Initially created: 2025-12-06T12:11:46.54+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command
Later learner of Tiāntái
The Shí clan, coming from Dàiběi, followed the King of Jìn as he rose in Tàiyuán;
then again, they gained control of the Central Plains by rising in Tàiyuán.
Tàiyuán governed Jìnyáng,
so the Qìdān then named it Jìn,
hence the state was named Jìn.
Gāozǔ Shèngwén Wǔmíng Déxiào Huángdì, the best of the best,
personal name Jìngtáng,
surname Shí.
His father, Nièlièjī,
originally came from among the barbarians.
From Zhūyé, he returned to the Táng,
and followed Zhūyé to live in Yīnshān.
As for his surname Shí,
the origin of its acquisition is unknown.
The Wǔdài Huìyào states: After Jìn obtained the empire,
it adopted Shí Què, Grand Master of Wèi, as its ancestor.
Tiānfú first year
(bǐngshēn, 936).
In the eleventh month of this year, the era name was changed, and he ascended the throne.
1 Spring,
first month.
Xú Zhīgào of Wú first established the Grand Marshal's Residence.
Wú appointed Xú Zhīgào as Grand Marshal,
see the autumn tenth month of the previous year in the preceding volume.
2 Dīngwèi,
the Táng lord enthroned his son Zhòngměi as King of Yōng.
3 Guǐchǒu,
the Táng lord held a banquet for the Qiānchūn Festival.
The Táng lord designated his birthday as the Qiānchūn Festival.
The Wǔdài Huìyào states: The emperor was born on the thirteenth day of the first month of Táng Guāngqǐ first year.
As the Jìn era name is used for dating,
the King of Lù is therefore referred to as the Táng lord.
He bid farewell and returned to Jìnyáng.
The emperor, drunk,
said:
"Why don't you stay a while?
Rushing back,
do you wish to rebel with Master Shí?!"
Shí Jìngtáng heard this
and grew more fearful.
4 Third month,
bǐngwǔ,
Mǎ Yìnsūn, Hanlin Academician and Vice Minister of Rites, was made Vice Minister of the Central Secretariat and Grand Councilor.
Yìnsūn was cautious and timid by nature.
Many matters in the Central Secretariat were delayed,
and he rarely received guests.
People at the time called him
"Three Shut-Offs,"
referring to his mouth, seal, and gate.
5 Shí Jìngtáng collected all his goods in Luòyáng and various circuits and returned to Jìnyáng,
claiming it was to aid military expenses.
Everyone knew he had ulterior motives.
At night, the Táng lord conversed casually with his close ministers, saying:
The Táng lord often conversed with his close ministers at night, see the previous year in the preceding volume.
Cóng,
pronounced qiānróng.
"Master Shí is a close relative of mine,
there is nothing suspicious about him;
but rumors persist,
and if by chance he becomes displeased,
how can I resolve it?"
No one replied.
Lǐ Sōng, Academician of the Duānmíng Hall and Attendant Censor, retired and said to his colleague Lǚ Qí:
Lǐ Sōng and Lǚ Qí were on duty together at the time.
"We have received profound kindness,
how can we be like common people,
indifferently waiting to see what happens?
What strategy should we adopt?"
Qí said:
"If Hédōng has a different scheme,
they will surely ally with the Qìdān for support.
The Qìdān empress, because Zànhuá is in China,
has repeatedly sought peace through marriage.
However, because their request for Cèlá, etc., has not been granted,
peace has not yet been achieved.
Zànhuá
was the eldest son of the Qìdān lord Ābǎojī.
His surrender is recorded in volume 277, Míngzōng's Chángxīng first year.
The request for Cèlá is recorded in the third year.
The Qìdān empress
refers to Empress Shùlǜ.
If we annually send them ceremonial gifts worth over a hundred thousand mín,
they will surely accept gladly.
If so,
even if Hédōng wishes to act audaciously,
they will be powerless."
Sōng said:
"This is also my intention.
However, money and grain all come from the Three Departments,
so we should discuss it further with Minister Zhāng."
So he informed Zhāng Yánlǎng.
Yánlǎng said:
"According to the Academician's plan,
not only can we control Hédōng,
but also save nine tenths of the border expenses.
Shí means ten, nine means nine.
If Your Majesty approves,
just entrust the matter to this old man,
and I will gather funds from outside the treasury to supply it."
Another evening,
the two secretly spoke to the emperor.
The emperor was greatly pleased,
praising their loyalty.
The two privately drafted a letter to the Qìdān to await his command.
After a long time,
the emperor informed Xuē Wényù, Academician of the Privy Council, of their plan.
Wényù replied:
"For the Son of Heaven,
to humble oneself and serve barbarians,
is that not a humiliation?
Furthermore,
if the barbarians follow precedent and seek to marry a princess,
how will you refuse them?"
From Emperor Tàizōng, the Táng granted imperial clan women as princesses to marry various foreign tribes,
which was called "harmonizing with the barbarians princesses."
Later, when the Uighurs rendered meritorious service to China,
even the emperor's daughters were given to them.
"Placing safety and danger on women."
The emperor's mind then changed.
Róng Yù
was a Táng person
and skilled in poetry.
Emperor Yuán of Hàn gave Wáng Zhāojūn in marriage to the Xiongnú.
Later generations pitied her
and competed to write songs and poems about her story.
He urgently summoned Sōng and Qí to the back building,
and in a great rage,
reprimanded them, saying:
"You all know ancient and modern affairs,
and wish to assist the ruler in achieving great peace;
yet now you devise such a plan!
My one daughter is still an infant,
do you wish to abandon her to the desert?
And you wish to send the funds for raising soldiers to the barbarian court!
Raising soldiers
means maintaining troops.
It means they want to cut the funds for maintaining troops to make peace with the barbarians.
The two were frightened,
sweat streaming down their backs,
and said:
"Our intention is to exhaust our foolishness to repay the country,
not to scheme for the barbarians.
We beg Your Majesty to discern this."
They bowed and thanked him countless times.
The emperor continued to rebuke them.
Lǚ Qí, exhausted,
paused his bowing slightly.
The emperor said:
"Lǚ Qí is stubborn,
does he still regard me as the ruler?!"
Qí said:
"Our plan was not good,
we ask Your Majesty to punish us,
what is the point of bowing more!"
The emperor's anger somewhat subsided,
he stopped their bowing,
and gave each a goblet of wine before dismissing them.
Bà,
meaning to make them leave for their residence.
Dīngsì,
Qí was made Imperial Censor-in-Chief,
which was to distance him.
Lǚ Qí's closeness to the Táng lord began in volume 277, Míngzōng's Chángxīng first year.
The Imperial Censor-in-Chief resided in the outer court
and was not allowed to serve inside the forbidden palace,
hence it is called distancing.
6 Xú Zhīgào of Wú appointed his son Jǐngtōng, Deputy Commander-in-Chief, as Grand Commandant and Deputy Marshal.
Sòng Qíqiū, Aide to the Commander-in-Chief, and Xú Jiè, Staff Officer, were made Left and Right Staff Officers of the Marshal's Residence.
7 Mǐn lord Chǎng changed the era name to Tōngwén,
and enthroned Consort Lǐ, née Lǐ Chūnyàn, as empress.
8 Mǎ Xī-gǎo, the Military Governor of Jìngjiāng and concurrently Grand Counselor, implemented good governance.
The supervising eunuch, Péi Rén-xù, slandered him to Chǔ Wáng Mǎ Xī-fàn,
saying that he was winning the hearts of the people.
Mǎ Xī-fàn grew suspicious.
In summer,
the fourth month,
the Hàn general Sūn Dé-wēi invaded Měng Zhōu and Guì Zhōu.
Měng Zhōu
was originally Lìpǔ County of Cāngwú Commandery under the Hàn dynasty.
The Suí dynasty separated Lìpǔ to establish Suíhuà County.
In the fourth year of Wǔdé of the Táng dynasty, it was changed to Lìshān [County].
Lì Zhōu was established in the county,
soon changed to Gōng Zhōu.
In the eighth year of Zhēnguàn, it was changed to Měng Zhōu.
To the east of the prefecture was Měng Shān,
and at the foot of the mountain was Měng Shuǐ.
Many people were surnamed Měng, hence the name.
In the fifth year of Xīníng of the Sòng dynasty, Měng Zhōu was abolished,
and Lìshān County was assigned to Zhāozhōu.
[Sūn Dé-wēi] personally led five thousand infantry and cavalry to Guì Zhōu.
Mǎ Xī-gǎo was afraid.
His mother, Lady Huá,
intercepted Mǎ Xī-fàn at Quányì Lǐng.
Quányì Lǐng was in Quányì County, Guì Zhōu,
which was also Shǐ'ān Lǐng.
"Xī-gǎo's administration has been inept,
causing bandits and invaders to enter the border,
troubling Your Highness to personally traverse dangerous terrain.
All of this is my fault.
I wish to have my fiefdom and stipend revoked,
and sweep the Yè Tíng,
to atone for Xī-gǎo's crime."
Mǎ Xī-fàn said,
"I have not seen Xī-gǎo for a long time.
I heard that his governance is particularly outstanding,
so I came to visit him.
There is no other reason."
The Hàn troops withdrew from Měng Zhōu.
Mǎ Xī-fàn transferred Mǎ Xī-gǎo to govern Láng Zhōu.
This laid the groundwork for Mǎ Xī-fàn to kill Mǎ Xī-gǎo.
9 Gāo Cóng-huì dispatched an envoy to present a memorial to Xú Zhī-gào,
urging him to ascend the imperial throne.
Gāo Cóng-huì, with his meager three prefectures situated between Táng, Wú, and Shǔ,
profited from their rewards and tributes,
paying homage to whomever he faced.
The various states called him
"Gāo Lài-zǐ" (Gāo the Scoundrel),
which was not without reason.
10 Initially,
Shí Jìng-táng wished to test the Táng ruler's intentions.
He repeatedly submitted memorials stating his frail health,
requesting to be relieved of military authority
and transferred to another circuit.
"Military authority"
refers to the post of Supreme Commander of the Northern Mounted and Infantry Armies.
He was to be transferred to Yùn Zhōu.
Fáng Gǎo, Lǐ Sōng, Lǚ Qí, and others all strongly advised against it,
believing it to be inappropriate.
The emperor hesitated for a long time.
In the fifth month,
on the night of Gēngyín,
Lǐ Sōng requested leave due to urgency and was out.
"Request leave due to urgency"
means to request leave.
The emperor discussed the affairs of Hédōng with [Wén] Yù.
[Wén] Yù said,
"There is a proverb: 'Building a house by the roadside
takes three years and is still unfinished.'
This matter must be decided by Your Sacred Will.
All your ministers consider their own interests;
how could they speak fully?
In my opinion,
Hédōng will rebel whether he is transferred
or not transferred,
it is only a matter of time.
It is better to plan for it in advance."
Before this,
diviners had said that the state this year would gain a worthy assistant,
who would produce extraordinary strategies,
and stabilize the realm.
The emperor believed Wén Yù was that person,
and upon hearing his words,
was greatly pleased,
saying,
"Your words truly enlighten my mind.
Success or failure, I will proceed with this."
He immediately prepared an appointment order,
and sent it to the Hanlin Academy to draft the imperial edict.
An appointment made personally by imperial decree without external consultation was called an 'appointment order' (chúmù);
one made after a prime minister's memorial and proposal was also called an 'appointment order.'
On Xīnmǎo,
Shí Jìng-táng was appointed Military Governor of Tiānpíng.
Sòng Shěn-qián, the Grand Commander of the Mounted Army and Military Governor of Héyáng, was appointed Military Governor of Hédōng.
Sòng Shěn-qián had followed the Táng ruler since his rise in Fèngxiáng,
thus he wanted to use him to replace Shí Jìng-táng.
When the two ranks heard Shí Jìng-táng's name being called out,
they looked at each other, paling.
"Two ranks"
refers to the civil and military officials.
On Jiǎwǔ,
Zhāng Jìng-dá, the Military Governor of Jiànxióng, was appointed Grand Commander of the Northwest Fān and Hàn Mounted and Infantry Armies,
urging Shí Jìng-táng to proceed to Yùn Zhōu.
Shí Jìng-táng grew suspicious and fearful,
and consulted his generals and aides, saying,
"When I came back to Hédōng,
the emperor personally promised that I would never be replaced.
The Táng ruler's words must have been at the beginning of his reign,
when Shí Jìng-táng entered court and was sent back to his post.
Is it not like what was said to the princess on this year's Qiānchūn Festival?
If I do not stir up trouble,
but the court instigates it,
how can I surrender and die on the roadside?
For now, I will submit a memorial claiming illness to observe their intentions.
If they are lenient with me,
I will serve them.
If they send troops against me,
I will make new plans."
Observing Shí Jìng-táng's words here,
his seeking aid from the Qìdān was a predetermined plan,
and Sāng Wéi-hàn's words merely coincided with his intention.
Shí Jìng-táng, considering his straightforwardness,
did not blame him.
The Judge of the Military Governor's headquarters, Zhào Yíng of Huáyīn, advised Shí Jìng-táng to go to Yùn Zhōu.
The Judge of the Surveillance Commissioner's headquarters, Xuē Róng of Píngyáo, said,
"I, Róng, am a scholar,
not accustomed to military matters."
The Chief Staff Officer, Liú Zhī-yuǎn, said,
"Lord, you have commanded troops for a long time
and have won the hearts of your soldiers.
Now you hold a strategically advantageous position,
and your soldiers and horses are strong and elite.
If you raise an army and issue a proclamation,
'raise'
means to start.
Why would you throw yourself into the tiger's mouth with a mere imperial decree?"
The Chief Secretary, Sāng Wéi-hàn of Luòyáng, said,
"When the emperor first ascended the throne,
and you, Lord, came to court,
did the emperor not know that a dragon should not be released into the deep abyss?
There is an ancient saying: 'A fish cannot be separated from the abyss.'
A divine dragon that loses its power
is no different from an earthworm.
This is Heaven's will granting you a potent weapon.
Míngzōng's benevolence remains in the hearts of the people,
but the present emperor, being of illegitimate descent, replaces him,
and the people's feelings are not attached.
You, Lord, are Míngzōng's beloved son-in-law,
and now the emperor treats you as a rebel.
This is not something that can be avoided by simply submitting to him.
You must strive to devise a plan for self-preservation.
The Qìdān
have always had a fraternal pact with Míngzōng.
Now their tribes are close by in Yún and Yìng.
The Qìdān royal tent had been encamped at Nàlā Pō since the third year of Chángxīng under Míngzōng.
Should an emergency arise,
they can be called in the morning and arrive in the evening.
What need to worry about not succeeding?"
Shí Jìng-táng's resolve was thus settled.
Before this,
the court, suspicious of Shí Jìng-táng,
appointed Yáng Yàn-xún, a General of the Yǔlín Guards, as Deputy Protector of Běijīng.
Báodǐng County was subordinate to Hézhōng Prefecture,
and was Fényīn County under the Hàn dynasty.
In the twenty-first year of Kāiyuán during Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng's reign, when sacrifices were made at Fényīn,
a precious cauldron was obtained,
and thus it was renamed.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: In the fourth year of Dàzhōng Xiángfú of the Sòng dynasty, Báodǐng was changed to Rónghé County,
located one hundred *lǐ* north of Hézhōng Prefecture.
[Yáng Yàn-xún] also informed him of the situation.
Yáng Yàn-xún asked,
"I don't know how much military provisions Hédōng has,
can it resist the imperial court?"
Those around [Shí Jìng-táng] requested to kill Yáng Yàn-xún.
Shí Jìng-táng said,
"Only the Deputy Envoy, I will protect him myself.
You all must not speak of this."
According to Xuē Shǐ, Yáng Yàn-xún was a calm and steady person,
which is likely how he survived.
On the *wùxū* day,
Huángfǔ Lì (皇甫立), Military Governor of Zhāoyì (昭義), reported that Shí Jìngtáng (石敬瑭) had rebelled.
The two prefectures of Bìng (幷) and Lù (潞) bordered each other,
so he knew of the matter and reported it first.
"The Emperor's adopted son
should not inherit the ancestral sacrifices.
I request that the throne be passed to Prince Xǔ (許王)."
Prince Xǔ was Cóngyì (從益),
Míngzōng's (明宗) son.
An imperial edict was issued in reply, saying:
"Your relationship with Prince È (鄂王) is certainly not distant.
The affair in Wèizhōu (衞州)
is known to all under Heaven;
it is said that Jìngtáng (敬瑭) killed all of Mǐndì's (閔帝) retainers,
leaving only the Emperor in Wèizhōu.
This event is found in the previous volume, Qīngtài (清泰) first year.
Prince È (鄂王) refers to Mǐndì (閔帝).
When Prince Lù (潞王) was enthroned,
by order of the Empress Dowager, Mǐndì (閔帝) was demoted to Prince È (鄂王).
Who would believe such a thing!"
On the *rénchén* day,
an imperial decree stripped Jìngtáng (敬瑭) of all his official titles and ranks.
On the *yǐsì* day,
Zhāng Jìngdá (張敬達) was concurrently made Inspector of the Four Sides of Tàiyuán (太原) and Commander of Formations;
Zhāng Yànqí (張彥琪), Military Governor of Héyáng (河陽), was made Grand Commander of Infantry and Cavalry;
Ān Shěnqí (安審琦), Military Governor of Ānguó (安國), was made Commander of Cavalry;
Xiānglǐ Jīn (相里金), Military Governor of Bǎoyì (保義), was made Commander of Infantry;
and Wǔ Tínghàn (武廷翰), Supreme General of the Right Gate Guard, was made Commander of Moats and Stockades.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
Zhāng Jìngdá (張敬達) was appointed Grand Commissioner for Military Affairs of the Four Sides of Tàiyuán (太原);
Yáng Guāngyuǎn (楊光遠), Military Governor of Yìwǔ (義武), was made his deputy.
This laid the groundwork for Yáng Guāngyuǎn (楊光遠) to kill Zhāng Jìngdá (張敬達) and surrender to the Jìn (晉).
On the *dīngwèi* day,
Zhāng Jìngdá (張敬達) was again appointed acting administrator of the Tàiyuán (太原) Branch Secretariat,
and Gāo Xíngzhōu (高行周), former Military Governor of Zhāngwǔ (彰武), was made Commissioner for Pacification and Formations of the Four Sides of Tàiyuán (太原).
After Guāngyuǎn (光遠) departed,
the Dìngzhōu (定州) army rioted,
and the *yájiàng* Qiānchéng Fāng Tài (千乘方太) pacified them.
The Hàn (漢) established the state of Qiānchéng (千乘).
Later it was renamed Lè'ān (樂安) Commandery.
The Suí (隋) abolished Lè'ān (樂安) Commandery and established Qiānchéng (千乘) County.
In the Táng (唐), it belonged to Qīngzhōu (青州).
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) states: Qiānchéng (千乘) County is eighty *lǐ* north of Qīngzhōu (青州).
*Chéng* (乘)
is pronounced *shéng zhèng* (繩證).
Zhāng Jìngdá (張敬達) led three thousand troops to camp in Jìn'ān (晉安) township.
Jìn'ān (晉安) township is south of Jìnyáng (晉陽) city.
The *Xuē Shǐ* (薛史) states: Jìn'ān (晉安) fort is south of Jìncí (晉祠).
On the *wùshēn* day,
Jìngdá (敬達) reported that Ān Shěnxìn (安審信), Commander of the Northwest Vanguard Cavalry, had rebelled and fled to Jìnyáng (晉陽).
Shěnxìn (審信) was
the nephew of Jīn Quán (金全).
Jìngtáng (敬瑭) had a long-standing relationship with him.
All the Ān (安) clan, including the followers of Shí Jìngtáng (石敬瑭), were originally from the Dàiběi (代北) region.
Ān Yuánxìn (安元信) of Mǎyì (馬邑), Commander of the Xióngyì (雄義),
led his unit of over six hundred men to garrison Dàizhōu (代州).
Zhāng Lǎng (張朗), the Prefect of Dàizhōu (代州), treated him well.
Yuánxìn (元信) secretly told Lǎng (朗):
"I observe that Lord Shí (石令公) is a superior man,
and his undertaking will surely succeed.
Why do you not secretly send someone to communicate your intentions,
so that you can preserve yourself?"
Lǎng (朗) did not agree,
which led to mutual suspicion.
Yuánxìn (元信) plotted to kill Lǎng (朗),
but failed.
He then led his troops to flee to Shěnxìn (審信).
Shěnxìn (審信) then led his several hundred cavalrymen and Yuánxìn (元信) to plunder Bǎijǐng (百井) and flee to Jìnyáng (晉陽).
Jìngtáng (敬瑭) asked Yuánxìn (元信):
"What advantage or disadvantage did you see
to abandon the strong and return to the weak?"
He replied:
"Yuánxìn (元信) does not know astrology or *qì* (氣);
I judge based on human affairs alone.
The most important thing for an emperor to govern the realm
is trustworthiness.
Now the present ruler has lost great trust with Lord Lìng (令公);
even those who are close and noble cannot preserve themselves.
Shí Jìngtáng (石敬瑭) is the Emperor's son-in-law,
which can be called close;
his office is Grand Councilor,
he holds a *jié* (節) and commands troops,
and he exclusively governs the northern frontier,
which can be called noble.
His downfall can be awaited by merely standing on tiptoe;
what strength does he have?"
Jìngtáng (敬瑭) was pleased
and entrusted him with military affairs.
Ān Chóngróng (安重榮), Northwest Inspector of Zhènnwǔ (振武), garrisoned Dàiběi (代北).
The *Ōu Shǐ* (歐史) states: Ān Chóngróng (安重榮) was Frontier Commander of Zhènnwǔ (振武).
*Shuài* (帥)
is read as *lǜ* (率);
likewise below.
He was from Shuòzhōu (朔州).
Sòng Shěnqián (宋審虔) was appointed Military Governor of Níngguó (寧國) and concurrently Grand Commander of the Palace Guard Cavalry.
Since Shí Jìngtáng (石敬瑭) did not accept his transfer,
Sòng Shěnqián (宋審虔) was therefore made to lead the *jié* (節) and oversee the palace guards.
Shěnqián (審虔) was a *yájiàng* (牙將) when the Táng (唐) ruler was stationed in Fèngxiáng (鳳翔).
Liú Yánhào (劉延皓), Military Governor of Tiānxióng (天雄), relying on the power of the Empress's clan,
became arrogant and indulgent.
Liú Yánhào (劉延皓) was the Táng (唐) ruler's Empress's brother.
He reduced the grants and rewards for his officers and soldiers
and indulged in excessive banquets.
Zhāng Lìngzhāo (張令昭), Patrol Commander of the Běngshèng (捧聖) Army, seized upon the soldiers' resentment and anger
and conspired to have Wèibó (魏博) respond to Hédōng (河東).
On the *guǐchǒu* day, before dawn,
he led his troops to attack the *yáchéng* (牙城)
and captured it.
Yánhào (延皓) escaped and fled,
and the mutinous soldiers plundered extensively.
Lìngzhāo (令昭) reported:
"Yánhào (延皓) failed in his management,
which led to military unrest.
I, to pacify the officers and soldiers,
temporarily lead the military government."
The *chén yǐ* (臣以)
of
*yǐ* (以)
should be
When Yánhào (延皓) reached Luòyáng (洛陽),
the Táng (唐) ruler was angry
and ordered him severely demoted.
The Empress interceded for him.
In the sixth month,
on the *gēngshēn* day,
it was merely ordered that Yánhào (延皓) be stripped of his official titles and ranks
and returned to his private residence.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Xú Jǐngqiān (徐景遷), Grand Preceptor of Wú (吳) and concurrently Grand Coordinator, was dismissed due to illness.
His brother Jǐngsuì (景遂) was appointed in his place as Vice Minister of the Chancellery and participant in government affairs.
On the *guǐhài* day,
the Táng (唐) ruler appointed Zhāng Lìngzhāo (張令昭) as General of the Right *Qiānniúwèi* (千牛衞) and acting administrator of the Tiānxióng (天雄) military government.
Lìngzhāo (令昭) accepted the new appointment
as the levies had not yet gathered.
Soon there was an edict to transfer him to Prefect of Qízhōu (齊州).
Lìngzhāo (令昭) excused himself by claiming he was retained by the soldiers,
but in reality, he was waiting to see the outcome in Hédōng (河東).
The Táng (唐) ruler sent an envoy to instruct him,
but Lìngzhāo (令昭) killed the envoy.
On the *jiǎxū* day,

Fàn Yánguāng (范延光), Military Governor of Xuānwǔ (宣武) and concurrently Grand Councilor, was made Grand Commander of Campaigns for the Four Sides of Tiānxióng (天雄) and acting administrator of the Wèibó (魏博) Branch Secretariat.
*Wèibó* (魏博)
should probably be
*Wèizhōu* (魏州).
Yáng Guāngyuǎn (楊光遠) was made his deputy.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Lǐ Zhōu (李周), Resident Administrator of Xījīng (西京), was made Deputy Grand Commander of Campaigns for the Four Sides of Tiānxióng (天雄) Army.
When Shí Jìngtáng's (石敬瑭) sons, Shí Chóngyīn (石重殷), Supreme General of the Right Guard, and Shí Chóngyì (石重裔), Deputy Palace City Commissioner, heard that Jìngtáng (敬瑭) had raised an army,
they hid in a civilian well.
His younger brother, Shí Jìngdé (石敬德), Commander of Yízhōu (沂州), killed his wife and daughter and fled.
He was later captured
and died in prison.
His cousin, Shí Jìngwēi (石敬威), Commander of Zhāngshèng (彰聖), committed suicide.
In autumn,
seventh month,
on the *wùzǐ* day,
Chóngyīn (重殷) and Chóngyì (重裔) were captured
and executed,
along with the families who had hidden them.
On the *gēngyín* day,
Chǔwáng Xīfàn (楚王希範) returned north from Guìzhōu (桂州).
He reached Guìzhōu (桂州) in the fourth month and
only returned in the seventh month.
*Huán* (還)
is pronounced *cóng xuān* (從宣),
also as it is.
Sāng Qiān (桑遷), Commander of the Yúnzhōu (雲州) Infantry, reported that Yǐn Huī (尹暉), Military Governor of Yìngzhōu (應州), had expelled Shā Yànxún (沙彥珣), Military Governor of Yúnzhōu (雲州),
and seized his troops to support Hédōng (河東).
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
Yànxún (彥珣) memorialized that Qiān (遷) was plotting rebellion in support of Hédōng (河東),
and led troops to besiege the inner city.
Yànxún (彥珣) broke through the siege and fled to Xīshān (西山),
occupying Léigōngkǒu (雷公口).
The next day,
he rallied his troops, entered the city, and attacked the mutinous soldiers.
Qiān (遷) was defeated and fled,
and the military city was again secure.
On the same day,
Yǐn Huī (尹暉) captured Qiān (遷) and sent him to Luòyáng (洛陽),
where he was executed.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
Fàn Yánguāng (范延光) captured Wèizhōu (魏州)
and executed Zhāng Lìngzhāo (張令昭).
An imperial edict ordered the execution of all his partisans in the seven divisions.
Zhāng Jìngdá (張敬達) dispatched the Zhāngshèng (彰聖) Army from Huáizhōu (懷州) to garrison Hǔběikǒu (虎北口).
Hǔběikǒu (虎北口) is north of the Fénshuǐ (汾水) River.
The Zhāngshèng (彰聖) Army was originally a garrison guard unit from Luòchéng (洛城).
Earlier, it was divided and stationed in Huáizhōu (懷州).
Then, from Huáizhōu (懷州), it was dispatched to Zhāng Jìngdá's (張敬達) army front.
Jìngdá (敬達) again dispatched it to garrison Hǔběikǒu (虎北口).
On the *bǐngchén* day,
an imperial edict ordered the complete extermination of their families.
19 Shí Jìngtáng (石敬瑭) sent secret envoys to seek aid from the Qìdān (契丹),
ordering Sāng Wéihàn (桑維翰) to draft a memorial declaring vassalage to the Qìdān (契丹) ruler,
and further requesting to serve him with the rites due to a father.
It was agreed that on the day of victory,
Lúlóng (盧龍) Circuit and all prefectures north of Yànmén Guān (鴈門關) would be ceded to him.
Liú Zhīyuǎn (劉知遠) advised,
“Declaring vassalage is acceptable,
but serving him as a father is excessive.
Lavishly bribing him with gold and silk
will be sufficient to bring his troops,
there is no need to promise him territory.
I fear this will become a great calamity for Zhōngguó (中國) in the future,
and by then it will be too late to regret.”
Jìngtáng (敬瑭) did not heed him.
Later, things turned out exactly as Liú Zhīyuǎn (劉知遠) had said.
This laid the groundwork for the Qìdān (契丹) entry into Zhōngguó (中國).
The Qìdān (契丹) ruler was overjoyed,
pleased that Zhōngguó (中國) had a weakness to exploit.
“My son recently dreamed that Shí Láng (石郎) sent an envoy,”
his mother was Empress Dàhòu Shùlǜ (述律太后).
“Bǐ (比)
(read as ‘pí zhì’),
means ‘recently’.
This is Heaven's will.”
From then on,
Liáo (遼) destroyed Jìn (晉),
Jīn (金) broke Sòng (宋),
(Sixteen characters missing in original text.)
The present borders,
extending west beyond Yì (益) and Níng (寧),
south to Jiāo (交) and Guǎng (廣),
and even overseas,
were all opened by Shí Jìngtáng (石敬瑭) by surrendering passes and barriers.
Was this truly Heaven's will?
He promised to mobilize his entire nation to provide aid in mid-autumn.
He would advance after the autumn was high and the horses were fat.
20 In the eighth month,
on the day Jǐwèi (己未),
Fàn Yán’guāng (范延光) was appointed Military Commissioner of Tiānxíong (天雄),
and Lǐ Zhōu (李周) was appointed Military Commissioner of Xuānwǔ (宣武) and Concurrently Grand Chancellor.
21 On the day Guǐhài (癸亥),
Yìngzhōu (應州) reported that three thousand Qìdān (契丹) cavalry attacked the city.
22 Zhāng Jìngdá (張敬達) built a long circumvallation to besiege Jìnyáng (晉陽).
Shí Jìngtáng (石敬瑭) appointed Liú Zhīyuǎn (劉知遠) as Commander-in-Chief of Cavalry and Infantry,
and the surrendered troops of Ān Chóngróng (安重榮) and Zhāng Wàndí (張萬迪) were all placed under his command.
Zhīyuǎn (知遠) enforced the law impartially,
treating everyone equally,
and thus no one harbored disloyal thoughts.
Jìngtáng (敬瑭) personally stood on the city wall,
sitting and sleeping under arrows and stones.
Zhīyuǎn (知遠) said,
“Observing Jìngdá (敬達) and his like with their high ramparts and deep moats,
they intend to wage a protracted war,
with no other unusual strategies,
so they are not worth worrying about.
I wish that Your Excellency would send out secret envoys in all directions
to manage external affairs.
Defending the city is very easy,
and I, Zhīyuǎn (知遠), can handle it alone.”
Jìngtáng (敬瑭) clasped Zhīyuǎn's (知遠) hand,
patted his back, and rewarded him.
23 On the day Wùyín (戊寅),
Dǒng Wēnqí (董溫琪), Military Commissioner of Chéngdé (成德), was appointed Deputy Commander of the Northeast Frontier Pacification Army,
to assist Zhào Déjūn (趙德鈞), Military Commissioner of Lúlóng (盧龍).
24 The Táng (唐) ruler sent Lǚ Qí (呂琦), Scholar of the Duānmíng Diàn (端明殿), to the Hédōng (河東) field headquarters to comfort the troops.
Yáng Guāngyuǎn (楊光遠) said to Qí (琦),
“I wish to report to His Majesty that
he may rest easy.
If the rebels have no reinforcements,
they will be subdued day and night;
if they draw in the Qìdān (契丹),
we should allow them to enter,
and defeat them in a single battle.”
Yáng Guāngyuǎn's (楊光遠) plan,
emboldened by Wáng Yànqiú's (王晏球) victory at Dìngzhōu (定州),
intended to let them enter and then fight them,
but he entirely failed to realize that victory in battle is not constant,
and passes and barriers must not be left unguarded.
Soon after, the Qìdān (契丹) entered directly,
the Táng (唐) army was defeated in one battle,
and subsequently found itself besieged.
The Emperor heard that the Qìdān (契丹) had promised Shí Jìngtáng (石敬瑭) aid in mid-autumn,
and repeatedly urged Zhāng Jìngdá (張敬達) to intensify his attack on Jìnyáng (晉陽),
but it could not be taken.
Whenever fortifications were built,
they were often met with wind and rain,
and the long circumvallation was again damaged by floods,
so it could not be completed.
Inside Jìnyáng (晉陽) city, the situation grew dire daily,
and food supplies gradually ran low.
If the Qìdān (契丹) reinforcements did not arrive,
Jìn (晉) would not be able to hold out.
25 In the ninth month,
the Qìdān (契丹) ruler, leading fifty thousand cavalry,
claiming three hundred thousand,
advanced south from Yángwǔ Gǔ (揚武谷).
Yángwǔ Gǔ (揚武谷) is in Guō Xiàn (崞縣) of Dàizhōu (代州).
Xuē Shǐ (薛史) states: Yángwǔ Gǔ (陽武谷) is south of Shuòzhōu (朔州).
Kǎoyì (考異) states: Dàizhōu (代州) now has Yángwǔ Zhài (楊武寨),
and to its north are Chángchéng Lǐng (長城嶺) and Shèngfó Gǔ (聖佛谷).
We now follow Hàn Gāozǔ Shílù (漢高祖實錄) to write
"Yángwǔ (揚武)".
Zhāng Lǎng (張朗), Administrator of Dàizhōu (代州), and Dīng Shěnqí (丁審琦), Administrator of Xīnzhōu (忻州), fortified their cities and defended themselves,
Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: Dàizhōu (代州) is 160 lǐ (里) south to Xīnzhōu (忻州);
Xīnzhōu (忻州) is 140 lǐ (里) south to Tàiyuán (太原).
and did not succumb to inducements or threats.
Shěnqí (審琦)
was from Míngzhōu (洺州).
On the day Xīnchǒu (辛丑),
the Qìdān (契丹) ruler arrived at Jìnyáng (晉陽)
and arrayed his forces at Hǔběikǒu (虎北口) north of the Fén (汾) River.
He first sent someone to Shí Jìngtáng (石敬瑭), saying,
“I wish to defeat the enemy today, may I?”
Jìngtáng (敬瑭) sent a rider to quickly report,
“The southern army is very strong,
one must not be rash.”
The Táng (唐) army came from the south to attack Jìnyáng (晉陽),
hence it was called the southern army.
Before the envoy arrived,
the Qìdān (契丹) had already engaged the Táng (唐) cavalry generals Gāo Xíngzhōu (高行周) and Fú Yànqīng (符彥卿) in battle.
Jìngtáng (敬瑭) then sent Liú Zhīyuǎn (劉知遠) with troops to assist them.
Zhāng Jìngdá (張敬達), Yáng Guāngyuǎn (楊光遠), and Ān Shěnqí (安審琦) arrayed their infantry at the foot of the mountain northwest of the city.
The Qìdān (契丹) sent three thousand light cavalry,
unarmored,
to directly assault their formation.
The Táng (唐) soldiers, seeing their weakness,
eagerly pursued them
to the bend of the Fén (汾) River,
where the Qìdān (契丹) crossed the water and departed.
The Táng (唐) soldiers advanced along the bank,
when Qìdān (契丹) ambush troops rose from the northeast,
charging the Táng (唐) army and splitting it in two.
Many of the infantry in the north were killed by the Qìdān (契丹),
while the cavalry in the south retreated to Jìn'ān Zhài (晉安寨).
The Qìdān (契丹) unleashed their troops to press the attack,
and the Táng (唐) army suffered a great defeat.
Nearly ten thousand infantry died,
only the cavalry remained intact.
Jìngdá (敬達) and others gathered the remaining troops and secured Jìn'ān (晉安).
The Qìdān (契丹) also withdrew their troops to Hǔběikǒu (虎北口).
Jìngtáng (敬瑭) obtained over a thousand surrendered Táng (唐) soldiers,
and Liú Zhīyuǎn (劉知遠) advised Jìngtáng (敬瑭) to kill them all.
Although the Táng (唐) army was defeated,
their forces were still strong,
and Liú Zhīyuǎn (劉知遠) feared that the surrendered soldiers would rebel and return.
Therefore, he advised killing them.
That evening,
Jìngtáng (敬瑭) exited the north gate,
meaning the north gate of Jìnyáng (晉陽) city.
The Qìdān (契丹) ruler clasped Jìngtáng's (敬瑭) hand,
regretting that they had met so late.
This was because they had not met before,
but also because Shí Jìngtáng's (石敬瑭) demeanor must have been impressive to him.
“Your Majesty has traveled a long distance,
your soldiers and horses are weary,
yet you immediately fought the Táng (唐) and won a great victory,
why is this so?”
The Qìdān (契丹) ruler said,
“When I first came from the north,
I thought Táng (唐) would surely block Yànmén (鴈門) and other routes,
ambushing us in dangerous defiles,
in which case I would not have been able to advance.
If Zhāng Jìngdá (張敬達) and others had indeed known to do this,
how could there be the predicament at Jìn'ān (晉安)?
But they did none of this,
so I drove deep directly,
knowing that the great undertaking would surely succeed.
Once the armies engaged,
my morale was high,
while theirs was low.
If I did not seize this moment to attack swiftly,
meaning to strike while our initial momentum was sharp.
then the outcome of victory or defeat would be unknown.
This is why I fought and won quickly,
it cannot be explained by the usual theories of exhaustion and freshness.”
Jìngtáng (敬瑭) greatly admired and was convinced by this.
On the day Rén-yín,
Shí Jìngtáng led his troops to join the Qìdān in besieging Jìn'ān Village.
They set up camp to the south of Jìn'ān,
stretching for over a hundred *lǐ*,
and fifty *lǐ* thick,
with many bells, ropes, and barking dogs set up,
so that not a single step could pass.
Zhāng Jìngdá's troops still numbered fifty thousand men,
and ten thousand horses,
looking around with nowhere to go.
The art of war states: "Place them in deadly ground, and they will live."
If Zhāng Jìngdá and others could have, before the encirclement fully closed,
encouraged and exhorted their officers and soldiers,
and fought with all their might to the death,
victory or defeat would have been unknown.
On the day Jiǎ-chén,
Zhāng Jìngdá sent an envoy to report the defeat to the Táng,
and from then on, communication ceased.
The Táng ruler was greatly alarmed,
and dispatched Fú Yànráo, Commander of the Zhāngshèng Directorate, to lead infantry and cavalry from Luòyáng to garrison Héyáng.
He issued an edict to Fàn Yánguāng, Jìedùshǐ of Tiānxíong and concurrently Minister of the Central Secretariat, to lead twenty thousand Wèizhōu troops via Qīngshān to Qū Yúcì.
Qīngshān
is the Qīngshān Pass in Xíngzhōu.
Qū
is pronounced Qī Yù.
He wanted them to emerge behind the Qìdān army,
and have Zhào Déjūn come out from Fēihú Pass to Dàizhōu,
to cut off the Qìdān's rear.
"Jiū"
is
the same as
"Jiū."
The Shuōwén says: "Three ropes combined make a *jiū*."
Therefore, any assembly of soldiers is called *jiūhé* or *jiūjí*.
"Western garrisons"
refers to the garrisons of Pú, Tóng and other western circuits.
All were to rescue Jìn'ān Village.
The Qìdān ruler moved his camp to Liǔlín;
Liǔlín should be south of Jìn'ān Village.
No Táng troops were seen.
On the day Dīng-wèi,
the Táng ruler issued an edict announcing his personal expedition.
Yōng Wáng Chóngměi said:
"Your Majesty's eye illness has not yet subsided,
and it is not advisable to travel far through wind and sand;
although I am young,
I wish to go north on Your Majesty's behalf."
The Emperor had no intention of going,
and upon hearing this,
was quite pleased.
Zhāng Yánlǎng, Liú Yánhào, and Liú Yánlǎng, Director of the Southern Bureau of the Xuanhui Directorate, all urged the Emperor to go.
The Emperor had no choice.
On the day Wù-shēn,
he departed Luòyáng,
saying to Lú Wénjì:
"I have long heard that you possess the qualities of a prime minister,
which is why I disregarded all opposition and first appointed you.
Now that disaster is upon us like this,
where are all your excellent strategies?"
Lú Wénjì merely bowed and expressed gratitude,
unable to reply.
On the day Jǐ-yǒu,
he dispatched Liú Yánlǎng to supervise Fú Yànráo, Commander of the Imperial Guard Infantry, to lead his army to Lùzhōu,
as a reserve force for the main army.
"Main army"
refers to the army at Jìn'ān Village.
"Jiān"
is pronounced Gǔ Xián.
"Tuīdài"
(support and enthrone) is mentioned in the previous volume, Qīngtài first year.
Fú Yànráo feared that they might cause trouble,
and dared not restrain them by law.
When the Emperor arrived at Héyáng,
his heart recoiled from traveling north.
He summoned the prime ministers and privy councilors to discuss strategies for advance.
Lú Wénjì, catering to the Emperor's wishes,
said:
"The foundation of the state,
more than half of it, lies in Hénán.
The Hu soldiers come and go swiftly,
and cannot stay long;
the great camp at Jìn'ān is very secure,
moreover, three routes of troops have already been dispatched to rescue it."
This refers to the armies of the three commanders: Fàn Yánguāng, Zhào Déjūn, and Pān Huán.
If the northern army were to attack Luòyáng,
they would have to cross the river from Héyáng,
hence this statement.
"Let us send a close minister to supervise the battle;
if the siege cannot be lifted,
it will not be too late to advance then."
Zhāng Yánlǎng wished to use this opportunity to allow Zhào Yánshòu to be relieved of his privy council duties.
Zhào Yánshòu was then a privy councilor,
and wished to be relieved but could not.
"What Lú Wénjì says is correct."
The Emperor asked others,
but no one dared to offer a differing opinion.
Liú Suìníng, Governor of Zézhōu,
was the son of Liú Xún.
He secretly communicated with Shí Jìngtáng.
In the early Yuánshùn era,
Liú Suìyōng, who resisted Wáng Sītóng in Cháng'ān and welcomed the Prince of Lù,
was also a son of Liú Xún;
these brothers repeatedly changed allegiance with the times to seek wealth and position,
like seizing gold in broad daylight,
seeing only the gold and not the people.
The Emperor discussed which close minister could be sent north.
Zhāng Yánlǎng and Hé Níng of Xūchāng, a Hanlin scholar, etc.,
Xūchāng
is the Xūchéng County under Yùnzhōu in the Jiǔyù Zhì.
This is because the Later Táng avoided the taboo name of Lǐ Guóchāng,
changing Xūchāng to Xūchéng,
but Ōu Yángxiū's history and the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn still use the old county name without change.
"Zhào Yánshòu's father, Déjūn, is coming with Lúlóng troops to respond to the crisis;
it is fitting to send Yánshòu to meet him."
On the day Gēng-xū,
he dispatched Zhào Yánshòu, Privy Councilor, Jìedùshǐ of Zhōngwǔ, General Commander of Imperial Escort Armies, and concurrently Chancellor, to lead twenty thousand troops to Lùzhōu.
On the day Xīn-hài,
the Emperor went to Huáizhōu.
He appointed Kāng Sīlì, Commander of the Right Divine Martial Army, as Commander of the Cavalry in the Northern Expeditionary Army,
to lead the accompanying cavalry to Tuánbǎi Valley.
Kāng Sīlì
was a Hú person from Jìnyáng.
The Emperor was worried about Jìn'ān,
and asked for strategies from his close officials.
Lóng Mǐn of Yǒngqīng, an Assistant Minister of Personnel, requested that Lǐ Zànhuá be enthroned as the Qìdān ruler.
In the first year of Rúyì of Táng, Wǔlóng County was established by dividing Āncì County.
In the first year of Jǐngyún, it was renamed Huìchāng.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo, it was renamed Yǒngqīng,
and belonged to Yōuzhōu.
The Xiōngnú should know: Yǒngqīng County is one hundred seventy *lǐ* southeast of Yōuzhōu.
Shùn appointed Lóng as a Nàyán,
and his descendants took his name as their surname,
or some believed they were descendants of the Huànlóng family.
Xiàng Yǔ had a general named Lóng Jū,
and the Hàn had Lóng Bógāo.
Lǐ Zànhuá
was the Qìdān ruler's brother;
he surrendered in the first year of Chángxīng of Míngzōng,
and was granted a new name.
He was in Luòyáng at the time.
He wanted Fàn Yánguāng and Zhào Déjūn to divide their forces to escort him.
If the court openly declared this in a proclamation,
the Qìdān ruler would surely have internal worries.
"Open proclamation"
means to make it known to the Qìdān.
Considering the later words of Qìdān Empress Dowager Shùlǜ reproaching Zhào Déjūn,
Lóng Mǐn's strategy was feasible,
but the Táng ruler regretfully did not adopt it.
This was also a strategy to lift the siege.
The Emperor greatly agreed with it,
but the high officials feared it would not succeed,
so the discussion was not resolved.
The Emperor's worry and dejection showed in his expression.
He only drank heavily and sang sorrowfully day and night.
Some close officials advised him to go north,
to which he would say:
"Gentlemen, say no more;
Master Shí has made my heart and guts fall to the ground!"
When Lǐ Sìyuán raised an army against Luòyáng, Emperor Zhuāngzōng was disheartened;
when Shí Jìngtáng rebelled with his army,
the Prince of Lù said he felt his heart and guts fall to the ground.
Why were they so brave when facing the enemy in peacetime,
but suddenly so timid and fearful?
This is because Emperor Zhuāngzōng and Emperor Míngzōng,
and the Prince of Lù and Emperor Jìnzǔ,
all engaged in military affairs.
Internally measuring their wisdom and strength,
they were not greatly superior to each other.
But when they seized an opportune moment and wielded power, it sometimes happened that they were not on par with each other,
and so their spirit was disheartened first.
In the winter of the 26th year,
tenth month,
on the day Rén-xū,
an edict was issued to widely conscript horses from officials, officers, and the common people throughout the realm;
also, people were conscripted as soldiers,
with one able-bodied man taken from every seven households.
The Kǎoyì states: "Xue's History says ten households."
Now following the Veritable Records of the Deposed Emperor.
They were called
"Righteous Army,"
and were expected to assemble by the eleventh month.
Láng Wànjīn, Governor of Chénzhōu, was ordered to teach them battle formations.
Láng Wànjīn
was a brave general of that time.
A total of over two thousand horses
and five thousand conscripted men were obtained,
which were of no real benefit,
but caused great unrest among the populace.
27 Previously,

Kào (犒) is pronounced kǔdào.
He procrastinated and did not advance,

31 Liú Jǐngyán (劉景巖), the former Cìshǐ (刺史) of Fāngzhōu (坊州),

Yáng Hànzhāng (楊漢章), the Zhāngwǔ Jiédùshǐ (彰武節度使), governed poorly,
losing the hearts of both "barbarians" and "Chinese."

The crowd,

32 The Qìdān (契丹) ruler said to Shí Jìngtáng (石敬瑭):

Rúzhōu (儒州) administered one county, Jìnshān (晉山).

I believe that for the prefectures north of Yànmén (鴈門),

Since Liú Shǒuguāng's (劉守光) usurpation

When Jìnyáng (晉陽) was under siege,

The Princess Zhǎng Gōngzhǔ (長公主) of the Jìn (晉) state was established as Empress.
Although the Qìdān (契丹) lord’s army was at Liǔlín (柳林),

Every evening, they would pack up

He was only a hundred *lǐ* (里) from Jìn’ān (晉安),

Déjūn repeatedly submitted memorials requesting the military governorship of Chéngdé (成德) for Yánshòu (延壽),

This meant that if Yánshòu were in Chángshān (常山),

Déjūn did not stop requesting,

The Zhànguócè (戰國策) says: Hánzǐlú (韓子盧) was the finest hound in the world,

Lú (盧) chased the *Jiaotu* (狡兔),
circled the mountains three times,
and leaped over mountains five times.
The rabbit died in front,
and the dog collapsed behind.
A farmer saw them and acquired both.
(The Táng lord) was displeased.
In the intercalary month,
Zhào Yánshòu (趙延壽) presented the imperial edict, armor, horses, bows, and swords bestowed by the Qìdān (契丹) lord.
He falsely claimed that Déjūn (德鈞) had sent an envoy with a letter to the Qìdān lord,
establishing good relations with the Táng,
and persuading him to withdraw his troops to his own country.
In reality, it was a separate secret letter,
heavily bribing the Qìdān lord with gold and silk,
saying:
“If I am established as emperor,

“Existing troops”
refers to the troops currently commanded by his father and son.
“見” (xiàn),
pronounced as *xián* (賢) and *biàn* (遍).
“And I will also promise that the Shí (石) clan will forever control Hédōng (河東).”
The Qìdān lord, realizing he was deep within enemy territory,

Déjūn’s (德鈞) army still strong,
Fàn Yánguāng (范延光) to his east,
and also fearing that the various prefectures north of the mountains might block his return route—
the various prefectures north of the mountains
refer to the prefectures of Yún (雲), Yìng (應), Huán (寰), Shuò (朔), etc.—
The Emperor heard of this

He immediately sent Sāng Wéihàn (桑維翰) to see the Qìdān lord,

Zhào Běipíng (趙北平) and his son are disloyal and untrustworthy.”
Zhào Déjūn (趙德鈞) was enfeoffed as King Běipíng (北平),

This means they are disloyal to Táng and untrustworthy to Qìdān.
“Moreover, they have long harbored rebellious intentions,
holding back their troops and observing developments.
They are not people who would die for their country.
Why should they be feared,
and why should you trust their deceitful and boastful words,
coveting a trivial profit?”
The tip of an autumn hair,
meaning extremely minute.
“Furthermore, if Jìn (晉) gains the empire,

The Qìdān lord said:

(Sāng Wéihàn) replied:

The Qìdān lord said:
“I have not violated the former agreement.”
means “to change.”

refers to allowing the Jìn emperor to rule Zhōngguó.
(Sāng Wéihàn) replied:
“Your Majesty, with integrity and righteousness, comes to the aid of those in distress.

The Zuǒzhuàn (左傳) says: Lord Jìn (晉) sent Hán Chuān (韓穿) to say that the fields of Wènyáng (汶陽) would be returned to Qí (齊).
Jì Wénzǐ (季文子) said:
“Within a year,
sometimes given, sometimes taken away,

“Your servant secretly believes Your Majesty should not do this.”
He knelt before the tent,
from dawn till dusk,
weeping and arguing.

Pointing to a stone in front of the tent, he said to Déjūn’s (德鈞) envoy:

When this stone rots,

“將” (jiàng),

Xiáng,
