Guāngyuǎn seized the opportunity when they were unprepared,
cut off Jìngdá's head,
and led the generals to submit a memorial surrendering to the Qìdān.
The Qìdān ruler had long heard of the generals' reputations,
and he consoled and rewarded all of them,
giving them furs and hats.
Then he joked with them, saying:
"You lot are also big villains!"
Northerners called southerners "Hàn."
"Big villains"
is like how people today call those who are fierce and violent "unpopular."
Wáng Zhāoyuǎn's so-called
"evil little boy"
also means this.
Guāngyuǎn and the others were greatly ashamed.
The Qìdān ruler praised Zhāng Jìngdá's loyalty,
ordered him to be buried and sacrificed to,
and said to his subordinates and the Jìn generals:
"As subjects, you
should emulate Jìngdá."
At that time, there were still nearly five thousand horses in Jìn'ān Zhài,
and fifty thousand sets of armor and weapons.
The Qìdān took all of them back to their country.
They handed all the Táng officers and soldiers to the emperor,
saying to them:
"Diligently serve your lord!"
Kāng Sīlì, Grand Commander of the Horse Army, died of indignation and sorrow.
The emperor, seeing that Jìn'ān had surrendered,
sent envoys to instruct the various prefectures.
Zhāng Lǎng, Prefect of Dàizhōu, beheaded the envoy.
Lǚ Qí, bearing the Táng ruler's edict, comforted the northern army.
"Northern army"
refers to the garrisons in the prefectures north of Yànmén that held firm.
He encountered a Jìn envoy
and also beheaded him.
He said to Prefect Dīng Shěnqí:
"The barbarians passed below the city walls without a glance.
Their intentions are clear.
When they return, there will surely be no chance of survival.
It would be better to lead the soldiers and people early from Wǔtái to Zhènzhōu."
From Wǔtái County southeast to Zhènzhōu is three hundred sixty lǐ,
taking the Fēihú Road.
Shuài,
read as shuài;
same below.
Shěn Qí regretted it,
and closed the inner city gate, refusing to comply.
The provincial troops wanted to attack him.
Qí said:
"With the country in such a state,
why should we further slaughter each other!"
So he led the provincial troops toward Zhènzhōu.
"Provincial troops"
means Xīnzhōu troops.
Qù,
read as qī yù.
36 The Qìdān ruler said to the emperor:
"Sāng Wéihàn has been loyal to you.
You should make him prime minister."
On the day of Bǐngyín,
Zhào Yíng was appointed Vice Director of the Department of the Palace Affairs,
and Sāng Wéihàn was appointed Vice Director of the Department of the Central Secretariat,
both concurrently as Grand Councilors.
Wéihàn also concurrently held the authority of Commissioner of Military Affairs.
Yáng Guāngyuǎn was appointed Grand Commander of the Palace Army (Horse and Foot).
Yáng Guāngyuǎn killed Zhāng Jìngdá and surrendered Jìn'ān Zhài,
hence he was promoted and employed.
37 The emperor and the Qìdān ruler were about to lead their armies south.
The emperor wished to leave one son to guard Hédōng,
and consulted the Qìdān ruler.
Deliberating matters is called "cī."
Today, northerners use "cī" to mean serious.
When the traveling bureaus and provinces send documents to the inner bureaus and provinces,
they generally call it "cī."
The emperor chose him himself.
The emperor's nephew Chóngguì,
whose father Jìngrú had died young,
was adopted by the emperor as his son.
He resembled the emperor but was short and small.
The Qìdān ruler pointed to him and said:
"This one with the big eyes is suitable."
So Chóngguì was appointed Resident Grandee of Běijīng.
The Qìdān ruler knew Chóngguì was capable.
Later, Jǐng Yán'guǎng indeed enthroned him.
However, "capable" here
means he was capable among the emperor's sons.
The Qìdān ruler had already observed him.
Appointing a Resident Grandee as Yǐn or commander
followed the old Táng system.
They advanced together with the surrendered soldiers.
"Surrendered soldiers"
refers to the Táng Jìn'ān Zhài troops.
On the day of Dīngmǎo,
they reached Tuánbǎi
and fought with the Táng army.
Zhào Déjūn and Zhào Yánshòu fled first.
Fú Yànráo, Zhāng Yànqí, Liú Yánlǎng, and Liú Zàimíng followed.
The soldiers were routed,
and tens of thousands died from trampling each other.
On the day of Jǐsì,
Yánlǎng and Zàimíng reached Huáizhōu.
The Táng ruler first learned that the emperor had ascended the throne and Yáng Guāngyuǎn had surrendered.
Public opinion was that
"the Tiānxíong Army Headquarters is still intact.
The Qìdān will surely be wary of Shāndōng
and will not dare to advance south."
The Tiānxíong Army was east of the Tàiháng Mountains.
The Táng ruler believed Lǐ Sōng had always been on good terms with Fàn Yánguāng.
At that time, Fàn Yánguāng was garrisoned in Wèizhōu.
Xuē Wényù, unaware, arrived immediately after.
Lǐ Sōng and Xuē Wényù were both on duty.
Wényù did not know Sōng was summoned alone,
thinking both were summoned,
so he arrived after Sōng.
His expression changed.
Sōng stomped on Wényù's foot,
and Wényù then left.
The Táng ruler said:
"When I saw that fellow, my flesh trembled.
I almost drew my sword to stab him."
Sōng said:
"Wényù is a petty man.
His shallow counsel has ruined the country.
Stabbing him would only make things uglier."
The Táng ruler had favored Xuē Wényù at the beginning of the uprising,
and upon ascending the throne,
he allowed him to participate in deliberations,
thwarting Lǐ Sōng's plan to make peace with the Qìdān,
and also supporting the Táng ruler's relocation of his garrison to Tiānpíng.
All of this was done by Wényù.
Now that things had failed, the blame was placed on him.
The Táng ruler agreed.
Luòyáng heard that the Northern Army had been defeated.
The Northern Army
refers to the troops of Zhào Déjūn and Fú Yànráo, etc., encamped at Tuánbǎi.
The residents poured out,
fleeing and hiding in the mountains and valleys.
The gatekeepers requested to forbid them.
The gatekeepers
were those guarding the gates of Luòchéng.
"The state is in great difficulty,
and cannot yet act as master for the people.
To forbid them from seeking survival
would only increase our bad reputation;
it is better to let them follow their own inclinations.
When peace is restored, they will return on their own."
So, an order was issued to allow them to go wherever they wished,
and the morale of the people was somewhat stabilized.
On Rénshēn,
the Táng ruler returned to Héyáng.
He ordered his generals to divide and guard the South and North cities.
Héyáng had three cities: South, North, and Middle Tān.
Guarding the South and North cities was for the purpose of defending the Héqiáo.
(He thought) this would allow him to connect his influence with Wèibó,
but the Táng ruler could not decide.
Zhào Déjūn and Zhào Yánshòu fled south to Lùzhōu.
The defeated Táng soldiers gradually followed them.
Their general Shí Sài led the light cavalry from Lúlóng eastward back to Yúyáng.
The Emperor had first sent Gāo Xíngzhōu, the Jìedùshǐ of Zhāoyì, back to prepare food,
sending him back to Lùzhōu
to first prepare provisions to await the army.
Seeing Déjūn and his son on the city wall,
Xíngzhōu said:
"I and the Great King are from the same region.
Zhào Déjūn was enfeoffed as the King of Běipíng,
hence Gāo Xíngzhōu addressed him as Great King.
Déjūn was from Yōuzhōu,
Xíngzhōu was from Guīzhōu,
both were Yān people,
hence he said 'from the same region.'
There isn't enough grain in the city to hold it,
it would be better to quickly welcome the imperial carriage."
On Jiǎxū,
the Emperor and the Qìdān ruler arrived at Lùzhōu.
Déjūn and his son welcomed and paid respects at Gāohé.
The Qìdān ruler comforted and appeased them.
The father and son bowed to the Emperor at his horse's head,
and advanced, saying:
"How have you been since we parted?"
The Emperor did not look at them,
nor did he speak to them.
(This was) because they had wanted to contend for the emperorship,
and he resented them for it.
"Where are the silver-saddled Qìdān guards you placed in Yōuzhōu?"
Déjūn pointed them out,
and the Qìdān ruler ordered them all killed in the western suburbs.
(This refers to) the western suburbs of Lùzhōu.
Then, he chained Déjūn and Yánshòu
and sent them back to their country.
Suǒ
is the same as Suǒ (鎖).
Déjūn met Empress Dowager Shùlǜ.
He presented all the treasures he had brought and registered his fields and residences to offer them.
The Empress Dowager asked:
"Why did you go to Tàiyuán recently?"
Déjūn replied:
"By the order of the Táng ruler."
The Empress Dowager pointed to the sky and said:
"You sought to be Emperor from my son,
why speak falsehoods!"
(This means) Déjūn raised troops and went to Tàiyuán
wishing to seek to be Emperor from the Qìdān ruler,
why then did he falsely claim to be acting on the Táng ruler's orders!
"This cannot be deceived."
She also said:
"When my son was about to leave,
I warned him, saying: If Great King Zhào leads his troops north towards Yúguān,
you must quickly retreat,
Tàiyuán cannot be saved.
If you wanted to be Emperor,
why didn't you first repel my son?
To plan slowly would not have been too late.
'Plan slowly'
means to slowly plan to become Emperor.
Since you betrayed your lord,
could not defeat the enemy,
and also wanted to take advantage of the chaos to gain profit,
with such actions,
how can you possibly ask to live?"
Déjūn bowed his head and could not respond.
She also asked:
"The precious artifacts are here."
(This refers to) what Déjūn brought to present.
Déjūn said:
"In Yōuzhōu."
The Empress Dowager said:
"To whom does Yōuzhōu belong now?"
He said:
"It belongs to Your Majesty."
The Empress Dowager said:
"If so, why offer them then?"
This is the meaning of Wèi Wáng Jìjí leaving Wáng Zōngbì's offerings,
meaning
"These are all our family's possessions."
From then on, he was depressed and ate little,
and died after more than a year.
Zhāng Lì and Yánshòu both entered Qìdān.
The Qìdān ruler reinstated him as Hàlín Xuéshì.
Zhāng Lì
was Hàlín Xuéshì during the reign of Táng Míngzōng.
The Táng ruler sent Lì to supervise Zhào Yánshòu in advancing the army at Tuánbǎi,
and thus he and Yánshòu both entered Qìdān.
He eventually died of illness in China.
When the Emperor was about to depart from Shàngdǎng,
the Qìdān ruler raised his cup and said to the Emperor:
"I came from afar to uphold righteousness.
Now that the great matter is accomplished,
if I were to go south,
the people of Hénán would certainly be greatly alarmed;
you should lead the Hàn troops south yourself,
and the people will not be too afraid.
I will order Tài Xiāng Wēn to lead five thousand cavalry to escort you to Hé Liang.
According to Tǔbō and Qìdān, both have Tài Xiāng.
Hé Liang is Héyáng Qiáo.
The 'Kǎo Yì' says: the 'Fèidì Shílù' records
'Gāo Móhàn',
Fàn Zhì's 'Xiàn Fān Jì' records
'Gāo Móhàn',
Ōuyáng Shǐ records
'Gāo Móuhàn'.
It is probably that his Fān name was Tài Xiāng Wēn,
and his Hàn name was Gāo Móhàn.
We now follow the 'Jìn Gāozǔ Shílù'.
I will stay here for now,
awaiting news from you.
If there is an emergency, I will come down the mountain to save you;
'come down the mountain'
means to descend the Tàiháng.
I will then return north."
He held the Emperor's hand and they wept together,
unable to part for a long time.
He untied his white sable fur coat and put it on the Emperor.
Sable originates from the north.
Black sable fur coats could still be obtained in the south,
but white sable fur coats were rare in the south.
Lù Diàn's 'Pí Yǎ' says: Sable is also a type of rodent,
with thick fur.
Its fur is warmer than fox or badger.
Yī
(pronunciation) is Fú Jì fān.
(He also gave) one thousand two hundred warhorses,
saying:
"May our descendants never forget each other, generation after generation."
He also said:
"Liú Zhīyuǎn, Zhào Yíng, and Sāng Wéihàn are all founding meritorious officials;
unless there is a major reason,
do not abandon them."
Earlier,
when Zhāng Jìngdá had set out with his army,
the Táng ruler sent Gāo Hànjūn, the Dà Jiāngjūn of Zuǒ Jīnwú from Lìshān, to guard Jìnzhōu.
There is Lìshān in Hédōng Xiàn, Hézhōng Fǔ.
Xuē Shǐ says: Gāo Hànjūn
was from Lìshān, Qízhōu.
This should be followed.
Zhāng Jìngdá, as the commander of Jìnzhōu, was sent to exclusively campaign in Tàiyuán,
so Gāo Hànjūn was made to guard Jìnzhōu.
Tián Chéngzhào, the Fùshǐ of Jiànxióng Jìedù, led his troops to attack Hànjūn at the prefectural office.
Hànjūn opened the gate and invited Chéngzhào in,
calmly saying:
"Both you and I have received appointments from the court,
why are you pressing me like this?"
Chéngzhào said:
"I wish to support you as Jìedùshǐ."
Hànjūn said:
"I am old,
and I will not be a leader of rebellion out of righteousness.
My life and death are yours to decide."
Chéngzhào signaled his attendants to kill him,
but the soldiers threw their blades to the ground, saying:
"Gāo Jīnwú is a man of accumulated virtue through several dynasties,
how can we harm him!"
Chéngzhào then apologized, saying:
"I was just joking with you."
He allowed Hànjūn to return to Luòyáng.
The Emperor met him on the road.
Gāo Hànjūn had probably come from Jìnzhōu through Hánkǒu to Héyáng,
while the Emperor had come south from Tàiháng,
hence they met on the road.
"I was worried that you would be harmed by the rebellious soldiers,
and I am very happy to see you now."
47 Initially,
Dǒng Wēnqí, the Jiedushi of Chéngdé, was greedy and tyrannical.
He amassed enormous wealth,
and used Mì Qióng, the Yánèi Dūyúhóu of Píngshān, as his confidant.
Píngshān County was subordinate to Zhènzhōu,
originally Fángshān County established by the Suí.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
Ān Lùshān rebelled,
Xuánzōng changed Lùquán County to Huòlù,
and Fángshān County to Píngshān.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Píngshān is sixty-five *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
Zhào Déjūn invited Dǒng Wēnqí to jointly rescue Jìn'ān,
and they both perished.
They were buried in one pit,
and their wealth was seized.
Like an elephant that is killed for its tusks,
this was due to bribery.
This lays the groundwork for Mì Qióng being killed by Fàn Yánguāng.
瘞 (yì),
rhymes with jì.
A memorial reported it as a military disturbance.
48 In Tóngzhōu, the junior officer Mén Duó killed Jiedushi Yáng Hànbīn,
and burned and plundered the prefectural city.
The Hénán Guānshì Zhì states: The Later Wèi changed the Chìmén clan to the Mén clan.
There was also the Tǔmén clan changed to the Mén clan,
and the Kùmén clan changed to the Mén clan.
校 (jiào),
rhymes with hù jiāo.
49 An imperial edict posthumously granted Lǐ Zànhuá the title of King of Yān,
and sent an envoy to return his remains to his country.
50 Zhāng Lǎng led his troops to the court.
When the Emperor first raised his army,
Zhāng Lǎng held Dàizhōu
and did not follow him.
將 (jiàng),
rhymes with jí liàng.
51 On *gēngzǐ* (the 37th day of the 60-day cycle),
Lú Wénjì, formerly the Táng Zhōngshū Shìláng, was made Lìbù Shàngshū.
Jìnyáng Zhōu Huái, the Huángchéng Shǐ, was made Dàjiāngjūn and concurrently Sāisī Shǐ;
Zhōu Huái declined, saying:
"I know my talent is not up to the task;
I would rather be rejected for avoiding responsibility
than suffer guilt by presuming on favor."
The Emperor granted his request.
52 The Emperor heard that Fáng Zhīwēn, the Jiedushi of Pínglú, had died,
and sent Wáng Jiànlì, the Jiedushi of Tiānpíng, with troops to pacify Qīngzhōu.
This was out of concern for a potential rebellion.
將 (jiàng),
rhymes with jí liàng;
the same applies below.
53 Xīngtáng Fǔ was renamed Guǎngjìn Fǔ.
The Later Táng changed Wèizhōu to Xīngtáng Fǔ.
After the Jìn rose,
it was again changed to Guǎngjìn Fǔ,
because the name of the prefecture was changed with the change of dynasty.
54 Lú Wénjìn, the Jiedushi of Ānyuǎn, heard that the Emperor had been installed by the Qìdān.
As he himself was a Qìdān rebel general,
Lú Wénjìn had fled from the Qìdān.
See volume 275, Míngzōng Tiānchéng first year.
On *xīnchǒu* (the 38th day of the 60-day cycle),
he abandoned his post and fled to Wú.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Ānzhōu is four hundred *lǐ* east of Huángzhōu,
and three hundred sixty *lǐ* southeast of Èzhōu.
Both Huáng and È were Wú territories.
He summoned his chief generals,
informed them of the situation,
and they all bowed, bid farewell, and withdrew.

55 Xú Zhīgào believed that Lǐ Déchéng, the Jiedushi of Zhènnán and Tàiwèi concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng, and Zhōu Běn, the Jiedushi of Déshèng concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng, held high positions and great prestige,
and wanted to use them to lead the multitude in supporting his ascension.
Zhōu Běn said:
"I received great kindness from the former king.
The 'former king' Zhōu Běn referred to
was Yáng Xíngmì.
帥 (shuài),
read as *shuài*.
I regret that I could not save the Yáng clan from danger;
how can you make me do this again?"
His son, Hóngzuò, pressed him,
and he had no choice but to join Déchéng in leading the generals to Jiāngdū to memorialize the Wú lord,
stating Zhīgào's merits and virtues,
and requesting the performance of the investiture ceremony;
they also went to Jīnlíng to urge him to ascend the throne.
Sòng Qíqiū said to Déchéng's son, Jiànxūn:
"Your esteemed father
was Tàizǔ's foremost meritorious minister.
Yáng Xíngmì of Wú was given the temple name Tàizǔ.
Therefore, there are many omens in the Wú palace."
The 'Wú palace'
refers to the Jiāngdū Palace.
妖 (yāo),
rhymes with yī yáo.
"Will the Wú dynasty then end?"
His attendants said:
"This is the will of Heaven,
not human affairs."
56 Wáng Jiàn, King of Gāolì, used his army to defeat Sīnlüó and Bǎijì.
Consequently, all the states of the Eastern Yi became subordinate to him.
He had two capitals,
six prefectures,
nine Jiedushi,
and one hundred twenty counties.
For Wáng Jiàn of Gāolì, see volume 271, Liáng Jūn Wáng Lóngdé third year.
Punctuation by Dèng Guǎngmíng, re-collated by Niè Chóngqí
Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial decree
Hòu Xué Tiāntái
Tiānfú 2nd year (Dīngyǒu, 937)
1 Spring,
1st month,
On *yǐmǎo* (the 52nd day of the 60-day cycle),
there was a solar eclipse.
The Kǎoyì states: The Shílù records:
"On *jiǎyín* (the 51st day of the 60-day cycle), the 1st day of the month,
on *yǐmǎo*, there was a solar eclipse."
The Shíguó Jìnián records:
"In Shǔ, on *yǐmǎo*, the 1st day of the month, there was a solar eclipse."
This is because the Jìn people changed their calendar to avoid a solar eclipse on the third day of the month.
2 An imperial edict made Ān Chóngróng, formerly the Běimiàn Zhāoshōu Zhǐhuīshǐ—
This refers to the military position Ān Chóngróng held during the siege of Jìnyáng,
hence "formerly."
重 (chóng),
rhymes with zhí lóng.
At that time, Mì Qióng himself was the Chéngdé Liúhòu,
and Ān Chóngróng was appointed to replace him.
祕 (Mì),
is a surname.
Between the Hàn and Wèi dynasties, there was Mì Yí of Nán'ān.
Chóngróng went to Zhènzhōu with the Qìdān general Zhào Sīwēn,
and Qióng dared not defy the order.
He feared the Qìdān.
On *bǐngchén* (the 53rd day of the 60-day cycle),
Chóngróng memorialized that he had taken up his duties.
This lays the groundwork for Ān Chóngróng's rebellion in Chéngdé.
He was a native of Xíngzhōu.
3 The Qìdān designated Yōuzhōu as their Nánjīng.
Ouwén Shǐ records: Yōuzhōu was made Yānjīng.
Referring to Zhào Sīwēn's position as Liúshǒu,
Nánjīng is correct.
4 Lǐ Sōng and Lǚ Qí hid among the common people in Yīquè.
The Emperor, when he first took control of Hédōng,
found Sōng to be helpful,
and appreciated him.
Lǐ Sōng proposed that the Emperor take control of Hédōng.
The matter is found in volume 278, Táng Míngzōng Chángxīng third year.
Lǐ Sōng and Lǚ Qí proposed an alliance with the Qìdān to control Hédōng.
See the previous volume, same year, 3rd month.
On *yǐchǒu* (the 2nd day of the 60-day cycle),
Qí was made Mìshū Jiān;
on *bǐngyín* (the 3rd day of the 60-day cycle),
Sōng was made Bīngbù Shìláng and concurrently Pàn Hùbù.
5 Initially,
when Fàn Yánguāng, the Tiānxíong Jiedushi concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng, was of humble status,
a fortune-teller named Zhāng Shēng told him:
"You will certainly become a general and prime minister."
After Yánguāng became prominent,
he trusted and respected him.
Yánguāng once dreamed that a snake entered his belly from his navel,
and he asked Zhāng Shēng about it.
Zhāng Shēng said:
"A snake is a dragon,
an omen of emperorship."
From then on, Yánguāng harbored ambitions beyond his station.
Lù Wáng of Táng had always been on good terms with Yánguāng.
When Zhào Déjūn was defeated,
Yánguāng led his troops back to Wèizhōu from Liáozhōu.
Zhào Déjūn's defeat is found in the previous volume, same year, intercalary 11th month.
Fàn Yánguāng garrisoned Liáozhōu, see same year, 10th month;
his return to Wèizhōu must also have been in the intercalary 11th month.
Feeling insecure,
he secretly sent a letter to Mì Qióng,
wanting to cause trouble with him;
Qióng received the letter but did not reply,
and Yánguāng resented him.
When Qióng was going to Qí,
passing through Wèi territory,
Yánguāng wanted to silence him,
and also coveted his wealth.
He sent soldiers to intercept him at Xiàjīn
and killed him.
This lays the groundwork for Fàn Yánguāng's rebellion in Wèi,
and his subsequent death at Yáng Guāngyuǎn's hands for his wealth.
Xiàjīn,
formerly the ancient Yú County,
was renamed Xiàjīn in the first year of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
and was subordinate to Bèizhōu;
in the Sòng dynasty, Xiàjīn was subordinate to Běijīng,
two hundred fifty *lǐ* northeast of Běijīng.
夏 (xià),
rhymes with hù yǎ.
On *dīngmǎo* (the 4th day of the 60-day cycle),
Yánguāng memorialized that the police at Xiàjīn had mistakenly killed Qióng;
the Emperor did not question it.
6 On the day *wùyín*,
Lǐ Sōng was appointed as *Zhōngshū Shìláng*, *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*,
and *Shūmìshǐ*,
and Sāng Wéihàn concurrently held the post of *Shūmìshǐ*.
At that time, the Jìn had just acquired the empire,
but many of the regional governors (fānzhèn) had not yet submitted;
or if they had submitted,
they were uneasy and restive.
After the ravages of war,
the state coffers were depleted,
the common people were impoverished,
and the Qìdān's demands were insatiable.
Wéihàn advised the emperor to deal with the fānzhèn with sincerity and put aside grievances,
to serve the Qìdān with humble words and generous gifts,
to train soldiers and repair weapons to strengthen military preparedness,
to promote agriculture and sericulture to fill the granaries,
and to facilitate commerce to enrich financial resources.
Within a few years,
China gradually stabilized.
History records Sāng Wéihàn's contributions to the early establishment of the Shíjìn dynasty in this way.
*Jiǎ*,
pronounced *gǔ*.
7 The Wú crown prince Liǎn married the daughter of Qí Wáng Zhī Gào.
Zhī Gào initially built the Great Ancestral Temple and altars of Soil and Grain,
and renamed Jīnlíng as Jiāngníng Fǔ.
Previously,
Wú had made Shēngzhōu into Jīnlíng Fǔ,
and now it was renamed again.
Halls were called *diàn*;
Sòng Qíqiū and Xú Jiè, formerly Left and Right *Sīmǎ*, were appointed Left and Right *Chéngxiàng*;
Zhōu Zōng, *Mǎbù Pànguān*, and Zhōu Tíngyù, *Nèishū Pànguān* from Yī, were appointed *Nèishūshǐ*.
Yī,
a Hàn county,
belonged to Shèzhōu during the Táng.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: it is one hundred fifty-three *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
Yī,
Yán Shīgǔ pronounced it *yī*,
Liú Xù pronounced it *yīng*.
Eight cavalry armies and
nine infantry armies were established.
8 In the second month,
the Wú ruler appointed Lú Wénjìn as *Xuānwǔ Jiédùshǐ*.
The Xuānwǔ Army's Biànzhōu,
at that time belonged to the Jìn,
so the Wú ruler only nominally appointed Lú Wénjìn.
9 On the day *wùzǐ*,
the Wú ruler sent Yíyáng Wáng Zǎo to the Western Capital.
Wú regarded Jīnlíng as the Western Capital, as seen in the previous year's entry in the previous volume.
*Zǎo*,
pronounced *zǐhào*.
The king received the imperial edict,
and a general amnesty was declared throughout the territory.
The edict referred to the king as the queen.
10 Qián Yuánguàn, King of Wúyuè, had a younger brother, Yuán Xiàng, who was *Shùnhuà Jiédùshǐ* and *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*. He incurred Yuánguàn's displeasure,
and was demoted to a commoner.
The beginning of Qián Yuánxiàng's offense is mentioned in volume 278, Táng Míngzōng, Chángxīng Fourth Year.
*Xiàng*,
pronounced *xiàng*.
11 The Qìdān ruler traveled from Shàngdǎng, passing through Yúnzhōu.
Shā Yànxún, *Dàtóng Jiédùshǐ*, went out to welcome him.
The Qìdān ruler detained him,
not allowing him to return to his post.
Wú Luán, *Jiédù Pànguān*, was in the city
and said to his followers:
"We belong to a people of propriety and righteousness;
how can we serve the barbarians (yídí)! "
The crowd elected Luán to manage the affairs of the prefecture,
closed the city gates, and refused the Qìdān's command.
The Qìdān attacked it,
but could not overcome it.
Guō Chóngwēi of Jīnchéng, *Mǎjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ* of Yìngzhōu, also felt ashamed to serve the Qìdān,
and bravely returned south.
The Hàn's Jīnchéng is the Táng's Wǔquán Xiàn of Lánzhōu.
The Táng's Jīnchéng was the land of Zhīyáng Xiàn in the Hàn.
Liáng established Guǎngwǔ Jùn;
Suí abolished the *jùn* and made it Guǎngwǔ Xiàn;
in the second year of Táng Qiányuán (759), it was renamed Jīnchéng,
belonging to Lánzhōu.
However, this is not the Jīnchéng of Lánzhōu,
but rather Jīnchéng Xiàn of Yìngzhōu.
Táng Míngzōng was born in Jīnfèngchéng, north of Dài,
and upon his ascension,
established Jīnchéng Xiàn in that area,
and also established Yìngzhōu,
where its administration was located.
Guō Chóngwēi was likely a local who served as the general of the local command.
Moreover, the *Xiōngnú Xūzhī* states: Yìngzhōu is eight hundred fifty *lǐ* east of Yōuzhōu;
Jīnchéng Xiàn is eight hundred *lǐ* northeast of Shuòzhōu.
As stated in the *Xūzhī*,
Yìngzhōu and Jīnchéng Xiàn appear to be two separate places,
as unrelated as north and south,
and it is not possible to verify its accuracy;
it should also be inquired from those who have traversed the area.
*Tǐng*,
meaning "to pull out" or "to brave."
The Qìdān ruler passed through Xīnzhōu,
and ordered Zhái Zhāng, *Wēisài Jiédùshǐ*, to collect one hundred thousand *mín* in military contributions.
Initially,
when the Qìdān ruler Ābǎojī was strong,
the Shìwéi, Xī, and Yíbó all submitted to him.
Xī Wáng Qùzhū suffered from Qìdān's greed and tyranny,
and led his followers to move west to Guīzhōu,
relying on Liú Rén'gōng and his son,
and were called the Western Xī.
The Eastern Xī lived in Pípáchuān;
the Western Xī moved to Guīzhōu,
residing along the northern mountains.
His son Sàolà succeeded him.
When Táng Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liú Shǒuguāng,
he bestowed upon Sàolà the surname Lǐ and the name Shàowēi.
Shàowēi married the elder sister of Qìdān Zhuíbùlǔ.
Zhuíbùlǔ incurred the Qìdān's displeasure,
and fled to Shàowēi.
Shàowēi took him in;
the Qìdān were enraged and attacked him,
but could not overcome him.
Shàowēi died,
and his son Zhuāilà succeeded him.
When the Qìdān ruler Déguāng returned north from Shàngdǎng,
Zhuāilà welcomed him and surrendered.
At that time, Zhuíbùlǔ had also died.
The Qìdān ruler said:
"You are truly blameless,
but Sàolà and Zhuíbùlǔ betrayed me."
He ordered their bones to be exhumed,
ground, and scattered.
The Xī people, fearing the Qìdān's cruelty,
mostly fled and rebelled.
The Qìdān ruler commended Zhái Zhāng, saying:
"I shall arrange a replacement for you,
and allow you to return south."
On the day *jǐhài*,
Zhāng submitted a memorial requesting to be summoned to the capital.
Subsequently, the Qìdān sent Zhāng to lead troops to suppress the rebellious Xī and attack Yúnzhōu.
He achieved success,
but the Qìdān kept Zhāng and did not release him.
Zhāng died in despondency.
Zhāng Lì fled from the Qìdān and returned,
but was captured by pursuing cavalry.
The Qìdān ruler reproached him, saying:
"Why did you leave me?"
He replied:
"Your servant is a Chinese person,
and my food and clothing are entirely different from here.
Life is worse than death;
I wish to be executed quickly."
The Qìdān ruler looked at the interpreter Gāo Yànyīng and said:
"I always warned you to treat this person well.
The Qìdān appointed interpreters to manage the Chinese people,
selecting those who understood Chinese customs and spoke Chinese.
Sòng Bái said: 'Those close confidants of the Qìdān ruler who could speak Chinese were called interpreters (*tōngshì*),
meaning they were thoroughly knowledgeable in all matters.'
If he is lost,
how can he be recovered!"
He flogged Yànyīng and apologized to Lì.
Lì served the Qìdān ruler with great loyalty and integrity,
always speaking his mind on matters,
without concealment or evasion.
The Qìdān ruler valued him greatly.
Historians say that the Qìdān ruler recognized and respected scholars.
12 Initially,
Qián Liú, King of Wúyuè, had a young son, Yuánshù,
who frequently distinguished himself in military campaigns.
Liú bestowed weapons upon him.
When Qián Yuánguàn, King of Wúyuè, ascended the throne,
Yuánshù was *Tǔkè Mǎbùjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ*
and concurrently *Zhōngshū Lìng*.
Relying on favor, he became arrogant and overbearing,
increasing his armed forces to several thousand,
and many people in the state attached themselves to him.
Yuánguàn was wary of him,
and had someone subtly suggest to Yuánshù that he should surrender his weapons
and go to govern Wēnzhōu.
Yuánshù did not comply.
A clerk from the Tóngguān Temple reported that Yuánshù had sent trusted followers to pray to the gods,
seeking to become the ruler of Wúyuè;
and also made wax pellets that passed through water channels,
to conspire with his elder brother Yuán Xiàng.
Wax pellets were written messages enclosed in wax,
with letters written and then sealed with wax on the outside.
On the day *wǔwǔ*,
Yuánguàn sent an envoy to summon Yuánshù to a banquet in the palace.
Upon his arrival,
his attendants claimed that Yuánshù had a blade concealed in his sash.
He was immediately seized and killed;
Yuán Xiàng was also killed.
Yuán Xiàng's imprisonment is mentioned in volume 278, Táng Míngzōng, Chángxīng Fourth Year.
His son Rénjùn remonstrated, saying:
"In the past, when Guāngwǔ defeated Wáng Láng,
and Cáo Gōng defeated Yuán Shào,
they both burned their correspondence to appease those who were wavering.
The incident involving Guāngwǔ is in volume 39, Hàn Gēngshǐ Second Year.
The incident involving Cáo Gōng is in volume 64, Xiàndì Jiàn'ān Fifth Year."
Yuánguàn agreed.
Thirty. Hánlín Xuéshì (翰林學士) and Lǐbù Shìláng (禮部侍郎) Hé Níng (和凝) was made Duānmíng Diàn Xuéshì (端明殿學士).
Níng (凝) closed his gate,
refusing to receive guests.
The former Yàozhōu Tuánliàn Tuīguān (耀州團練推官) Zhāng Yì (張誼) of Xiāngyì (襄邑)
Xiāngyì (襄邑) County was subordinate to Sòngzhōu (宋州).
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) says: It is one hundred and seventy *lǐ* southeast of Dàliáng (大梁).
considered
"The proximate offices are the eyes and ears of the Son of Heaven.
They should be aware of the advantages and disadvantages of the four directions.
How can one refuse guests!
Although it is convenient for personal safety,
how can one betray the state!"
Níng (凝) was impressed by him,
and recommended him to Sāng Wéihàn (桑維翰).
Not long after,
he was appointed Zuǒ Shíyí (左拾遺).
Yì (誼) submitted a memorial, stating:
"The northern *dí* (狄) have rendered services of support and establishment.
It is advisable to outwardly strengthen good faith,
and inwardly be cautious with border defenses.
One must not indulge in ease,
thereby inciting the *róng* (戎) heart."
The emperor deeply approved of this.
Thirty-one. The Qìdān (契丹) attacked Yúnzhōu (雲州),
and could not take it for half a year.
Wú Luán (吳巒) sent an envoy through a secret path to present a memorial seeking rescue.
The emperor wrote a letter to the Qìdān (契丹) ruler to request it.
The Qìdān (契丹) ruler then ordered Zhái Zhāng (翟璋) to lift the siege and depart.
The emperor summoned Luán (巒) back,
appointing him Wǔníng Jiédù Fùshǐ (武寧節度副使).
Thirty-two. On the *dīngwèi* day,
Yang Guāngyuǎn (楊光遠), the Shìwèishǐ (侍衞使), was appointed Wèifǔ Sìmiàn Dūbùshǔ (魏府四面都部署).
Shìwèishǐ (侍衞使) here means Shìwèi Dūjūnshǐ (侍衞都軍使),
and the historian used an abbreviated form. Zhāoyì Jiédùshǐ (昭義節度使) Gāo Xíngzhōu (高行周) led his own army to garrison Xiāngzhōu (相州),
becoming Wèifǔ Xīmiàn Dūbùshǔ (魏府西面都部署).
Xiāngzhōu (相州) is west of Wèizhōu (魏州),
so Gāo Xíngzhōu (高行周) was ordered to lead troops from Lùzhōu (潞州) to garrison Xiāngzhōu (相州) to confront Fàn Yánguāng (范延光).
The soldier Guō Wēi (郭威) was formerly subordinate to Liú Zhīyuǎn (劉知遠).
He was to accompany Yáng Guāngyuǎn (楊光遠) on the northern campaign. Going from Dàliáng (大梁) to campaign against Wèizhōu (魏州) was considered a northern campaign.
Xuē Shǐ (薛史) in the Zhōujì (周紀) states that
Guō Wēi (郭威) initially served Lǐ Jìtāo (李繼韜);
after Jìtāo (繼韜) was executed,
he was assigned to the Mǎzhí (馬直).
Jìn Zǔ (晉祖) took charge of the Fùshìwèi (副侍衞),
summoned him to his command,
and thus he came to serve Hàn Zǔ (漢祖).
When people asked him why,
Wēi (威) said:
"Duke Yáng (楊公) has the talent for treachery and cunning,
but lacks the spirit of a hero.
What use would he have for me?
The one who can use me is perhaps Duke Liú (劉公)!"
This sets the stage for Guō Wēi (郭威) assisting Liú Zhīyuǎn (劉知遠) in founding his dynasty.
Thirty-three. An imperial edict ordered Zhāng Cóngbīn (張從賓) to dispatch several thousand Hénán (河南) soldiers to attack Fàn Yánguāng (范延光).
Hénán (河南) soldiers means the troops from Hénánfǔ (河南府).
Zhāng Cóngbīn (張從賓) was then Luòyáng Xúnjiǎnshǐ (洛陽巡檢使),
hence he was ordered to dispatch them.
Cóngbīn (從賓) then rebelled together with them,
killing the imperial prince and Héyáng Jiédùshǐ (河陽節度使) Zhòngxìn (重信),
and appointing the senior general Zhāng Jìzuò (張繼祚) as Héyáng Liúhòu (河陽留後).
Jìzuò (繼祚) was
the son of Quányì (全義).
Zhāng Quányì (張全義) had been Yǐn (尹) of Hénán (河南) since the end of the Táng (唐) dynasty,
spanning the Táng (唐) and Liáng (梁) dynasties. He also killed the imperial prince and provisional Dōngdū Liúshǒu (東都留守) Zhòngyì (重乂),
appointing Dōngdū Fùliúshǒu (東都副留守) and Dū Xúnjiǎnshǐ (都巡檢使) Zhāng Yánbō (張延播) to manage affairs of Hénánfǔ (河南府),
and join his army.
He took money and silk from the imperial treasury to reward his soldiers;
Lìushǒu Pànguān (留守判官) Lǐ Xiá (李遐) refused to comply,
and the soldiers killed him.
Cóngbīn (從賓) led his troops to block Sǐshuǐ Guān (汜水關).
Sǐshuǐ Guān (汜水關) is named after the county,
and is actually Hǔláo Guān (虎牢關).
See the Biànwù (辯誤) for details.
An imperial edict ordered Fèngguó Dūzhīhuīshǐ (奉國都指揮使) Hóu Yì (侯益) to lead five thousand imperial guards to join Dù Zhòngwēi (杜重威) in attacking Zhāng Cóngbīn (張從賓);
another edict ordered Xuānhuīshǐ (宣徽使) Liú Chùràng (劉處讓) to divide his troops from Líyáng (黎陽) to attack him.
At that time, urgent dispatches flew everywhere,
and all officials accompanying the emperor in Dàliáng (大梁) were terrified.
"Urgent dispatches flew everywhere" means military documents piled up.
The families of the accompanying officials were all left in Dōngdū (東都),
while the emperor was in Biàn (汴),
so their roots had been pulled up,
hence their fear.
Zòng (縱) is pronounced *zǐróng*.
Cóng (從) is pronounced *cáiyòng*.
Xiōng (恟) is pronounced *xǔgǒng*.
(Sāng Wéihàn's) expression remained calm and composed,
and he received guests
without changing his usual demeanor,
which somewhat reassured the public.
The historian says Sāng Wéihàn (桑維翰) was able to maintain composure and stabilize affairs.
that a white dragon was seen at night on Luófēng (螺峯);
the Mǐn (閩) ruler built Báilóng Sì (白龍寺).
At that time, numerous projects were underway,
and expenses were insufficient.
The Mǐn (閩) ruler said to Lìbù Shìláng (吏部侍郎) and Pàn Sānsī (判三司) Cài Shǒuméng (蔡守蒙) of Hòuguān (候官):
The Latter Hàn (後漢) established Hòuguān (候官) County.
The Suí (隋) dynasty abolished it and merged it into Mǐn (閩) County.
The Táng (唐) dynasty re-established Hòuguān (候官) County,
which was subordinate to Fúzhōu (福州).
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) says: It is governed from within the prefectural city.
"I hear that officials responsible for appointments all accept bribes,
is this true?"
He replied:
"Such popular rumors are not to be trusted."
The Mǐn (閩) ruler said:
"I have known this for a long time.
Now I entrust this to you,
choose the worthy and appoint them,
but do not refuse the unworthy and those who deceive and usurp [appointments].
Wǎngmào (罔冒) refers to those who deceive and falsely usurp to seek official positions.
Deceiving a superior with something that is not factually possible is called *wǎng* (罔);
falsely claiming another's possessions to fabricate is called *mào* (冒).
Record them and present them to me."
Shǒuméng (守蒙) was always honest,
and considered this unacceptable;
the Mǐn (閩) ruler became angry,
and Shǒuméng (守蒙), fearing, complied.
From then on, appointments were made solely based on the amount of wealth offered.
This sets the stage for Cài Shǒuméng (蔡守蒙) being executed for selling offices.
Tángdié (堂牒)
is what people nowadays call *shěngzhá* (省劄).
"Empty names" means
that the name of the appointed person was not yet written,
but filled in after the sale for money.
Kōng (空) is pronounced *kǔgòng*.
There was no satiety.
An edict also decreed that those who concealed their age would be flogged,
those who concealed their household members would be executed,
and fugitives' families would be exterminated.
Fruits, vegetables, chickens, and pigs
were all heavily taxed.
Thirty-five. Autumn,
seventh month.
Zhāng Cóngbīn (張從賓) attacked Sǐshuǐ (汜水),
killing Xúnjiǎnshǐ (巡檢使) Sòng Tínghào (宋廷浩).
The emperor donned military attire,
prepared light cavalry,
and was about to flee to Jìnyáng (晉陽) to avoid him.
Sāng Wéihàn (桑維翰) kowtowed and earnestly advised:
"Although the rebel's momentum is strong,
it cannot last long.
Please wait a little longer;
you must not move rashly."
The emperor then stopped.
The historian says Sāng Wéihàn (桑維翰) possessed courage and strategy,
and the Jìn (晉) court relied on him for the stability of the state.
Shǎo (少) is pronounced *shàozhǎo*.
Thirty-four. A *fāngshì* (方士) told the Mǐn (閩) ruler
Yòu Wǔwèi Shàngjiāngjūn (右武衞上將軍) Lóu Jìyīng (婁繼英) and Yòu Wèi Dàjiāngjūn (右衞大將軍) Yǐn Huī (尹暉), who were in Dàliáng (大梁),
and Wēn Tāo's (溫韜) sons Yánjùn (延濬), Yánzhǎo (延沼), and Yánjùn (延袞), who resided in Xǔzhōu (許州),
all responded.
Yǐn Huī (尹暉) had surrendered his entire army to Lù Wáng (潞王) to obtain a *jiézhèn* (節鎮),
but now resided as a security guard,
hence he was an official without a substantial post.
Wēn Tāo (溫韜) had been executed during the Táng Míngzōng (唐明宗) era,
and his sons were discarded;
Lóu Jìyīng's (婁繼英) daughter-in-law was Wēn Yánzhǎo's (溫延沼) daughter,
and Jìyīng (繼英) also held an honorary post,
so they all responded to Yánguāng (延光).
Their followers had already reached a thousand people.
Jìyīng (繼英) and Huī's (暉) conspiracy was exposed,
and they both fled.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
an imperial decree stated that Yánguāng's (延光) cunning plot
slandered loyal and virtuous people.
From now on, if Yánguāng's (延光) spies are captured,
the captors will be rewarded,
the spies killed,
and any
wax letters
must not be reported.
This was to avoid knowing the names of those he enticed,
thereby reassuring those who were wavering.
(Yǐn Huī (尹暉)) was killed by someone.
Jìyīng (繼英) fled to Xǔzhōu (許州),
taking refuge with the Wēn (溫) clan.
Zhōngwǔ Jiédùshǐ (忠武節度使) Cháng Cóngjiǎn (萇從簡) made extensive preparations against them,
so Yánjùn (延濬) and the others could not take action.
They wanted to kill Jìyīng (繼英) to clear their names,
but Yánzhǎo (延沼) stopped them,
and they then fled together to Zhāng Cóngbīn (張從賓).
Jìyīng (繼英) knew their plan,
and persuaded Cóngbīn (從賓) to capture the three Wēns (溫),
and execute them all.
37 Bái Fèngjìn (白奉進) was in Huázhōu (滑州).
In the sixth month of that year, Bái Fèngjìn (白奉進) was sent to garrison Bǎimǎ (白馬).
Bǎimǎ (白馬)
was the seat of Huázhōu (滑州).
They were captured,
five men were caught.
Three of them belonged to Fèngjìn (奉進),
and two belonged to Fú Yànráo (符彥饒).
Fèngjìn (奉進) beheaded them all.
Yànráo (彥饒) was furious
because Fèngjìn (奉進) had not informed him first.
The next day,
Fèngjìn (奉進), with a few horsemen, went to Yànráo (彥饒) to apologize.
Yànráo (彥饒) said:
"Each division in the army has its own jurisdiction.
How can you seize soldiers from Huázhōu (滑州) and behead them all?
Is there no sense of guest and host at all!"
Fú Yànráo (符彥饒) considered himself the master by garrisoning Huázhōu (滑州),
and Bái Fèngjìn (白奉進) garrisoning Huázhōu (滑州) as a guest.
"When soldiers break the law,
how can there be 'them' and 'us'?
I have already admitted my fault and apologized to you,
yet you remain angry.
Do you wish to rebel with Yáng Yán'guāng (楊延光)?"
He flicked his sleeves and rose.
Yànráo (彥饒) did not detain him.
The armored soldiers under the tent roared loudly,
seized Fèngjìn (奉進),
and killed him.
His horsemen fled,
shouting outside.
The various armies scrambled to don armor and wield weapons,
creating an uncontrollable uproar.
Mǎ Wàn (馬萬), the Commander of the Left Wing of Fèngguó (奉國), was bewildered and did not know what to do.
He led his infantry, intending to join the chaos.
He met Lú Shùnmì (盧順密), the Commander of the Right Wing, who was leading his troops out of the camp.
Shùnmì (順密) sternly said to Wàn (萬):
"Fú Gōng (符公) has killed Bái Gōng (白公),
he must be colluding with Wèichéng (魏城).
From here to the temporary palace is only two hundred *lǐ*.
Wèichéng (魏城)
refers to Wèizhōuchéng (魏州城).
At that time, Fàn Yán'guāng (范延光) was rebelling from Wèizhōu (魏州).
According to *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志): Huázhōu (滑州) is two hundred *lǐ* south of Dàliáng (大梁).
At that time, the Emperor was in Dàliáng (大梁).
Why do you not think of repaying the state,
but instead wish to aid the rebellion
and bring about the extermination of your own clan!
Today, we should collectively seize Fú Gōng (符公),
send him to the Son of Heaven,
and achieve a great merit.
Those soldiers who obey orders will be rewarded,
and those who defy orders will be executed.
Hesitate no more!"
Some soldiers under Wàn (萬)'s command were still shouting and jumping.
Shùnmì (順密) killed several of them,
and no one dared to move.

Wǔ Jǔ (伍舉) of Chǔ (楚) and Shēng Zǐ (聲子) were good friends.

All of Fú Cúnshěn (符存審)'s sons were talented and spirited,

Yànráo (彥饒) was unable to control his subordinates,

His brothers had no prior collusion.
The crime does not extend to others (罪不相及)
is an ancient principle.
Yáng Guāngyuǎn (楊光遠) led his troops from Báigāo (白皋) towards Huázhōu (滑州).

*Jiàng* (降),
pronounced *hù jiāng fān* (戶江翻).
That is a true rebel."

Wèi (魏),

The Emperor consulted Liú Zhīyuǎn (劉知遠) for a plan.
He replied:
"The rise of an emperor

Your Majesty, when you were in Jìnyáng (晉陽),

Powerful foreign enemy

With both benevolence and severity evident,

Zhīyuǎn (知遠) then strictly implemented prohibitions and regulations.
*Kē* (科)
means "rule."
A soldier stole a bundle of paper money.
The owner seized him.
The owner
refers to the owner of the paper money.
Zhīyuǎn (知遠) said:
"I will punish his intent,
not consider its value."
He ultimately killed him.
According to Táng (唐) law,
the punishment for theft was determined by the value of the stolen goods.
Liú Zhīyuǎn (劉知遠) used severe punishment to awe the masses,
wanting to subdue their hearts to suppress any nascent rebellion.
This is not something that can be ordinarily practiced in peaceful times.
On the day *Yǐmǎo* (乙卯),
Yáng Guāngyuǎn (楊光遠) was appointed Grand Commander of all armies in the Wèifǔ (魏府) temporary camp and concurrently acting prefect of the temporary government.

Hóu Yì (侯益) was appointed Military Governor of Héyáng (河陽).

Between the Jìn (晉) and Hàn (漢) dynasties,

Féng Huī (馮暉) and Sūn Ruì (孫銳) led their troops to Liùmíngzhèn (六明鎮).

They attacked them halfway across the river.
Huī (暉) and Ruì (銳)'s forces were greatly defeated,
many drowned,

Huī (暉) and Ruì (銳) fled back to Wèi (魏).
Dù Chóngwēi (杜重威) and Hóu Yì (侯益) led their troops to Sìshuǐ (汜水).

They fought,
capturing and beheading almost all of them.
They then took Sìshuǐ (汜水).
Cóngbīn (從賓) fled,
crossing the river on horseback,

His confederates Zhāng Yánbō (張延播), Jìzuò (繼祚), and Lóu Jìyīng (婁繼英) were captured,
sent to Dàliáng (大梁),
and executed.
Their clans were exterminated.
Fú Yànráo (符彥饒), Zhāng Cóngbīn (張從賓), and others were all dead,
Féng Huī (馮暉) and Sūn Ruì (孫銳) were also defeated,
Fàn Yán'guāng (范延光)'s position was isolated and weakened.
Zhāng Quányì (張全義) had the merit of rebuilding Luòyì (洛邑),
details are in Volume 257, the third year of Guāngqǐ (光啟) of Emperor Xīzōng (僖宗) of Táng (唐).
Therefore, only Jìzuò (繼祚)'s wife and children were executed.
Tāo (濤)

40 Ānzhōu Wēihé Zhǐhuīshǐ Wáng Huī
According to the Wǔdài Huìyào, in the Táng Dynasty there were the Wēihé and Gǒngchén Nèizhí armies,
which were renamed Xìngshùn Zuǒjūn and Yòujūn in the sixth year of Tiānfú of the Jìn Dynasty.
Wáng Huī killed Ānyuǎn Jiédùshǐ Zhōu Huái,
and took over the army himself.
He intended to attach himself to Fàn Yánguāng if Fàn Yánguāng was victorious,

The Emperor dispatched Yòulǐngjūn Shàngjiàngjūn Lǐ Jīnquán with a thousand cavalry to Ānzhōu to inspect,

41 Fàn Yánguāng knew that the situation was hopeless,

Sūn Ruì had advised Fàn Yánguāng to rebel six years prior.
On the day Wùyín,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn reported this,
but the Emperor did not approve.
42 Wú Tóngpíngzhāngshì Wáng Lìngmóu went to Jīnlíng to persuade Xú Gào to accept the abdication,

Wáng Huī extensively plundered Ānzhōu,

In the eighth month,
on the day Guǐsì,
the report was submitted.
Lǐ Jīnquán arrived in Ānzhōu,

Lǐ Jīnquán persuaded and exhorted them,

As Yànhé was about to die,

Although the Emperor knew Lǐ Jīnquán's true intentions,

when the door closed, the two leaves closed.

Yáng Shì was removed from the imperial genealogy.

Pú nèi fān,

Fú yòu fān.

Lí zhēn fān.

on the day Jiǎshēn,
Qí Wáng Gào ascended the imperial throne in Jīnlíng,

"Your Majesty responds to Heaven and follows the people,

Gǒng,

Although Qíqiū was Left Chancellor,

Hearing the imperial edict's wording,
"a friendship of commoners,"

on the yǐmǎo day,
Táng King of Wú Jǐngtōng changed his name to Jǐng.

is pronounced "shuài"

52On the wùchén day,
an edict added the title Deputy Marshal of All Armies of the Realm to Wúyuè King Yuán Guàn,

The Study of Differences says: The Veritable Records state:
"In the eleventh month of Tiānfú Second Year,
Yuán Guàn was promoted to Deputy Marshal and King,
and Chéng Xùn and others were sent as envoys for the bestowal of grace.
On the bǐngwǔ day of the tenth month of the Fourth Year,
due to Chéng Xùn's death at sea,
the court was suspended,
and posthumous offices were granted."
Chéng Xùn's biography states:
"In the autumn of Tiānfú Third Year, he was an envoy to Wúyuè;
on his return, he drowned."
Yuán Guàn's biography states:
"In Tiānfú Third Year, he was enfeoffed as King of Wúyuè."
It is likely that the edict was issued in the winter of the Second Year,
and Xùn and others arrived in Hángzhōu in the Third Year.
The exact year of his drowning is unknown, but the Jìn court first heard of it in the tenth month of the Fourth Year.
The Comprehensive History of Wúyuè states:
"In the fourth month of Tiānfú Second Year, an imperial edict dispatched Chéng Xùn and others to bestow upon the King the titles of Deputy Marshal and King.
On the jiǎwǔ day,
the King ascended the throne,
using the ceremonies for establishing a state,
following the precedent of Tóngguāng.
In this year, Chéng Xùn returned to the capital
and drowned at sea."
According to records, when Yuán Guàn first ascended,
he claimed Liú's dying wish and only used the rites of a regional commander.
The next year, Míngzōng enfeoffed him as King of Wú.
In the beginning of Yìngshùn, Emperor Mǐn enfeoffed him as King of Wúyuè.
Therefore, he ascended the throne as King in Tiānfú Third Year.
The Comprehensive History, however, mistakenly states that he ascended the throne after being granted the titles of Marshal and King.
This is an error.

The Emperor heard of this,
and replaced him with the honest official Jiǎ Rénzhǎo,

written as "Rénshào";

Hànjūn conspired with the Judicial Investigator Zhāng Wěi,
using flattery to deceive Jīnquán,

Lǐ Jīnquán's plan to rebel and defect to Southern Táng was thus settled.

5 In the second month,

"When emperors encounter natural disasters, they often grant general amnesties,
calling it 'cultivating virtue.'
Suppose there are two people in prison who receive an amnesty;
then the guilty one fortunately escapes,
while the innocent one harbors resentment.
This resentment rises to heaven,
which is precisely what causes disaster,
not what mitigates it."
An edict praised him.
The Emperor delighted in hearing honest words
and decreed that all officials should submit memorials,
ordering Minister of Personnel Liáng Wénjù and ten others to establish a Deliberation Office to examine them.
Those not adopted were to be kept within the palace,

Several months later,
fewer than ten people responded to the decree.
On the yǐwèi day,
another imperial rescript was issued urging them.
6 In the third month,
on the dīngchǒu day,
an imperial edict prohibited commoners from making copper vessels.
Initially,
during the Táng dynasty, there were thirty-six mints throughout the realm for casting coins.
This refers to the era of Later Táng.
In the era of Prosperous Táng,
there were over ninety copper mints throughout the realm.
All of these were abolished,
and coins became increasingly scarce.
Many commoners melted down coins to make copper vessels,
hence the prohibition.

A treasury clerk

Cáng (藏),
pronounced 'cú làng'.

A Zhūjì Dàjiàng (朱記大將)

“Your Majesty acts in accordance with Heaven and humanity,

The Lord of Táng (唐) agreed.

The Emperor accepted his words

13 On the jǐchǒu (己丑) day,
Jīnbù Lángzhōng (金部郎中) Zhāng Zhù (張鑄) memorialized:
“I have observed that among the wandering households in the countryside,
Wandering households
refer to those who do not have permanent residence and are not registered in a fixed place;
it means they drift like tumbleweeds and duckweeds,
not having a fixed dwelling,
as if floating on water.
It is not that they do not wish to live in peace,
but because their planted trees have not yet matured for ten years,
their reclaimed fields have not yet reached three qǐng (頃) (a unit of area),
and just as they seem to have established a livelihood,
they are already collected by the county authorities for labor service,
burdened with heavy taxes,
and threatened with severe punishments.
Therefore, they are forced to abandon their efforts and livelihoods

I request that from now on, if commoners reclaim five qǐng (頃) or more of land,

This was approved.

(Receiving Heaven's bright mandate, only virtue will truly prosper).

and its inscription reads: ‘Huángdì shòumìng,
yǒu dé zhě chāng (皇帝受命，有德者昌)’ (The Emperor receives the mandate, those with virtue prosper).”
The imperial edict designated
“Shòu tiān míng mìng,
wéi dé yǔn chāng (受天明命，惟德允昌)”
as the inscription.
According to the Táng Liùdiǎn (唐六典), the Shòumìng Bǎo (受命寶)

"Xù",

Guāngyuǎn personally memorialized about Wéihàn's usurpation of power;

then sent Wéihàn out to lead Ānyáng,
and Guāngyuǎn became the Protector of the Western Capital."
Now, according to the "Jìn Gāozǔ Shílù",
on the Rénchén day of the tenth month of the third year of Tiānfú,
Wéihàn and Sōng were dismissed as Privy Council commissioners.
On the Gēngzǐ day,
Guāngyuǎn first entered the court
and held an audience in the private hall;
on the Wùshēn day of the eleventh month,
Guāngyuǎn became the Protector of the Western Capital.
On the Rénshēn day of the intercalary seventh month of the fourth year of Tiānfú,
Wéihàn was sent out to be the Jíedùshǐ of Xiāngzhōu.
This indicates an error in the biographies of Chǔràng and Guāngyuǎn.
The "Jìn Shàodì Shílù" and Xuē Shǐ's biography of Sāng Wéihàn describe Guāngyuǎn's memorializing for Wéihàn to be sent out to Xiāngzhōu after Guāngyuǎn was garrisoned in Luòyáng,
which is correct.
"Now the Eastern Capital has been established,
but the ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain are all in the Western Capital.
We request they be moved to Dàliáng."
An imperial edict stated:
"For now, maintain the old arrangement."
a general amnesty was declared.
"Yánshì"
should be
"Tíngyì".
(Jiǎo Gōngxiàn killing Yáng Tíngyì is recorded in the previous year of this volume.)
Liú Xù said: Àizhōu is four hundred sixty *lǐ* east to Xiǎohuáng Jiāngkǒu, where it enters Jiāozhōu territory.
Based on the following text,
the character "公" (gōng)
should be
before
"xiàn".
(Chapter: The Yǐ-eleven-line edition indeed has
the character "公"
there.)
The Hàn ruler made his son Wàn Wáng Hóngcāo the Jìnghǎi Jíedùshǐ,
and transferred his enfeoffment to Prince of Jiāo,
stating that Jiāozhōu would be the territory for Hóngcāo to rule.
The Hàn ruler personally led his troops to garrison at Hǎimén,
providing support for them.
The Hàn ruler asked for strategy from Xiāo Yì, the Commissioner of Chongwen.
Yì said:
"The continuous rain has lasted for ten days,
and the sea route is treacherous and distant.
Wú Quán is cunning and fierce;
he should not be taken lightly.
The main army should proceed cautiously,
using many local guides,
and only then can it advance."
The ruler did not listen.
He ordered Hóngcāo to lead battleships from Bái téng Jiāng towards Jiāozhōu.
(Bái téng Jiāng should be within the territory of Fēngzhōu.
From here, they advanced to Huābù,
reaching Fēngzhōu.)
Wú Quán, based in Jiāozhōu,
led his troops to meet the enemy.
He first planted many large stakes at the mouth of the sea,
sharpened their tips,
covered them with iron,
and sent light boats to challenge the enemy during high tide, then feigned retreat.
A short while later, the tide receded,
and all the Hàn ships were obstructed by the iron stakes and could not return.
The Hàn army suffered a great defeat,
with more than half of the soldiers drowning.
Hóngcāo died.
The Hàn ruler wept bitterly,
gathered the remaining troops, and returned.
Earlier,
Hóu Róng, Assistant Editor of the Bureau of Historiography, had advised the Hàn ruler to cease military action and bring peace to the people.
When the army failed at this time,
the ruler retrospectively blamed Róng,
opened his coffin, and exposed his corpse.
Yì was the grandson of Fǎng.
Lady Péng was unsightly in appearance but had effective methods for managing the household,
and King Xīfàn of Chǔ feared her.
After her death,
Xīfàn began to indulge in sensual pleasures,
holding all-night feasts,
with no distinction between inside and outside the palace.
There was a beautiful merchant's wife,
and Xīfàn killed her husband and seized her.
The wife swore not to be disgraced
and hanged herself.
The historian recorded this event because the woman upheld her chastity,
but lost her surname,
while Mǎ Xīfàn's licentiousness and cruelty cannot be concealed.
Fàn Yánguāng entered the court from Yùnzhōu.
(Fàn Yánguāng surrendered, moved from Wèi to Yùn, and now entered the court from Yùnzhōu.)
On the *bǐngwǔ* day (33),
Mǐn Zhǔ Chǎng was made King of the State of Mǐn.
Writing "Mǐn Zhǔ" (Lord of Mǐn)
indicates that he had already usurped a great title;
writing "King of the State"
signifies a Jin appointment.
Chǎng was bestowed a scarlet robe.
The scarlet robe,
worn by the Son of Heaven,
was bestowed upon him, thus permitting his usurpation of the title.
On the *wùshēn* day,
Wáng Jìgōng, the Military Governor of Wēi Wǔ, was made Prince of Línhǎi Commandery.
The Lord of Mǐn, hearing of this,
sent the attendant officer Lín Ēn to inform the executive officials,
stating that since he had already assumed the imperial title,
he declined the imperial册命(*cèmìng*, enfeoffment order) and the envoy.
Huáng Fěng, the Grand Master of Remonstrance for Mǐn, considering the Lord of Mǐn to be dissolute and tyrannical,
bid farewell to his wife and children and entered to remonstrate.
The Lord of Mǐn wished to flog him.
Fěng said,
"If I, your subject, have been disloyal to the state through confusion,
I would die without regret;
but to be flogged for direct remonstrance,
your subject will not accept it."
The Lord of Mǐn was enraged
and demoted him to commoner status.
The Emperor was troubled by the unruly and uncontrollable Military Governor of Tiānxíong, Yáng Guāngyuǎn.
Sāng Wéihàn requested to divide the forces of Tiānxíong
and promote Guāngyuǎn to Grand Commandant, Retainer of Xījīng, and concurrently Military Governor of Héyáng.
Guāngyuǎn was consequently resentful
and secretly sent bribes to the Qìdān, pleading his case.
He maintained over a thousand personal troops
and always harbored rebellious ambitions.
Although Yáng Guāngyuǎn harbored rebellious ambitions,
as long as the Emperor and Qìdān were on good terms,
he had no opportunity to act.
But when the Emperor provoked a rift with the Qìdān,
he would call upon the Qìdān for aid and hasten disaster.
On the *xīnhài* day,
Yèdū was established at Guǎngjìn Fǔ.
When Emperor Zhuāngzōng of Táng first ascended the throne,
he established Dōngjīng at Wèizhōu,
making Wèizhōu Xīngtáng Fǔ.
Later it was renamed Yèdū.
In the fourth year of Tiānchéng (929) of Emperor Míngzōng, it was abolished.
When the Jìn received the Mandate,
Wèizhōu was made Guǎngjìn Fǔ.
Now Yèdū is re-established.
Chán and Wèi were subordinated to it.
Zhāngdé Jūn
had been established during the Zhēnmíng reign of the Liáng dynasty,
but was soon abolished during Zhāng Yàn's rebellion.
Now it is re-established.
Bó and Jì were subordinated to it.
Bèi and Bó from Tiānxíong,
and Jìzhōu from Chéngdé, were merged to form Yǒngqīng Jūn.
The Emperor, fearing the Qìdān would become a problem for future generations,
sent Liú Jìxūn, a native of Jǐ and former Cǐzhōu Administrator, to relocate Chánzhōu across the Désheng Fording,
along with Dùnqiū.
Chánzhōu was originally administered from Dùnqiū County.
Now both the prefecture and county have been relocated to Désheng.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì, Chánzhōu is 130 *lǐ* from Wèizhōu.
The Chánzhōu at Désheng,
according to Jìn discussants, is 150 *lǐ* from Wèizhōu,
a difference of 20 *lǐ*.
This is because from the northern wall of Chánzhōu to Wèizhōu is only 130 *lǐ*.
If one crosses the river from the southern wall and includes the pontoon bridge,
the distance is calculated as 150 *lǐ*.
Wáng Tíngyìn, the Defense Commissioner of Bèizhōu, was made Military Governor of Zhāngdé.
Wáng Zhōu, the Right Commander of Shénwǔ, was made Military Governor of Yǒngqīng.
Bèizhōu was initially promoted to Yǒngqīng Jūn.
He was the grandson of Chǔcún.
At the end of Táng, Wáng Chǔcún garrisoned Yìdìng.
He was a native of Yèdū.
Fàn Yánguāng repeatedly requested to retire.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
an imperial edict allowed him to retire as Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince.
He resided in Dàliáng.
He frequently attended banquets,
no different from other favored officials.
When Yánguāng rebelled,
Wáng Jǐng, the Administrator of Xiāngzhōu and a native of Yè, resisted and did not comply.
Fàn Yánguāng commanded Tiānxíong,
and Xiāngzhōu was within his jurisdiction.
Yè
was a Hàn county,
and in Táng was under Láizhōu.
Xiāng is pronounced *xìliàng fān*.
On the *wùwǔ* day,
Jǐng was made Circuit Intendant of Yàozhōu.
On the *guǐhài* day,
an imperial edict permitted both public and private minting of copper coins,
with no mixing of lead or iron.
Every ten coins were to weigh one *liǎng*.
The inscription was to be
"Tiānfú Yuánbǎo",
and the Salt and Iron Office was ordered to distribute the standard molds.
"Salt and Iron" refers to the Salt and Iron Commissioner's office.
*Xià* is pronounced *hùjià fān*.
Chóngguì, the Grand General of the Left Golden Guard, was enfeoffed as King of Zhèng,
and appointed Mayor of Kāifēng.
The Tōngjiàn often uses "enfeoffed" (*fēng*) when referring to the enfeoffment of imperial sons and nephews as kings,
but sometimes uses "established" (*lì*).
This is because the historians of the time wrote it down as it happened,
without a fixed rule.
On the *guǐhài* day,
an imperial edict, having previously allowed public and private minting,
and fearing that copper would be difficult to obtain,
permitted flexibility in weight,
as long as they were not incomplete or leaky.
Allowing private minting
was already not a sustainable policy,
much less allowing flexibility in weight.
For then people would certainly mint light coins.
How could anyone mint heavy ones?
The only concern would be that they might not be light and thin enough.
If they were extremely light and thin,
they would inevitably become incomplete or leaky.
How could such coins be used for long?
On the *xīnchǒu* day,
the abdicated Emperor of Wú passed away.
He was thirty-eight years old.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Both Xuē Shǐ and Táng Yú Lù state that Pǔ abdicated the throne and died in confinement more than a year later.
Ouyáng Shǐ only says he "died".
The Jiǔguó Zhì says:
"Pǔ was able to hand over the mandate and bring an end to his reign
without suffering the disaster of usurpation and murder,
showing deep insight."
The Shíguó Jìnián says:
"On the *xīnchǒu* day,
the people of Táng assassinated the abdicated Emperor."
As the matter is not clear,
we only say he "died" here.
The Lord of Táng, upon the death of the former ruler,
imitating the Hàn dynasty court officials who wore mourning for their ruler for a number of days instead of months, abolished court for a number of days.
Since ancient times,
among rulers who changed dynastic names, only the Lord of Táng seemed to show generosity towards the former ruler.
Judging the intention to determine the guilt,
this is like twisting a brother's arm to snatch his food.
After snatching his food,
one then pulls his arm and massages it,
saying,
"I love my brother!"
*Zhāo* is pronounced *zhíyáo fān*.
In this year,
the Lord of Táng relocated Wú Wáng Jǐng to be Qí Wáng.
Lǐ Cóngyǎn, the Military Governor of Fèngxiáng,
favored scholars but slighted military men,
and loved peasants but was strict with soldiers.
Consequently, his generals and soldiers resented him.
It happened that troops were dispatched to garrison the western border.
As soon as they left the city,
they mutinied,
burst through the gate into the city,
and plundered the markets.
They burst through the city gate and entered to plunder.
*Piāo* is pronounced *pǐmiào fān*.
The mutinous troops were defeated
and fled east,
intending to appeal to the imperial court.
When they reached Huázhōu,
Zhāng Yànzé, the Military Governor of Zhèngguó,
intercepted them
and executed them all.
