Hòuxué Tiāntái
Fourth Year of Tiānfú (Gǐhài, 939)
1. Spring,
First month,
On the *xīnhài* day,
Zhāng Cóng'ēn of Tàiyuán, Defense Commissioner of Chánzhōu, was appointed Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs.
2. Zhāng Xīchóng, Military Governor of Shuòfāng, died.
The Qiāng and Hú bandits raided,
no longer feeling fear or hesitation.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
Féng Huī, Military Governor of Yìchéng, was made Military Governor of Shuòfāng.
Tuòbá Yànchāo, the leader of the Dǎngxiàng, was the most powerful.
When Huī arrived,
Yànchāo came to congratulate him,
entering Língzhōu city from his tribe to offer congratulations.
Because Huī built a residence for him in the city,
furnishing it lavishly with clothes and trinkets,
and kept him there, not letting him go,
the territory within the frontier became peaceful.
By holding Yànchāo hostage in the city,
the various Dǎngxiàng tribes dared not raid or act violently outside,
thus peace was maintained.
3 Táng yuánchén (唐元臣) Jiāngwáng (江王) Zhīzhèng (知證) and others repeatedly submitted memorials requesting the Táng (唐) ruler to revert to the surname Lǐ (李),
and establish the Táng (唐) ancestral temple.
On the day Yǐchǒu (乙丑),
the Táng (唐) ruler granted their request.
The yuánchén (元臣) again requested to bestow an honorific title.
The Táng (唐) ruler said,
"Honorific titles are empty flattery,
and moreover, not in accordance with ancient practice."
So he did not accept it.
Thereafter, his descendants all followed his example,
not accepting honorific titles,
nor allowing maternal relatives to assist in government,
and eunuchs were not permitted to participate in affairs.
These were all things other states could not achieve.
In the second month,
on the day Yǐhài (乙亥),
the temple name of Tàizǔ (太祖) was changed to Yìzǔ (義祖).
When the Táng (唐) ruler first accepted the abdication,
he honored Xú Wēn (徐溫) as Tàizǔ (太祖);
now that he had reverted to the surname Lǐ (李),
he considered Wēn (溫) his adoptive father,
hence the temple name was changed to Yìzǔ (義祖).
On the day Jǐmǎo (己卯),
the Táng (唐) ruler mourned for his Lǐ (李) ancestors,
and he and the empress wore sackcloth and dwelled in a mourning hut,
following the rites for a primary mourning,
mourning morning and evening for a total of fifty-four days.
Jiāngwáng (江王) Zhīzhèng (知證) and Ráowáng (饒王) Zhī'è (知諤) requested to also wear sackcloth;
this was not permitted.
Zhīzhèng (知證) and Zhī'è (知諤) were both sons of Xú Wēn (徐溫).
It was like mourning for one's own parents.
The wife of Lǐ Jiànxūn (李建勳)
was Xú Wēn's (徐溫) daughter;
where power and advantage lay,
one became close even without blood kinship.
Zhǎng (長),
read as zhī liǎng fān (知兩翻).
On the day Xīnsì (辛巳),
an imperial edict instructed Qíwáng (齊王) Jǐng (璟) to thoroughly deliberate and decide on state affairs,
only reporting on military matters.
On the day Gēngyín (庚寅),
the Táng (唐) ruler changed his name to Biàn (昪).
An edict commanded all officials to discuss the rites for conjointly honoring the two lineages.
The two lineages
refer to the ancestors of the Xú (徐) and Lǐ (李) surnames.
On the day Xīnmǎo (辛卯),
Sòng Qíqiū (宋齊丘) and others proposed that Yìzǔ (義祖) should be placed in the easternmost of the seven chambers.
The Táng (唐) ruler ordered Gāozǔ (高祖) to be placed in the western chamber,
Tàizōng (太宗) next,
and Yìzǔ (義祖) next to him,
all to be permanent ancestral lords.
The yuánchén (元臣) said,
"Yìzǔ (義祖) was a feudal lord,
and should not be honored alongside Gāozǔ (高祖) and Tàizōng (太宗). We request a separate temple be built behind the main hall of the Grand Temple to offer sacrifices to him."
The Emperor said:
The Zīzhì Tōngjiàn (資治通鑑) already refers to Emperor Jìn (晉);
this character 'dì' (帝) is confused with Jìn Dì (晉帝).
This is also due to the old history of Jiāngnán (江南),
which failed to make corrections.
"I was entrusted to Yìzǔ (義祖) from a young age,
the details of which can be found in Volume 260, Qíanníng (乾寧) second year of Táng Zhāozōng (唐昭宗).
How could I have initiated this enterprise of restoration?"
The yuánchén (元臣) then dared not speak.
The Táng (唐) ruler wished to claim Wúwáng (吳王) Kè (恪) as his ancestor.
Someone said,
"Kè (恪) was executed,"
Wúwáng (吳王) Kè (恪) died during the reign of Táng Gāozōng (唐高宗),
implicated by Fáng Yí'ài (房遺愛),
which was not his crime.
The Táng (唐) ruler ordered the officials concerned to investigate the descendants of the two princes.
Since Wúwáng (吳王)'s grandson Yī (禕) had merits,
and Yī's (禕) son Xiàn (峴) was chancellor,
Xìn'ānwáng (信安王) Yī (禕) had military achievements on the border during the Xuánzōng (玄宗) era,
and Xiàn (峴) served as chancellor for Sùzōng (肅宗).
Xiàn (峴),
read as hù diǎn fān (戶典翻).
It is said that from Xiàn (峴) to his father Róng (榮) were five generations.
Their names were mostly compiled by the relevant officials.
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: The Shìzōng Shílù (世宗實錄) of Zhōu (周) and Xuē Shǐ (薛史) state that Biàn (昪) was a descendant of Yǒngwáng (永王) Lín (璘), the sixth son of Táng Xuánzōng (唐玄宗).
The Jiāngnán Lù (江南錄) states he was a great-grandson of Jiànwáng (建王) Kè (恪), the eighth son of Xiànzōng (憲宗).
Lǐ Hào's (李昊) Shǔ Hòuzhǔ Shílù (蜀後主實錄) states:
"Táng Sī Xuēwáng (唐嗣薛王) Zhīróu (知柔) served as Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Lǐngnán (嶺南),
and died in office.
His son Zhīgào (知誥) wandered to Jiānghuái (江淮),
and subsequently became an adopted son of Xú Wēn (徐溫)."
The Wú Yuè Bèishǐ (吳越備史) states:
"Biàn (昪) was originally of the Pān (潘) clan,
from Ānjí (安吉), Húzhōu (湖州).
His father was a commander of the Ānjí (安吉) fortress.
Wú (吳) general Lǐ Shénfú (李神福) attacked Yīyǐn Jūn (衣錦軍),
passing through Húzhōu (湖州),
captured Biàn (昪) and brought him back,
to be a servant.
Xú Wēn (徐溫) once visited Shénfú (神福),
appreciated Biàn's (昪) diligence and honesty,
and asked for him as an adopted son.
Because a prophecy stated, 'A carp from the Eastern Sea flies up to heaven,'
Biàn (昪) first served Shénfú (神ú),
later returned to Wēn (溫),
and thus adopted the surname Lǐ (李) to fulfill the prophecy."
Liú Shù (劉恕) believed that Biàn's (昪) reversion to the surname Lǐ (李) and attachment to the ancestors was certainly not a claim to be of the Lǐ (李) clan,
but since Wú Yuè (吳越) and the Táng (唐) people were enemies,
it was also not a true record.
Biàn (昪) was orphaned young and experienced chaos,
so his ancestral lineage was unknown;
Biàn's (昪) great-grandfather Chāo (超) and grandfather Zhì (志) had the same names as Yìzǔ's (義祖) great-grandfather and grandfather,
indicating that these were all fabrications.
It is doubted that ten generations are too few.
An official said,
"Thirty years constitute a generation.
Your Majesty was born in Wéndé (文德),
which was already fifty years ago."
Wéndé (文德)
was the reign title at the end of Táng Xīzōng's (唐僖宗) reign.
It means that fifty years had passed from the Táng (唐) ruler's birth to that year.
4 Lú Sǔn (盧損) arrived in Fúzhōu (福州).
Lú Sǔn (盧損) was sent as an envoy with imperial decrees to Mǐn (閩) in the eleventh month of the previous year,
and now he arrived in Fúzhōu (福州).
He commanded his younger brother Jìgōng (繼恭) to manage it.
He sent his Lǐbù yuánwàiláng (禮部員外郎) Zhèng Yuánbì (鄭元弼) with Jìgōng's (繼恭) memorial to enter the court with Sǔn (損) as tribute.
The Mǐn (閩) ruler was impolite to Sǔn (損).
A scholar, Lín Shěngzōu (林省鄒), privately told Sǔn (損),
"Our ruler does not serve his lord,
does not love his relatives,
does not care for his people,
does not respect his gods,
does not get along with his neighbors,
and is impolite to his guests,"
'guests' referring to Lú Sǔn (盧損).
"I will don monastic robes and flee north;
we shall meet in the 'Upper Kingdom.'"
At that time, those who claimed sovereignty in remote areas referred to the Central Plains as the 'Upper Kingdom'.
In my view,
Lín Shěngzōu (林省鄒) was also not a good scholar;
he had the ambition of Fán Ruòshuǐ (樊若水) but could not fulfill it.
5 In the third month,
on the day Gēngxù (庚戌),
the Táng (唐) ruler posthumously honored Wúwáng (吳王) Kè (恪) as Dìngzōng Xiàojìng Huángdì (定宗孝靜皇帝),
and posthumously bestowed temple names and posthumous titles upon all his ancestors from his great-grandfather downwards.
6 On the day Jǐwèi (己未),
an edict bestowed upon Guīdé Jìedùshǐ (歸德節度使) Liú Zhīyuǎn (劉知遠) and Zhōngwǔ Jìedùshǐ (忠武節度使) Dù Chóngwēi (杜重威) the concurrent title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事).
Zhīyuǎn (知遠) considered himself to have rendered service in establishing the dynasty,
while Chóngwēi (重威) rose from being a maternal relative
and had no great achievements.
He was ashamed to be treated equally with him;
'treated equally' refers to receiving the imperial edict.
Huáng Zhōng (黃忠) had merits,
yet Guān Yǔ (關羽) was still ashamed to be ranked with him;
what kind of person was Dù Chóngwēi (杜重威)?
How could Liú Zhīyuǎn (劉知遠) be willing to be treated equally with him!
The strong-willed spirit of heroes
is largely like this.
Dù (杜) submitted four memorials declining the appointment.
The Emperor was enraged
and said to Zhào Yíng (趙瑩),
"Chóngwēi (重威) is my brother-in-law.
Although Zhīyuǎn (知遠) has rendered service,
how can he firmly refuse an imperial command!
His military authority can be revoked."
Liú Zhīyuǎn (劉知遠) was then in command of all palace guard armies.
Yíng (瑩) bowed and pleaded, saying,
"When Your Majesty was in Jìnyáng (晉陽) in the past,
your troops were no more than five thousand,
yet you were attacked by over a hundred thousand Táng (唐) troops,"
the event is described in the previous volume, last year.
"If not for Zhīyuǎn's (知遠) iron will,
how could such a great undertaking have been accomplished!
Why abandon him over a minor fault!
I fear that if these words are heard outside,
it would not serve to demonstrate the magnanimity of a ruler."
The Emperor's anger then subsided,
and he ordered Duānmíng Diàn Xuéshì (端明殿學士) Hé Níng (和凝) to go to Zhīyuǎn's (知遠) residence to convey the imperial decree.
Zhīyuǎn (知遠) was terrified
and rose to receive the order.
When a ruler humbles himself to appease his minister,
the minister also repents.
To tame the strong-willed spirit of meritorious veterans,
one cannot but do so.
7 Wáng Yànzhōng, the defending general of Língzhōu, rebelled by occupying Huáiyuǎn City.
Huáiyuǎn County was subordinate to Língzhōu.
Zhào Xún's Jùmǐtújīng says: "The Táng dynasty's Huáiyuǎn Garrison was about a hundred li north of Língzhōu."
During the Sòng dynasty, the Xī Xià was powerful,
and established Xīngzhōu in that area.
Ninety li west of it was Hèlán Shān.
Yànzhōng surrendered,
but Yánzuò killed him.
The emperor was enraged and said:
"Since I ascended the throne,
I have never broken faith with anyone.
Yànzhōng had already laid down his arms and come out to surrender,
how could Yánzuò kill him?!"
Yánzuò was stripped of his title,
severely bastinadoed, and exiled.
Commentators still believed that Yánzuò should not have been spared from death.
Because by killing a surrendered man, he broke faith,
and following this, there would be no way to win over the people of Huáiyuǎn.
8 On the day Xīnyǒu,
Rénměi, the Khagan of the Huíhú, was enfeoffed as Fènghuà Kèhán.
At that time, the Huíhú had for years sent envoys to pay tribute,
hence the enfeoffment.
According to Wǔdài Huìyào: "The Huíhú, after being defeated by the Xiájiásī during the Huìchāng reign of the Táng dynasty,
fled west and settled in Gānzhōu.
In the first year of Qiānhuà of the Liáng dynasty, they sent envoys to offer tribute.
By the fourth month of the second year of Tóngguāng of the Táng dynasty,
Rénměi, their acting Khagan, sent envoys to pay tribute.
Zhèng Jì and Hé Yánsì were ordered to carry the credentials and enfeoff Rénměi as Yīngyì Kèhán.
In the eleventh month of that year,
Rénměi died,
and his younger brother Díyín succeeded him,
sending Commander Ān Qiān and others to come to court and pay tribute.
Díyín died,
and Āduōyù succeeded him,
also sending envoys to pay tribute.
In the third year of Tiānchéng,
Rén yù, their acting Khagan, sent envoys to pay tribute.
In the third month of that year,
an envoy was dispatched to enfeoff Rén Yù as Shùnhuà Kèhán.
In the third year of Tiānfú of the Jìn dynasty,
they sent envoys to pay tribute;
in the third month of the fourth year,
they again sent envoys to court,
also presenting local products."
In that month,
Xíng Dézhāo, the Grand Master of the Imperial Equipage, was ordered to carry the credentials and enfeoff him as Fènghuà Kèhán.
If based on the Huìyào,
then
"Rénměi"
should be
"Rén yù."
9 Summer,
fourth month.
Xú Zhīzhèng, Prince of Jiāng of Táng, and others requested to also adopt the surname Lǐ;
they wished to change their original surname to the imperial surname to show their closeness.
10On the day Xīnsì,
the Táng sovereign offered sacrifices at the southern suburb;
on the day Guǐwèi,
there was a great amnesty.
11Since Liáng Tàizǔ,
the emperor often discussed major military and state affairs with the Chóngzhèng and Shūmì Envoys.
Liáng discussed with the Chóngzhèng Envoy,
and Táng discussed with the Shūmì Envoy.
The Chóngzhèng Envoy's duties were the same as the Shūmì Envoy.
They merely issued imperial edicts,
lectured on precedents,
and managed civil affairs.
The emperor, learning from the tyranny of Ān Chónghuǐ during the reign of Táng Míngzōng—
details of the tyranny can be found in the Táng Míngzōng Jì.
Héng is pronounced Hù-mèng-fān—
only appointed Sāng Wéihàn concurrently as Shūmì Envoy.
When Liú Chǔràng became Shūmì Envoy,
his reports and replies often failed to satisfy the emperor—
Liú Chǔràng's seizing Sāng Wéihàn's Shūmì Envoy position is mentioned in the previous volume's previous year.
Chēng is pronounced Chǐ-zhèng-fān.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
the Privy Council was abolished,
its seal was handed over to the Central Secretariat,
and all council affairs were entrusted to the chancellors for division and judgment.
Vice-Envoy Zhāng Cóng'ēn was appointed Xuānhuī Envoy.
Zhíxuèshì and Cāngbù Lángzhōng Sītú Xǔ, and Gōngbù Lángzhōng Yán Kàn were both dismissed from their original posts.
Zhèng Qiáo's Shìzúlǜe says: "According to Dìwáng Shìjì, Shùn was Yáo's Sītú,
and his descendants took this as their surname."
Zhíxuèshì refers to the Shūmì Zhíxuèshì.
The original posts of the two men were Cāngbù and Gōngbù.
Kàn is pronounced Kǔ-hàn-fān.
Accustomed to old practices,
they always wished to restore it.
Historians say that when emperors appoint chancellors,
they should completely entrust them with governmental affairs,
and should not set up a Shūmì Envoy to divide their power.
12The emperor, seeing that the Táng ministers who had been stripped of their titles and were in the two capitals were all impoverished—
the stripping of titles of Lǐ Zhuānměi and others is seen in the first year of the previous volume.
Cuì is pronounced Qín-zuì-fān—
on the day Bǐngxū,
appointed Hán Zhāoyìn as Minister of War,
Mǎ Yìnsūn as Prince's Guest,
and Fáng Gǎo as Grand General of the Right Valiant Guard,
all retiring.
13The Mǐn sovereign was jealous of the talent and reputation of his uncle, the former Prefect of Jiànzhōu, Yánwǔ, and Minister of Revenue, Yánwàng.
The sorcerer Lín Xīng, who had a grudge against Yánwǔ,
claimed that spirits spoke, saying:
"Yánwǔ and Yánwàng will rebel."
The Mǐn sovereign did not question it further,
and had Xīng lead strong men to their residences to kill them,
along with their five sons.
The Mǐn sovereign, acting on Chén Shǒuyuán's advice,
built the Sānqīng Hall within the palace walls—
Taoists consider Shàngqīng, Yùqīng, and Tàicīng as the Sānqīng.
He played music day and night,
burned incense, offered sacrifices,
and sought elixirs of immortality.
All governmental matters, great or small,
were decided by Lín Xīng, who transmitted the "imperial command."
14On the day Wùshēn,
Prince Xīfàn of Chǔ was promoted to Tiāncè Shàngjiāngjūn,
bestowed with a seal,
and allowed to establish an administration and appoint officials.
In the fourth year of Kāipíng of the Liáng dynasty, Prince Yīn of Chǔ had already been promoted to Tiāncè Shàngjiāngjūn;
now the Jìn dynasty again bestowed this title upon his son, Xīfàn.
15On the day Xīnhài,
the Táng ruler transferred Prince Jǐngsuì of Jí to be Prince of Shòu,
and established Jǐngdá, Duke of Shòuyáng, as Prince of Xuānchéng.
16On the day Yǐmǎo,
Liáng Huáiwáng Xú Zhī'è, Commissioner of Zhènhǎi and concurrently Chancellor, died.
17The Táng people moved the clan of Rànghuáng to Tàizhōu,
naming it Yǒngníng Palace,
and guarded them very strictly.
Tàizhōu was originally Hǎilíng County of Yángzhōu.
During the Qiánzhēn reign of Wú, a Zhìzhìyuàn was established;
in the first year of Shēngyuán of Southern Táng, it was elevated to Tàizhōu.
Kǎoyì says: "Shíguó Jìnián:
'The Táng people moved the clan of Rànghuáng to Tàizhōu,
naming it Yǒngníng Palace,
and guarded them very strictly,
not daring to intermarry with the common people.
Over time, men and women paired among themselves.'
Jiāngbiǎo Zhì:
'Rànghuáng's son, at five years old,
was sent an imperial envoy to be appointed an official
and granted court attire,
and died on the same day.'
According to Táng Lièzǔ's acceptance of the abdication,
he made Rànghuáng reside in the old palace
and called himself a subject submitting memorials,
in pursuit of a reputation for benevolence and generosity.
If he hated the Yáng clan, he should have simply exterminated them;
why such a roundabout approach?
Other books have not mentioned this,
and it is unknown what source the Jìnián used,
so it is not adopted here."
He returned to Yǒngníng Palace.
Kānghuà Garrison was also a military governorship established by Wú within its jurisdiction,
or perhaps by Southern Táng;
its location is now untraceable.
On the day Yǐchǒu,
Yáng Lián, Commissioner of Pínglú and concurrently Chancellor, was made Commissioner of Kānghuà;
Lián firmly declined,
requesting to observe the full mourning period,
which was the mourning for Rànghuáng.
18The Táng sovereign was about to establish Prince Jǐng of Qí as Crown Prince,
but he firmly declined;

so he was made Grand Marshal of All Armies and Cavalry, concurrent Superintendent of the Six Armies and Guards, Grand Commandant, and Director of Affairs of the Secretariat, and Governor of Shēng and Yáng Prefectures.
Southern Táng designated Shēng Prefecture as the Western Capital
and Yáng Prefecture as the Eastern Capital,
hence the establishment of governors for these two prefectures.
19Prince Jìyán of Jiàn, Superintendent of the Six Armies and Guards of Mǐn, had gained the support of the soldiers.
The Mǐn sovereign was jealous of him,
and in the sixth month,
deprived him of his military authority,
and renamed him Jìyù;
his younger brother Jìróng
was made Superintendent of the Six Armies,
with the "Guards" character removed.
Lín Xīng's deception was discovered,
and he was exiled to Quánzhōu.
A diviner who observed portents said there would be disaster in the palace.
On the day Yǐwèi,
the Mǐn sovereign moved his residence to Chángchūn Palace.
20Autumn,
seventh month.
On the first day of the month, Gēngzǐ,
there was a solar eclipse.
21 Ān Zhòngróng, the Jìedùshǐ of Chéngdé, came from the ranks of soldiers.
He was rough and reckless by nature.
Cū [rough],
is the same as cū [rough].
He often said to people:
"The Son of Heaven in this age
is simply whoever has strong armies and sturdy horses."
Ān Zhòngróng was merely a rough and violent fellow.
Even if he were tyrannical, what could he achieve!
However, the reason he was so tyrannical
was also because he had often witnessed the events of the time,
and thus conceived ambitious aspirations.
He once held a bow and arrows and said to his attendants:
"If I can hit the dragon
on the top of the pole,
it must be the will of Heaven."
With one shot, he hit it.
Because of this, he became even more conceited.
When the Emperor dispatched Zhòngróng to replace Mì Qióng,
see Volume One, second year.
(He said:) "If Qióng does not accept the replacement,
I will assign you another prefecture.
Do not take it by force,
lest it lead to deeper trouble."
Zhòngróng, from then on, considered the Emperor timid,
and said to people:
"Mì Qióng is just a common fellow,
yet the Son of Heaven fears him.
How much more so should I, with the importance of a general and a minister,
and the multitude of my soldiers and horses!"
Most of his requests exceeded his proper station,
and were approved or denied by the ruling officials.
If approved, he would comply;
if denied, he would not.
He then gathered fugitives
and purchased warhorses,
harboring ambitious intentions.
The Emperor knew of this.
Huángfǔ Yù, the Jìedùshǐ of Yìwǔ, was related by marriage to Zhòngróng.
On the Jiǎchén day,
Yù was transferred to become Jìedùshǐ of Zhāoyì.
Zhèn and Dìng were contiguous.
Fearing they might unite and cause trouble,
he moved him farther away to separate them.
22 On the Yǐsì day,
a fire broke out in the northern palace of Mǐn,
burning almost all the palace buildings.
23 On the Wùshēn day,
Xuē Róng and others presented the compiled statutes they had finalized,
and they were put into effect.
In the third year,
Xuē Róng and others were ordered to carefully finalize the compiled statutes.
Now they are finally presented and put into effect.
Shàng,
reads shí zhǎng fān.
24 On the Bǐngchén day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Previously, all private and public minting of coins in the empire was permitted,
see Volume One, previous year.
Those that are small, weak, flawed, or thin
should all be prohibited.
Only government offices are to be permitted to mint them."

25 Yáng Guāngyuǎn, the Liúshǒu of Xījīng, memorialized that Sāng Wéihàn, the Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, had made unfair appointments and transfers, and had set up shops and market stalls in both capitals,
competing with the common people for profit.
The Emperor, having no choice,
in the intercalary month,
on the Rénshēn day,
sent Wéihàn out to become Jìedùshǐ of Zhāngdé and concurrently Shìzhōng.
26 Originally,
Wáng Wēi, the son of Wáng Chǔzhí, the Jìedùshǐ of Yìwǔ,
fled to Qìdān to escape the trouble with Wáng Dū.
The trouble with Wáng Dū
refers to the imprisonment of Chǔzhí,
see Volume Two Hundred Seventy-One, Liáng Jūn Wáng Lóngdé First Year.
Nán,
reads nǎi dàn fān.
There was a vacancy for the commander of Yìwǔ,
as Huángfǔ Yù had been moved to Lù.
Hence, Yìwǔ lacked a commander.
Shuài,
reads suǒ lèi fān.
(The Qìdān ruler said:) "I request that Wēi succeed to his father's territory,
according to the law of our dynasty."
"Our dynasty"
refers to Qìdān's self-designation.
Cháo,
reads zhí yáo fān.
(The Emperor replied:) "The law of the Central Plains dictates that one must progress through ranks, from Cìshǐ, Tuánliàn, Fángyù, up to Jìedùshǐ.
I request that Wēi be sent here,
and gradually advanced in promotion."
The Qìdān ruler was angry,
and sent another envoy to say:
"You yourself became Son of Heaven from a Jìedùshǐ.
Was there a hierarchy then?"
The Emperor feared that the trouble would escalate endlessly,
so he generously bribed Qìdān,
and also requested that Chǔzhí's elder brother's grandson, Tíngyìn, the Jìedùshǐ of Zhāngdé, be made Jìedùshǐ of Yìwǔ to satisfy their wishes.
The Qìdān's anger somewhat subsided.
27 Originally,
Mǐn Huìzōng had established the Gǒngchén and Kònghè divisions from the founder's original followers.
Mǐn Wáng Shěnzhī's temple name was Tàizǔ.
Cóng,
reads cái yòng fān;
the same below.
He further recruited two thousand strong warriors as his confidants,
called the Chénwèi Division,
whose salaries and rewards were all more generous than those of the other two divisions.
Some said that the two divisions were resentful
and planning a rebellion.
The Mǐn ruler wanted to assign them to Zhāng and Quán prefectures.
The two divisions became even more angry.
The Mǐn ruler was fond of continuous night drinking,
and forced his ministers to drink.
When drunk, he would order his attendants to look for their mistakes.
His cousin Jìlóng was executed for disrespect while drunk.
He frequently executed members of the imperial clan out of suspicion and anger.
His uncle Yánxī, the Zuǒ Púyè and Tóng Píngzhāngshì, pretended to be mad and foolish to avoid disaster.
The Mǐn ruler bestowed on him a Taoist robe
and placed him in the Wǔyí Mountains.
Wǔyí Mountains are thirty lǐ south of Chóng'ān County in Jiàn Prefecture.
Zhū Yuánhuì's preface to the Wǔyí Map says: The name of Wǔyí Jūn [Lord Wǔyí]
has been recorded since the Hàn era.
He was worshipped with dried fish,
but it is unknown what god he actually was.
Today there is a mountain in Chóng'ān named Wǔyí,
traditionally believed to be the dwelling of immortals.
Its peaks, ridges, cliffs, and valleys
are outstanding and magnificent.
The clear stream has nine bends,
flowing through it.
The two banks have sheer cliffs,
in places inaccessible to human footprints,
where often withered wooden structures are inserted into rock fissures,
used to hold boats and coffins.
The remains inside the coffins,
with pottery vessels arranged outside,
are still intact.
It is somewhat suspected that in ancient times, when the roads were impassable
and the rivers were blocked and not yet cleared,
it was a dwelling place for barbarian customs.
And the one worshipped by the Hàn was their chieftain,
who was probably a hermit.
While alive, he was revered by the masses,
and after his death, he was said to be an immortal.
There is a Taoist temple in Wǔyí Mountain.
The Mǐn ruler probably placed Yánxī in the temple.
He was confined to his private residence.
The Mǐn ruler repeatedly insulted Zhū Wénjìn of Yǒngtài and Lián Chóngyù of Guāngshān, the commanders of the Gǒngchén and Kònghè armies.
The two resented him.
Coinciding with the fire in the northern palace,
the arsonist could not be found.
The Mǐn ruler ordered Chóngyù to lead the inner and outer camp soldiers to clear away the ashes and embers.
Ten thousand men were put to work daily,
and the soldiers suffered greatly.
He also suspected Chóngyù knew of the arson plot
and wanted to execute him.
Chén Tán, an inner scholar, secretly informed Chóngyù.
On the night of Xīnsì,
Chóngyù, on duty,
led the soldiers of the two divisions to burn Chángchūn Palace
and attack the Mǐn ruler.
He sent men to welcome Yánxī from among the ruins
and shouted "Long live!"
He then summoned the outer camp soldiers to jointly attack the Mǐn ruler.
Only the Chénwèi Division resisted.
The Mǐn ruler then fled with Empress Lǐ to the Chénwèi Division.
Empress Lǐ
was Lǐ Chūnyàn.
Rú
means "to go to."
The rebel soldiers burned the Chénwèi Division.
The Chénwèi Division was defeated,
and over a thousand remaining troops escorted the Mǐn ruler and Empress Lǐ out through the northern gate,
arriving at Wútóng Lǐng.
The troops gradually scattered.
Yánxī sent his elder brother's son, Jìyè, the former Cìshǐ of Tíngzhōu, to lead troops in pursuit.
They caught up with him in a village house.
The Mǐn ruler was skilled in archery
and drew his bow, killing several people.
Soon, the pursuing troops gathered like clouds.
The Mǐn ruler knew he could not escape,
so he threw down his bow and said to Jìyè:
"Where is your loyalty as a minister!"
Jìyè replied:
"If the lord lacks the virtue of a lord,
how can a minister possess the loyalty of a minister!
The new lord
is my uncle,
the former lord
is my cousin.
Who is closer, who is more distant?"
The Mǐn ruler said nothing more.
Jìyè returned with him.
Upon reaching Tuózhuāng,
he gave him wine to drink,
and when he was drunk, he strangled him.
Empress Lǐ and all their sons, including Wáng Jìgōng, were also killed.
The remaining Chénwèi troops fled to Wúyuè.
Chǔ Wáng Mǎ Xīfàn (馬希範) first established the Tiāncè Fǔ (天策府).
In the summer of that year, he was promoted to Tiāncè Shàngjiāngjūn (天策上將軍),
and only then did he establish the Fǔ (府).
Officials such as Wèi (尉)
and Lǐngjūn Sīmǎ (領軍司馬)
were filled by his younger brothers and military officers.
He also appointed eighteen of his advisors as academicians, including Tuòbá Héng (拓跋恆), Lǐ Hónggāo (李弘皋), Liào Kuāngtú (廖匡圖), and Xú Zhòngyǎ (徐仲ǎ).
This emulated Táng Tàizōng's (唐太宗) Tiāncè Fǔ Wénxué Guǎn (天策府文學館) in appointing academicians.

Lù Zhèn's (路振) Jiǔguó Zhì (九國志) records Lǐ Duó (李鐸), Pān Qǐ (潘起), Cáo Zhuì (曹梲), Lǐ Zhuāng (李莊), Xú Mù (徐牧), Péng Jìyīng (彭繼英), Péi Háng (裴頏), Hé Zhòngjǔ (何仲舉), Mèng Xuáncuī (孟玄暉), Liú Zhāoyǔ (劉昭禹), Dèng Yìwén (鄧懿文), Lǐ Hóngjié (李弘節), Xiāo Zhū (蕭洙), Péng Jìxūn (彭繼勳), along with Tuòbá Héng (拓跋恆) and four others, totaling eighteen individuals.
Héng (恆),
is pronounced hù dēng (戶登) fan.
Liú Qíng (劉勍) and others attacked Xīzhōu (溪州).
Péng Shìchóu's (彭士愁) forces were defeated,
and he abandoned the prefecture to defend his mountain stronghold.
The stone cliffs were sheer on all four sides.
Qíng (勍) used ladders and trestles to ascend and besiege him.
Liào Kuāngqí (廖匡齊) died in battle.
Chǔ Wáng Mǎ Xīfàn (楚王馬希範) sent someone to condole with his mother.
His mother did not weep,
and told the envoy:
"Three hundred members of the Liào (廖) clan have received the King's kindness and sustenance.
For the whole clan to die in service
would not be enough to repay him,
let alone one son!
I pray the King does not dwell on this."
The King considered his mother virtuous,
and provided generously for her family.
In the twelfth month,
on the day of bǐng xū (丙戌),
the construction of Buddhist temples was prohibited.
Mǐn Wáng Wáng Xī (閩王王曦) built a new palace
and moved into it.
The northern palace of Mǐn (閩) was destroyed by fire,
so Xī (曦) rebuilt a new palace and moved into it.
That year,
Zhào Guāngyì (趙光裔), Menxià Shìláng (門下侍郎) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事) of Hàn (漢), told the Hàn Zhǔ (漢主):
"Since Empress Mǎ (馬) passed away,
the Hàn Zhǔ (漢主) has married into Chǔ (楚).
Empress Mǎ (馬) died in the first year of Táng Qīngtài (唐清泰).
The old good relations between relatives and neighbors
must not be forgotten."
Liú (劉) and Mǎ (馬) were connected by marriage,
hence "relatives";
Tán (潭) and Guǎng (廣) bordered each other,
hence "neighbors."
Hǎo (好)
is pronounced hū dào (呼到) fan.
The Hàn Zhǔ (漢主) agreed;
Chǔ (楚) also sent envoys to return the courtesies.
Guāngyì (光裔) served as chancellor of Hàn (漢) for over twenty years;
the state treasury was full,
and there was no danger on the borders.
Upon his death,
the Hàn Zhǔ (漢主) again appointed his son Sǔn (損), who was Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ (翰林學士承旨) and Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (尚書左丞), as Menxià Shìláng (門下侍郎) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事).
In spring,
in the first month,
the Emperor granted an audience to the Mǐn (閩) envoy Zhèng Yuánbì (鄭元弼) and others.
Yuánbì (元弼) said:
"Wáng Chǎng (王昶) is a ruler of barbarians;
he knows nothing of ritual and righteousness.
It is not worthy of joy if Your Majesty receives good words from him,
nor worthy of anger if Your Majesty receives bad words.
This servant has failed in his mission.
I wish to submit to execution by ax and saw to atone for Chǎng's (昶) crimes."
The Emperor pitied him.
On the day of xīn wèi (辛未),
an edict was issued to release Yuánbì (元弼) and others.
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: The Luòzhōng Jìyì (洛中紀異) says:
"After Chǎng (昶) was reprimanded by the imperial court,
he sent an envoy across the sea to Khitan (契丹),
offering confiscated goods as tribute.
Jìn Zǔ (晉祖) was then humbly serving the tribal ruler,
who issued a false edict saying: 'All gifts from the Mǐn (閩) state shall be given to Qiáo Róng (喬榮),
and their envoys are to be sent back to their own country.'
Jìn Zǔ (晉祖) dared not refuse.
Subsequently, Chǎng (昶) again sent an envoy to Khitan (契丹) to request horses,
traveling south via the Cāng (滄), Qí (齊), and Huáidiàn (淮甸) routes.
From then on, such exchanges were frequent,
and the people were universally indignant."
According to records, Chǎng (昶) was assassinated in the intercalary seventh month of the fourth year of Tiānfú (天福).
In the tenth month, Yuánbì (元弼) and others arrived in the capital and were imprisoned.
How could Chǎng (昶) have known this and informed Khitan (契丹)!
This account is not accepted now.
Chǔ's (楚) Liú Qíng (劉勍) and others, taking advantage of a strong wind,
used fire arrows to burn Péng Shìchóu's (彭士愁) stronghold and attacked it.
Shìchóu (士愁) led his subordinates and fled into the deep mountains of Jiǎng (獎) and Jǐn (錦).
On the day of yǐ wèi (乙未),
he sent his son Shīhào (師暠) to lead the various chieftains to present the seals of Xī (溪), Jǐn (錦), and Jiǎng (獎) three prefectures,
requesting to surrender to Chǔ (楚).
This provides context for Péng Shīhào's (彭師暠) ultimate loyalty to the Mǎ (馬) clan.
Shuài (帥)
is pronounced as lǜ (率).
In the second month,
on the day of gēng xū (庚戌),
Ān Yànwēi (安彥威), Beīdū Liúshǒu (北都留守) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事), came to court.
Beīdū (北都) had been established in Tàiyuán (太原) since the Later Táng (後唐) dynasty.
"What I value are trust and righteousness.
Formerly, Khitan (契丹) saved me with righteousness;
I now repay them with trust.
I hear their demands are ceaseless.
If you can humble yourself and serve them,
it deeply pleases my intention."
He replied:
"Your Majesty, for the sake of the common people,
still uses humble words and rich gifts to serve them.
What humbling is there for your servant to do!"
The Emperor was pleased.
Liú Qíng (劉勍) led his troops back to Chángshā (長沙).
Chǔ Wáng Mǎ Xīfàn (楚王馬希範) relocated Xīzhōu (溪州) to a more convenient location.
"Convenient location" means
moving it closer to the Chǔ (楚) border,
making it easier to control.
He appointed Liú Qíng (劉勍) as Jǐnzhōu Cìshǐ (錦州刺史).
From then on, all the barbarians submitted to Chǔ (楚).
Xīfàn (希範) called himself a descendant of Fúbō (伏波).
Mǎ Yuán (馬援) of Hàn (漢) was Fúbō Jiāngjūn (伏波將軍).
A pillar twelve feet tall,
six feet of which were buried in the ground,
with an inscription and oath on it,
was erected in Xīzhōu (溪州).
Today, there is a bronze column about one li southwest of Huìxīchéng (會溪城) in Chénzhōu (辰州),
which was erected by Mǎ Xīfàn (馬希範).
The inscription was written by Lǐ Gāo (李皋), an academician of the Tiāncè Fǔ (天策府).
Yáng Lián (楊璉), Jiédu Shǐ (節度使) and Zhongshū Lìng (中書令) of Táng Kānghuà (唐康化), returned after visiting Pínglíng (平陵).
Pínglíng (平陵)
was presumably the tomb of Yáng Lián's (楊璉) father, Ràng Huáng (讓皇).
Huán (還)
is pronounced cóng xuān (從宣) fan,
and also as written.
He was heavily drunk
and died in his boat.
This was caused by the Táng Zhǔ (唐主).
Lù Zhèn's (路振) Jiǔguó Zhì (九國志) says: Yáng Lián (楊璉) visited the tomb,
reached Zhúxiǎo Kǒu (竹篠口),
moored his boat, got heavily drunk,
and died overnight.
He was posthumously enfeoffed and given the posthumous title Hóngnóng Jìng Wáng (弘農靖王).
Because the Yáng (楊) clan's ancestors were enfeoffed in that prefecture, he was posthumously enfeoffed as Hóngnóng Wáng (弘農王),
with the posthumous title Jìng (靖).
After Mǐn Wáng Wáng Xī (閩王王曦) ascended the throne,
he became arrogant, licentious, cruel, and tyrannical,
suspicious of his relatives,
and often sought out old grievances.
His younger brother, Yánzhèng (延政), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Jiànzhōu (建州), repeatedly advised him by letter.
Xī (曦) was enraged and
replied with an abusive letter.
He sent his close official Yè Qiáo (業翹) to supervise the Jiànzhōu (建zhōu) army.
Shǐ Zhào (史炤) says:
"Yè (業)"
should be
According to Fēngsú Tōng (風俗通), Hàn (漢) had Liáng Lìng Yè Fèng (梁令鄴鳳).
Jiān (監)
is pronounced gǔ xián (古銜) fan.
It is recorded that northwestern Fúzhōu (福州) borders Jiànzhōu (建zhōu).
The Mǐn Zhǔ (閩主) probably established the Nánzhèn Jūn (南鎮軍) at the border between Fú (福) and Jiàn (建) two prefectures,
controlling the vital passes for traffic.
Therefore, after this, Wáng Yánzhèng (王延政) attacked Nánzhèn (南鎮) and all the border guards in the western outskirts of Fúzhōu (福zhōu) were routed.
From this, the brothers accumulated mutual suspicion and hatred.
One day,
Qiáo (翹) and Yánzhèng (延政) disagreed on a matter.
Qiáo (翹) rebuked him, saying:
"Are you rebelling!"
Yánzhèng (延政) was furious
and wanted to execute Qiáo (翹).
Qiáo (翹) fled to Nánzhèn (南鎮).
Yánzhèng (延政) dispatched troops to attack it
and defeated its garrison.
Qiáo (翹) and Hàn Chóng (漢崇) fled to Fúzhōu (福州),
and all the border guards in the western outskirts were routed.
In the second month,
Xī (曦) sent Pān Shīkuí (潘師逵) and Wú Xíngzhēn (吳行真), Tǒngjūnshǐ (統軍使), leading forty thousand troops to attack Yánzhèng (延政).
Shīkuí's (師逵) army encamped west of Jiànzhōu (建zhōu) city,
and Xíngzhēn's (行真) army encamped south of the city.
Both set up camps obstructed by water
and burned the houses outside the city.
Yánzhèng (延政) sought help from Wúyuè (吳越).
On the day of rén xū (壬戌),
Wúyuè Wáng Qián Yuánguàn (吳越王錢元瓘) sent Yǎng Rénquán (仰仁詮), Níngguó Jiédu Shǐ (寧國節度使) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事).
Xuānzhōu Níngguó Jūn (宣州寧國軍) at that time belonged to Nán Táng (南唐);
Yǎng Rénquán (仰仁詮) as Wúyuè (吳越) envoy only held a nominal title,
and many such cases occurred among the various states at that time.
Yǎng (仰)
is a surname;
the Hè Shì Xìngyuàn (何氏姓苑) has this surname.
Premier Lín Dǐng (林鼎) remonstrated,
but was not listened to.
In the third month,
on the day of wù chén (戊辰),
Shīkuí (師逵) divided three thousand troops,
sending Cài Hóngyì (蔡弘裔), Dūjūnshǐ (都軍使), to lead them in battle.
Yánzhèng (延政) sent his generals Lín Hànchè (林漢徹) and others to defeat them at Cháshān (茶山),
beheading over a thousand.
Cháshān (茶山) is twenty-five li east of Jiànzhōu (建zhōu),
now also called Fènghuáng Shān (鳳凰山);
the Beǐyuàn Chábèi (北苑茶焙) is located there.
7 Ān Yánwēi and Wáng Jiànlì both requested retirement,
but it was not granted.
On the day Xīnwèi,
Liú Zhīyuǎn, the Jiedushi of Guīdé, the Supreme Commander of the Imperial Guards of Cavalry and Infantry, and a Grand Councilor, was made the Grand Administrator of Yèdū.
Yánwēi was transferred to be the Jiedushi of Guīdé
and additionally granted the title of Attendant Counselor.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
Jiànlì was transferred to be the Jiedushi of Zhāoyì
and elevated to the rank of Prince of Hán.
As Jiànlì was from Liáozhōu,
Liáozhōu and Qìnzhōu were detached and placed under Zhāoyì.
Since the Táng dynasty, Liáozhōu and Qìnzhōu had always belonged to the Hedong Jiedushi.
Qìn,
read as "wǔ zhèn" (午鴆).
8 Ān Cóngjìn, the Jiedushi of Shānnán Dōngdào and a Grand Councilor, relied on the formidable defenses of
Xiāngyáng, which possessed the strategic advantage referred to by Qū Wán as
"Fāngchéng as its rampart
and the Hànshuǐ as its moat."
Thus, Ān Cóngjìn relied on these to defy the imperial court.
He seized tribute goods from Húnán.
These Húnán tribute goods
were those presented by Mǎ Xīfàn.
He increased his armed forces.
Wáng Lìngqiān, the Metropolitan Commander of the Personal Retainers, and Pān Zhīlín, an Attendant Officer, remonstrated,
but both were killed.
When Wáng Jiànlì was transferred to Lùzhōu,
the emperor sent a messenger to ask him,
"I am reserving Qīngzhōu for you."
Qīngzhōu was the Pínglújūn.
Cóngjìn replied,
"If Qīngzhōu were moved to Hànnán."
Xiāngyáng was south of the Hànshuǐ.
The emperor did not rebuke him.
The emperor was not one to be lenient for the sake of peace;
rather, he reflected internally with displeasure on how he had gained control of the Central Plains,
and considered how he might secure it.
Apprehensive,
he therefore treated with humility and appeased all the rebellious regional commanders.
9 On the day Dīngchǒu,
Wáng Yánzhèng recruited over a thousand death-defying warriors.
They crossed the water by night
and secretly infiltrated Pān Shīkuí's camp.
Taking advantage of the wind, they set fires.
The drums and shouts from the city walls responded to them.
Chén Huì of Jiàn'ān, the Commander of the Battle Boats, killed Shīkuí.
Jiàn'ān
was the land of Hàn Yěxiàn.
Wú established Jiàn'ānxiàn.
During the Táng, it was under Jiànzhōu.
On the day Wùyín,
(Yánzhèng) led his troops to attack Wú Xíngzhēn's stronghold.
The Jiàn people had not yet crossed the water,
but Xíngzhēn and his officers abandoned the camp and fled,
with ten thousand casualties.
Yánzhèng, emboldened by victory, captured the two cities of Yǒngpíng and Shùnchāng.
Wú divided Jiàn'ān and established Nánpíngxiàn.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn changed it to Yánpíngxiàn.
Wáng Shěnzhī established Yánpíngzhèn.
His son Yánhàn changed its name to Yǒngpíngzhèn.
The seat of Nánjiànzhōu is now that very place.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states
that Nánjiànzhōu administered Shùnchāngxiàn,
which was 180 li west of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Shùnchāngxiàn was originally the Xiàoxiāng area of Jiàn'ānxiàn.
In the third year of Yǒng'ān of Wú, Jiānglèxiàn was established.
During the Suí, it was merged into Shàowǔ.
During the Táng, it was re-established.
In the second year of Jǐngfú, Jiāngshuǐzhèn was also established,
renamed Yǒngshùnchǎng,
and soon after made Shùnchāngxiàn.
10 In summer,
in the fourth month,

Zhào Jìliáng, the Grand Tutor of Shǔ, concurrently Secretary of the Department of the Palace Gate, and a Grand Councilor, requested to divide the administration of the Three Judicial Offices with Wú Zhāoyì, Secretary of the Department of the Palace Gate and a Grand Councilor, and Zhāng Yè, Secretary of the Department of the Chancellery and a Grand Councilor.
On the day Guǐmǎo,
the Ruler of Shǔ ordered Jìliáng to administer the Ministry of Revenue,
Zhāoyì to administer the Salt and Iron Monopoly,
and Yè to administer the Department of Finance.
11 On the day Gēngxū,
Mǎ Quánjié, formerly the Jiedushi of Hénghǎi, was made the Jiedushi of Ānyuǎn.
This was to replace Lǐ Jīnquán.
12 On the day Jiǎzǐ,
Hóngzūn, the Filial and Virtuous Heir Apparent of Wúyuè, passed away.
13 Wúyuè forces under Yǎng Rénquán reached Jiànzhōu.
Wáng Yánzhèng, knowing that the Fúzhōu troops had already been defeated and retreated,
presented beef and wine to comfort them
and requested them to return to their homeland.
Rénquán and others did not comply,
instead encamping northwest of the city.
Yánzhèng was afraid.
Seeing Yǎng Rénquán pressing the city and encamping,
with the intention of taking Jiànzhōu,
he was therefore afraid.
The Prince of Mǐn appointed Wáng Jìyè, the Prefect of Quánzhōu, as the Commander-in-Chief of the Campaigning Army,
leading twenty thousand troops to relieve them.
He also sent a letter to rebuke Wúyuè,
which was a frank rebuke by attributing the fault.
It happened that there was prolonged rain.
The Wúyuè forces
ran out of provisions.
In the fifth month,
Yánzhèng dispatched troops to attack,
severely defeating them,
capturing and beheading tens of thousands.
On the day Guǐwèi,
Rénquán and others fled by night.
14 Hú Hànjūn, having already disobeyed the imperial edict by not appearing at the court,
also heard that Jiǎ Rénzhǎo's two sons intended to appeal to the court.
Jiǎ Rénzhǎo's death is mentioned in the second year of the previous volume.
Cháo,
read as "zhí yáo" (直遙).
Hànjūn deceived Jīnquán, saying,
"The Presenting Official sent someone by express route to say
(The Presenting Official
refers to the chief clerk of the Ānyuǎnjūn's Presenting Office in Dàliáng.)
that an investigation into Jiǎ Rénzhǎo's death
would surely reveal ulterior motives."
Jīnquán was greatly alarmed.
Hànjūn then persuaded Jīnquán to defy the imperial order
and surrender to Táng.
Jīnquán agreed.
On the day Bǐngxū,
the emperor, hearing of Jīnquán's rebellion,
ordered Mǎ Quánjié to lead troops from Biàn, Luò, Rǔ, Zhèng, Shàn, Sòng, Chén, Cài, Cáo, Pú, Shēn, and Táng to suppress him.
This meant that all the troops from the various prefectures south of the Yellow River and west of the Jì River were dispatched.
Shàn,
pronounced "shàn."
Pú,
pronounced "pú."
Shěn Huī
was Shěn Qí's elder brother.
Lǐ Jīnquán dispatched the investigating officer Zhāng Wěi to present a memorial requesting surrender to Táng.
The Ruler of Táng sent Lǐ Chéngyù and Duàn Chǔgōng, the commanders of the Èzhōu garrison, with three thousand troops to meet him.
15 The Ruler of Táng sent Shàng Quángōng, the Attendant of the Guest Department, to Mǐn
to mediate between Mǐn ruler Xī and Wáng Yánzhèng.
In the sixth month,
Yánzhèng sent his tooth-general and a slave girl carrying an oath letter and an incense burner to Fúzhōu,
where they swore an oath with Xī at Xuānlíng.
In ancient times, when swearing oaths,
a pit was dug for sacrifices,
the written oath was placed on top,
and blood was smeared to appeal to Heaven, Earth, spirits, and deities.
For ancestral temple sacrifices,
only burning mugwort and combining fragrant spices were used.
As for libations, fresh spirits were poured,
and food was seasoned with pepper.
Xún Qīng spoke of "fragrant like pepper and orchid."
Han empresses' chambers were called "pepper chambers,"
taking their name from the fragrance.
Court officials held chicken-tongue incense when presenting memorials.
The Xījīng Zájì records that the skillful artisan Dīng Huǎn of Cháng'ān made "incense burners for placing under the clothes."
Liú Xiàng inscribed "Bóshān burners."
Han official records state that secretarial officials were given two female scribes to hold incense burners and burn incense.
None of these were used to serve spirits and deities.
The Hàn Wǔ Nèichuán records the descent of Xīwángmǔ,
burning many types of "infant incense."
It is suspected that these are all later additions and fabrications.
Fàn Yè of the Sòng dynasty wrote "Incense Preface,"
detailing various incenses to satirize contemporary people;
yet when he compiled the Hòuhànshū,
he also did not record the Han people's practice of burning incense.
It is suspected that the custom of offering incense to deities
originated in the Wèi and Jìn dynasties or later.
Chéng Dàchāng's Yǎnfánlù states: Emperor Wǔ of Liáng was the first to use agarwood for sacrifices to Heaven;
it was not used in ancient times.
For sacrifices to Earth, "shànghé incense" was used.
The note states: As Earth is close to humans,
various fragrances should be added,
meaning various incenses were combined,
not just one type of incense.
Mǐn ruler Lín's grand proclamation was to honor the tomb of his father, Shěnzhī, as Xuānlíng.
16th day, guǐmǎo.
Táng Lǐ Chéngyù and others arrived at
Ānzhōu.
That evening,
Lǐ Jīnquán led several hundred men from his command to the Táng army.
His singing girls, concubines, and wealth were all seized by Chéngyù.
Chéngyù entered and occupied Ānzhōu.
On the jiǎchén day,
Mǎ Quánjié advanced from Yìngshān to Dàhuàzhèn.
Yìngshān,
anciently Yìngguó,
during the Hàn dynasty belonged to Suíxiàn county;
the Liáng dynasty separated Suíxiàn and established Yǒngyángxiàn county;
the Suí dynasty renamed it Yìngshān,
and during the Táng dynasty it belonged to Ānzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: it is 180 lǐ north of the prefecture.
Dàhuàzhèn belonged to Yìngshānxiàn county.
They were greatly defeated.
Chéngyù plundered Ānzhōu and fled south.
Quánjié entered Ānzhōu.
On the bǐngwǔ day,
Ān Shěnhuī pursued and defeated the Táng troops at Huánghuāgǔ.
Duàn Chǔgōng was killed in battle.
On the dīngwèi day,
Shěnhuī again defeated the Táng troops in Yúnmèngzé.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Ānzhōu's Ānlùxiàn county has Yúnmèngzhèn town.
Today, 50 lǐ south of Ānlùxiàn county is Yúnmèngzé.
Sòng Bái said: Ānzhōu's Yúnmèngxiàn county was originally Hān Ānlùxiàn county's territory.
In the 16th year of Dàtǒng of the Later Wèi, Yúnmèngxiàn county was established at the ancient city of Yúnchéng.
Defeated,
read bǔmài.
The Táng general Zhāng Jiànchóng occupied Yúnmèngqiáo to resist,
so Shěnhuī returned.
and sent the Supervising Military Affairs Dù Guāngyè and 507 others to Dàliáng.
The Emperor said:
"What crime have these people committed!"
He bestowed horses and equipment upon them all and sent them home.
Initially,
when Lú Wénjìn fled to Wú,
the event is detailed in Volume 280, 1st year.
He gave orders not to enter Ānzhōu city,
but to arrange troops outside the city,
await Wénjìn's exit,
act as his rear guard on the return,
and not engage in plunder.
From Lú Wénjìn until this point,
it all refers to the Táng ruler's affairs when he was allied with Wú.
Rear guard,
read dīngliàn.
Plunder,
read pǐmiào.
He instructed them like Quán'ēn;
Chéngyù was greedy and plundered,
fought with the Jìn army and was defeated,
losing 4,000 men.
The Táng ruler grieved for several days,
considering that his instructions had not been properly heeded.
When Dù Guāngyè and others arrived in Táng,
the Táng ruler, seeing that they had disobeyed orders and been defeated,
did not accept them,
but sent them back north of the Huái River,
and sent a letter to the Emperor saying:
"Border officials were greedy for merit,
and seized the opportunity to occupy the stronghold."
He also said:
"Military law and court regulations,
both sides cannot allow this."
Meaning, if judged by military law,
then those who lost troops must be executed here,
and those who raided the border cannot be pardoned there;
if judged by court regulations,
then neither state can tolerate their presence at court.
Court,
read zhíyáo.
The envoy was about to cross the Huái from Tóngxū.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Sùzhōu's Qíxiàn county has Tónglúzhèn town.
From Tónglú southward,
upon reaching Guōkǒu, one crosses the Huái.
The Jīnrén Jiāngyù Tú states: Tóngxū is in Sùzhōu's Línhuànxiàn county.
Then he returned.
The Emperor granted official positions to all the Táng generals,
made their soldiers the Xiǎnyì Dū,
and ordered the former general Liú Kāng to lead them.
Former general,
refers to those who rose with him from Jìnyáng.
Your servant Guāng says:
Those who disobeyed orders were the generals; the soldiers merely followed the generals' commands,
so what crime have they committed!
To accept them and execute their generals to apologize to the enemy,
to mourn the soldiers and comfort them,
that would have been appropriate.
Why abandon the people to aid an enemy state!
17th day. The Táng ruler sent a eunuch to sacrifice at Lúshān.
Lúshān is in Jiāngzhōu's Xúnyángxiàn county.
South of the mountain is the Táng Dūchāngxiàn county,
north of the mountain is the Táng Xúnyángxiàn county.
Dūchāng is now Nánkāngjūn,
15 lǐ north of the military city is Lúshān.
He comforted him, saying:
"Your journey on this occasion was very pure and clean."
The eunuch replied:
"Since receiving the imperial edict, your servant has eaten only vegetables until now."
The Táng ruler said:
"On such-and-such a day, you bought fish from such-and-such a place for stew,
and on such-and-such a day, you bought meat for a dish.
Why do you say you ate only vegetables?"
The eunuch was ashamed and submitted.
At the end of the year, the granary officials presented a surplus of over ten thousand shí.
The Táng ruler said:
"Income and expenditure have their proper limits.
If not for exploiting the people and deducting from the army,
how could there be a surplus!"
18th day. Autumn,
7th month.
Mǐn Lord Xī fortified the western wall of Fúzhōu in preparation for the Jiàn people.
He also registered commoners as monks.
Many commoners became monks to avoid heavy taxes.
A total of 11,000 people were registered.
Alas,
if registering monks truly brought merits and benefits,
then the Mǐn state might still exist today.
19th day, yǐchǒu.
The Emperor bestowed silk upon Zhèng Yuánbì and others,
and sent them back.
Sent them back to Mǐn.
He had imprisoned them in the 10th month of the previous year;
now he released and sent them away.
20th day. When Lǐ Jīnquán rebelled,
the Ānzhōu cavalry and infantry deputy commander Sāng Qiān, the Wēihé commander Wáng Wànjīn, and Chéng Yànwēn refused to follow and died.
The cavalry and infantry commander Páng Shǒuróng mocked their foolishness,
to curry favor with Jīnquán.
On the jǐsì day,
an edict posthumously granted official titles to Jiǎ Rénzhǎo and Sāng Qiān and others,
and an envoy was sent to execute Shǒuróng in Ānzhōu.
Lǐ Jīnquán arrived in Jīnlíng,
but the Táng ruler treated him very poorly.
Lǐ Jīnquán was deluded by traitorous generals,
betrayed his parents' state,
and entrusted himself to a foreign land;
it was fitting that he was treated poorly.
21st day, dīngsì.
The Táng ruler established Qí Wáng Jǐng as crown prince,
also Grand Marshal,
and in charge of the Department of State Affairs.
22nd day. The retired Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince, Fàn Yánguāng, requested to return to his private residence in Héyáng.
Fàn Yánguāng served the Táng dynasty and previously had a private residence in Héyáng.
Yánguāng traveled with heavy baggage.
The Western Capital's Resident Commissioner Yáng Guāngyuǎn also held the post of Héyáng's overseer.
He coveted Yánguāng's wealth,
and also feared him as a future threat to his descendants.
When Fàn Yánguāng surrendered from Guǎngjìn,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn was the Marshal,
and must have bullied him in some way,
hence he feared him as a future threat to his descendants.
"Yánguāng is a rebel subject,
not settling in Biàn or Luò but going to an outer dependency.
I fear he might escape to an enemy state;
he should be eliminated early!"
The Emperor did not permit it.
Guāngyuǎn requested an edict ordering Yánguāng to reside in the Western Capital.
This was granted.
Guāngyuǎn sent his son Chéngguì with armed soldiers to surround Yánguāng's residence,
forcing him to commit suicide.
Alas!
Wealth burdens people to such an extent.
Mì Qióng used this to kill Dǒng Wēnqí's family,
Fàn Yánguāng in turn used this to kill Mì Qióng,
and Yáng Guāngyuǎn again used this to kill Fàn Yánguāng,
yet Guāngyuǎn also ultimately could not escape.
Wealth truly burdens people to such an extent!
"The Son of Heaven is above,
he granted me an iron certificate,
promising me immunity from death."
Granted an iron certificate,
see Volume 3, 3rd year.
On the jǐwèi day,
Chéngguì, with drawn blades, forced Yánguāng onto a horse.
Upon reaching Fúliáng,
he pushed him into the river.
Guāngyuǎn reported that Yánguāng had committed suicide by drowning.
The Emperor knew the truth,
but, intimidated by Guāngyuǎn's power,
dared not question him;
he suspended court for Yánguāng
and posthumously granted him the title of Grand Preceptor.
23rd day. Táng Qí Wáng Jǐng firmly declined the position of Crown Prince.
Holding the position of eldest son of the legitimate consort, he should have been Crown Prince; declining it was not the way to secure the hopes of officials and commoners.
On the yǐchǒu day,
the Táng ruler permitted it,
and issued an edict to all within and without the court to offer congratulatory memorials according to the rites for a Crown Prince.
24th day, dīngmǎo.
Hé Níng, Hanlin Academician, Acting Chief, and Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Revenue, was appointed Minister of the Central Secretariat and Co-acting Grand Chancellor.
25th day, jǐsì.
Liú Zhīyuǎn, Resident Commissioner of Yèdū, entered court.
In the second month of this year,
Liú Zhīyuǎn replaced Ān Yànwēi in garrisoning Wèizhōu.
On the 26th day of the Xīnwèi month,
Lǐ Sōng presented a memorial:
"The grain in the granaries of various prefectures,
has a considerable surplus beyond what is accounted for in the ledgers."
The term "ledgers"
refers to the accounts drawn up annually and submitted to the Three Departments.
Granary officials profit from the difference in measurements when receiving grain,
and then privately appropriate that profit when issuing it;
this is a corrupt practice perpetuated by officials in collusion,
and it continues to this day.
One can only know the surplus after measuring it,
but the process of measuring itself is prone to much corruption.
I suspect Lǐ Sōng also presented this memorial because people were already talking about it.
"Illegally taxing the populace
is a crime equivalent to perverting the law.
Granary officials should be spared death,
but severely punished."
I do not know what kind of severe punishment was meant at the time;
ultimately, it was spoken of but could not be implemented.
On the 27th, Hanlin Academician Lǐ Hàn
was frivolous,
and frequently made mistakes due to drink.
The emperor disliked him.
On the Bǐngzǐ day,
he was dismissed as Hanlin Academician,
and his duties were merged with those of the Secretariat Drafters.
Hàn
was Tāo's younger brother.
On the 28th, Yáng Guāngyuǎn came to court.
The emperor wanted to move him to another command,
and said to Guāngyuǎn:
"In the campaign of encircling Wèi,
all your subordinates rendered meritorious service,
but have not yet been rewarded."
For "encircling Wèi," see the second and third years of the previous volume.
Consequently, several of his generals and officers were made regional governors.
This was to divide Yáng Guāngyuǎn's faction and weaken his influence.
On the Jiǎshēn day,
Guāngyuǎn was transferred to be Jìedùshǐ of Pínglú,
and promoted to Prince of Dōngpíng.
At the beginning of Kāiyùn,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn indeed rebelled from Pínglú.
On the 29th, in winter,
the tenth month,
on the Dīngyǒu day,
Wúyuè King Qián Yuánquàn was given the titles of Generalissimo of All Armies Under Heaven and Grand Mentor.
On the 30th, on the Rén'yín day,
the Southern Táng granted a general amnesty.
An edict was issued that no memorial from within or outside the court should contain the characters
"Ruì"
or
"Shèng";
offenders would be prosecuted for disrespect.
The diviner Sūn Zhìyǒng, seeing four stars gathered in Dǒu, predicted disaster in the corresponding astronomical region,
and advised the Táng ruler to tour the Eastern Capital,
specifically suggesting a tour to Jiāngdū.
On the Yǐsì day,
the Táng ruler ordered Qí King Lǐ Jǐng to supervise the state.
Chén Jué, Deputy Commissioner of Guāngzhèng and Junior Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud, out of personal grudge, memorialized that Chǔ Rénkuī, the Prefect of Tàizhōu, was greedy and cruel.
Tàizhōu
was the Hǎilíng Granary territory of the Wú Kingdom during the Hàn dynasty;
in the Eastern Jìn, Hǎilíng Commandery was established by dividing Guǎnglíng;
in the early Táng, Wú Prefecture was established,
and Hǎilíng County was renamed Wúlíng County;
in the seventh year of Wǔdé, Wú Prefecture was abolished,
and it reverted to Hǎilíng County;
the Southern Táng elevated it to Tàizhōu.
On the Bǐngwǔ day,
Rénkuī was dismissed and made Commander of the Imperial Escort.
Jué then began to wield power.
This laid the groundwork for Chén Jué to disrupt the Táng government.
On the Gēngxū day,
the Táng ruler departed from Jīnlíng;
on the Jiǎyín day,
he arrived in Jiāngdū.
On the 31st, Mǐn King Wáng Xī sent a memorial through merchants to clear his name;
stating that he had never assumed a grand title.
The one who assumed a grand title
was Wáng Chǎng.
On the Jiǎshēn day,
Xī was made Jìedùshǐ of Wēiwǔ,
concurrently Grand Mentor,
and enfeoffed as King of Mǐn.
On the 32nd, the Táng ruler wished to reside permanently in Jiāngdū,
but due to the freezing of the water,
grain transport became insufficient,
so he returned.
In the twelfth month,
on the Bǐngshēn day,
he arrived in Jīnlíng.
On the 33rd, Zhāng Yánhàn, the Táng Right Grand Mentor concurrently Junior Minister of the Department of the Palace Gate and Grand Councillor, passed away.
On the 34th, in this year,
Zhào Sǔn, the Hàn Junior Minister of the Department of the Palace Gate and Grand Councillor, passed away.
Nánchāng King Mǎ Dìngbǎo, Jìedùshǐ of Níngyuǎn, was made Junior Minister of the Secretariat and Grand Councillor,
but he also passed away within a year.
On the 35th, initially,
the emperor ceded the region north of Yànmén to the Khitans as a bribe.
See the first year of volume 280.
Suffering from their greed and cruelty,
they wished to return to China.
Ān Chóngróng, Jìedùshǐ of Chéngdé, further enticed them,
whereupon the Tǔyùhùn, leading over a thousand households, defected from Wǔtái.
Ōuyáng Xiū said: The Tǔyùhùn originally lived in Qīnghǎi.
During the Zhìdé reign of the Táng, they were attacked by the Tubo,
and their tribes scattered.
Those who submitted to the Táng were settled in Héxī.
In the late Táng,
their leader Hèlián Duó became Jìedùshǐ of Dàtóng,
but was defeated by Jìn King Lǐ Kèyòng.
The tribes further dwindled,
scattering in the vicinity of Wèizhōu.
I observe that during the time of Táng Gāozōng,
the Tǔyùhùn were defeated by the Tubo,
abandoned Qīnghǎi, and migrated inland.
By the Zhìdé reign,
there were no longer Tǔyùhùn in Qīnghǎi.
As the Tubo expanded eastward to Hélǒng,
the Tǔyùhùn again moved eastward,
settling between Yúnzhōu and Wèizhōu.
Their defection from Wǔtái
likely means they took the Fēihú pass to Zhènzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: The Tǔyùhùn were called Tuìhùn,
likely due to a rapid pronunciation.
After Shènglì,
the Tubo conquered Ānlèzhōu,
and their people migrated eastward,
scattering in Shuòfāng.
In the first year of Kāichéng, Hèlián Duó brought his three thousand households to Fēngzhōu.
Emperor Wénzōng ordered Liú Miǎn, Jìedùshǐ of Zhèníwǔ, to settle them in good land.
When Miǎn moved his command to Hédōng,
they then scattered in the area of Chuān,
and by phonetic corruption were called Tuìhùn.
Thereafter, the Bái clan of Tǔyùhùn were all of Hèlián's tribe.
Hèlián Duó, having been driven out by Lǐ Kèyòng,
returned to Lǐ Kuāngchóu in Yōuzhōu,
and subsequently settled in the Wèizhōu area.
The tribes were established generation by generation,
but their surname was not constant.
After Zhuāngzōng, Bái Chéngfú became a Grand Governor.
He established a stockade relying on the North Mountains and North Stone Gate,
and was granted the plaque "Níngshuò Prefecture,"
and the Grand Governor was made Jìedùshǐ.
Envoys were sent to reprimand the emperor for harboring rebels.
The Khitans' constant reproaches
laid the groundwork for the emperor's eventual depression and death.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the Bǐngyín day,
the emperor dispatched Palace Attendant Zhāng Chéng with two thousand soldiers to search for the Tǔyùhùn in the mountain valleys of Bīng, Zhèn, Xīn, and Dài prefectures,
and drive them back to their former homeland.
2. Wáng Yánzhèng fortified Jiànzhōu,
with a circumference of twenty *lǐ*.
He requested from Mǐn King Wáng Xī
to designate Jiànzhōu as Wēiwǔ Command,
and himself to be Jìedùshǐ.
Xī, noting that Wēiwǔ Command was Fúzhōu,
instead designated Jiànzhōu as Zhèn'ān Command,
made Yánzhèng its Jìedùshǐ,
and enfeoffed him as Prince of Fùshā.
Jiànzhōu was originally part of Hàn Yě County territory,
later the southern part of Yě territory was divided off and called Jiàn'ān;
the Táng established Jiànzhōu.
There was an ancient Fùshā post station in the prefecture.
Also, there was Fùshā Hamlet within Nánjiàn Prefecture's jurisdiction.
3. In the second month,
on the Rénchén day,
a pontoon bridge was built at Déshèngkǒu.
This became the Yellow River Bridge at Chánzhōu.
4. Zhāng Yànzé, Jìedùshǐ of Zhāngyì, wanted to kill his son.
Zhāng Shì, his chief secretary, was usually favored by Yànzé,
and advised against it.
Yànzé became enraged and
shot at him.
His entourage, who disliked Shì,
then slandered him further.
Shì, fearing for his life,
pleaded illness and departed.
Yànzé sent troops to pursue him.
When Shì reached Bīnzhōu,
Lǐ Zhōu, Jìedùshǐ of Jìngnàn, reported it.
The emperor, for Yànzé's sake,
exiled Shì to Shāngzhōu.
Yànzé sent Zhèng Yuánzhāo, his Army Supervisor, to the imperial court to demand Shì's return,
and further said:
"If Yànzé does not have Zhāng Shì,
I fear unforeseen consequences."
He threatened the emperor with rebellion.
Shì was given to him.
On the Guǐwèi day,
when Shì arrived in Jīngzhōu,
Yànzé ordered his mouth to be cut open, his heart to be extracted,
and his four limbs to be severed.
5 In the military rebellion in Liángzhōu,
Li Wénqiān, the acting governor, closed the gates and immolated himself.
Zhào Xún’s "Gathering Rice and Illustrating the Classics" states: From Liángzhōu, east to Huìzhōu is six hundred *lǐ*,
west to Gānzhōu is five hundred *lǐ*,
south to Shànzhōu is three hundred sixty *lǐ*,
and north to the former Tǔjué territory is three hundred *lǐ*.
Sòng Bái’s "Continued Comprehensive Institutions" states the four directions are the same but the distances in *lǐ* differ.
6 Since Shǔ established its state,
in the first year of Táng Qīngtài,
Shǔ was established as a state.
Or, holding other posts, they remained in Chéngdū,
entrusting their subordinates to manage the duties of the post,
specializing in extortion,
with state affairs neglected,
and the people having nowhere to complain.
The Shǔ ruler, aware of these abuses,
on the *bǐngchén* day,
promoted Zhào Tíngyǐn to Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Guards and Cavalry, Military Commissioner of Wǔdé, and concurrently Minister of the Central Secretariat.
Shǔ renamed Dōngchuān as Wǔdé Army,
to settle Dǒng Zhāng,
conquer Zǐzhōu,
and chose "Seven Virtues of Military Prowess" as the army's name.
And dismissed their military commissioner posts.
In the third month,
on the *jiǎxū* day,
Lǐ Hào, Academician-in-Waiting and Bearer of the Imperial Edict, was appointed to govern Wǔníng
Command;
Liú Yīngtú, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, to govern Bǎoníng Command;
Cuī Luán, Remonstrance Grandee, to govern Wǔxìn Command;
Xiè Cóngzhì, Supervising Secretary, to govern Wǔtài Command;
and Zhāng Zàn, Director of the Imperial Works, to govern Níngjiāng Command.
They were each made to oversee military commissioner affairs,
not as principal commanders.
7 In summer,
in the fourth month,
Mǐn King Xī appointed his son Yàchéng as Concurrently Manager of Affairs and Administrator of the Six Armies and Imperial Guards.
Xī suspected his younger brother Yánxǐ, Governor of Dīngzhōu, of conspiring with Yánzhèng.
Dīng and Jiàn border each other,
hence the suspicion.
He arrested Yánxǐ and brought him back.
8 The Táng ruler appointed Chén Jué and Wànnián Cháng Mèngxí as Deputy Commissioners of Xuanhui.
9 On the *xīnsì* day,
Lǐ Déqióng, Protector of Běijīng, sent his牙校 (yáxiào, aide-de-camp) with Bái Chéngfú, a chieftain of the Tǔyùhùn, to court.
Since Zhāng Chéng had already been dispatched to expel the Tǔyùhùn from the valleys of the four prefectures,
yet their chieftain was allowed to enter court,
was this not permitting the great and expelling the small?
Jìn Gāozǔ and the Qìdān ruler
met through stratagem.
Qióng (珫) pronounced *chāngzhōng*.
10 The Táng ruler sent Ōuyáng Yù, a palace usher (*tōngshì shèrén*), to request passage to communicate with the Qìdān;
the Emperor did not permit it.
When Qìdān requested passage to communicate with Huái and Zhè,
Jìn had no objection;
but when Táng requested passage to communicate with Qìdān,
it was not permitted.
This was responding according to what was considered important or insignificant.
11 Since Huáng Cháo attacked Cháng'ān,
Huáng Cháo entered Cháng'ān in the first year of Táng Xīzōng’s Guǎngmíng era.
Afterwards, various states each had their own territories,
and warfare gradually ceased.
When the Táng ruler ascended the throne,
Jiāng and Huái enjoyed consecutive years of abundant harvests,
with surplus soldiers and provisions.
His ministers eagerly argued:
"Your Majesty’s restoration is at hand!
Now the north is fraught with difficulties;
it is fitting to dispatch troops to recover our former territories."
The Táng ruler said:
"I have grown up in military camps
and have seen how deeply warfare harms the people.
I cannot bear to speak of it again.
If their people are at peace,
then our people will also be at peace.
What more could one seek!"
The Hàn ruler sent envoys to Táng
to plot jointly to take Chǔ
and divide its territory;
the Táng ruler did not permit it.
Historians say the Táng ruler was able to protect his borders and bring peace to his people.
12 Ān Cóngjìn, Military Commissioner of Shānnán Dōngdào, plotted rebellion,
sending an envoy with a memorial to Shǔ,
requesting the dispatch of troops to Jīn and Shāng as support;
from Jīn and Shāng, taking the route through Jūn and Fáng, one would reach Xiāngyáng.
On the *dīnghài* day,
the envoy arrived in Chéngdū.
The Shǔ ruler discussed it with his ministers,
all of whom said:
"Jīn and Shāng are remote and perilous.
Sending a small force would be insufficient to subdue the enemy,
and a large force would face inadequate logistics for transport."
Water transport is called *cáo*,
land transport is called *wǎn*.
*Wǎn* (輓) pronounced *wǎn*.
He also sought aid from Jīngnán.
Gāo Cónghuì sent a letter to Cóngjìn,
explaining the consequences of fortune and misfortune;
Cóngjìn was enraged
and retaliated by falsely accusing Cónghuì in a memorial.
Wáng Bǎoyì, Army Supervisor of Jīngnán, urged Cónghuì to fully report the situation
and request to dispatch troops to assist the court in suppressing him;
Cónghuì agreed.
13 Ān Chóngróng, Military Commissioner of Chéngdé, was ashamed to be a vassal of the Qìdān.
When he saw Qìdān envoys,
he would always sit disrespectfully with legs spread and curse them.
If envoys passed through his territory,
he would sometimes secretly send men to kill them.
The Qìdān complained to the Emperor,
who made humble apologies for him.
In the sixth month,
on the *wùwǔ* day,
Chóngróng seized the Qìdān envoy Zhuáilá,
sent cavalry to raid the southern border of Yōuzhōu,
and camped at Bóyě.
Bóyě County belonged to Dìngzhōu.
In the fourth year of Sòng Yōngxī, Níngbiān Army was established in its territory.
In the first year of Jǐngdé, it was renamed Yǒngdìng Army.
In the seventh year of Tiānshèng, it was renamed Yǒngníng Army.
Jīn elevated it to Lízhōu.
Its territorial map states: North to Yànjīng is four hundred ninety *lǐ*.
"The Tǔyùhùn, the two Tǔjué, Hún, Qìbì, and Shātuó, each leading their tribes, have come to pledge allegiance.
The two Tǔjué are
the Eastern Tǔjué and the Western Tǔjué.
帥 (shuài) is
read as *shuài*.
They say they have been oppressed by the barbarians,
and they also say that since the second month,
they have been ordered to prepare elite armor and strong horses,
and will, in the early autumn, invade the south.
Early autumn refers to the seventh month.
We wish to be destroyed with them.
I am willing to prepare one hundred thousand troops
to jointly attack Qìdān with Jìn."
Furthermore, Zhào Chóng, Deputy Military Commissioner of Shuòzhōu, has expelled Liú Shān, the Qìdān Military Commissioner.
Shuòzhōu was not formerly a military governorship;
it was established by the Qìdān.
Your subjects have successively reported this.
"Your Majesty has repeatedly ordered your subjects to serve the Qìdān
and not to provoke trouble themselves.
But how can the Way of Heaven and human hearts
be resisted or defied?
The opportunity must not be missed;
the time will not come again.
Those military commissioners who have perished in the barbarians' court,
these refer to Zhào Déjūn, Dǒng Wēnqí, Shā Yànxún, Zhái Zhāng, etc.
are truly lamentable.
I wish you would make a decision soon."
The memorial had several thousand words,
largely criticizing the Emperor for serving the Qìdān as a father
and exhausting Zhōngguó to appease the insatiable barbarians.
He also wrote letters with this intent to court nobles
and various military governors,
stating that he had already mobilized his troops
and would certainly fight a decisive battle with the Qìdān.
The Emperor was greatly troubled by Chóngróng, who then wielded a strong army
and could not be controlled.
At that time, Liú Zhīyuǎn (劉知遠), the Commander-in-chief of the Palace Guards for Cavalry and Infantry and the Defense Commissioner of Yèdū (鄴都), was in Dàliáng (大梁);
last year, Liú Zhīyuǎn came to court from Wèi (魏),
and at that time, he was still residing in Dàliáng.
Moreover, he feared that the court would again violate his wishes.
"Zhòng (重)"
means "nán (難)" (difficult).
"Your Majesty escaped the calamity of Jìnyáng (晉陽) and gained the empire,
all thanks to Qìdān (契丹)'s efforts.
You must not betray them.
Now, Zhòngróng (重榮) relies on his bravery and underestimates the enemy;
Tǔhún (吐渾) uses this as an opportunity to take revenge.
None of these are beneficial to the state,
and should not be permitted.
Your servant secretly observes that for several years now, Qìdān
has possessed elite cavalry and strong soldiers,
devouring its neighbors on all sides.
They are victorious in every battle
and capture every city they attack.
They seize territories from Zhōngguó (中國)
and collect weaponry from Zhōngguó.
This refers to the time when Yáng Guāngyuǎn (楊光遠) surrendered and Zhào Déjūn (趙德鈞) was captured.
Their officials, high and low, are harmonious;
their cattle and sheep thrive.
Their country is free from natural disasters.
Therefore, they are not to be made enemies of.
Moreover, Zhōngguó has just suffered defeats;
this refers to Zhāng Jìngdá (張敬達)'s defeat at Jìn'ān (晉安)
and Zhào Déjūn's defeat at Tuánbǎi (團柏).
To confront Qìdān with their momentum of victory,
the disparity in strength is immense.
Furthermore,
since the peace through marriage alliance has been broken,
we should dispatch troops to guard the borders.
If the troops are few, they will be insufficient to withstand the invaders;
if the troops are many, provisions and transport will not be able to sustain them.
When we march out, they retreat;
when we retreat, they arrive.
Your servant fears that the imperial guards will be exhausted by constant deployments,
and the lands of Zhèn (鎮) and Dìng (定) will be devoid of inhabitants.
Since Yōu (幽), Zhuó (涿), Yíng (瀛), and Mò (莫) already belong to Qìdān,
Zhèn, Dìng, Cāng (滄), and Jǐng (景) will all become border garrisons.
The lands of Cāng and Jǐng are close to the sea and low-lying,
and also have many marshes.
The barbarian cavalry cannot enter there.
When they invade, they mostly rely on the mountains to reach Zhèndìng (鎮定),
so this area is a critical point for barbarian attacks.
treasury is depleted,
and the common people are struggling and exhausted.
"Zhēng (蒸)"
means "zhòng (衆)" (multitude).
Even then, we fear failure;
how can we act rashly?
The kindness and righteousness between Qìdān and our state are not slight;
the oaths and pledges are clearly established.
They have no grievance
yet we ourselves initiate conflict.
Even if we succeed,
future troubles will be heavier.
If by any chance we fail,
the great cause will be lost.
Those who argue that the annual tribute of silk is a waste and a detriment,
and that showing deference is humiliation,
do not realize that if wars are prolonged without end,
and disasters are intertwined without resolution,
our financial resources will be exhausted;
what could be a greater waste and detriment than that?
If we engage in war, military officials and meritorious subjects will demand excessive leniency,
and distant border garrisons and prefectures will become arrogant.
The lower ranks will usurp the upper ranks,
what could be a greater humiliation than that?
Sāng Wéihàn (桑維翰) weighs the severity of advantages and disadvantages in his speech;
this is a perspective for the current situation.
By nurturing the army and resting the people,
waiting until the country has no internal worries
and the people have surplus strength,
then observing the opportune moment to act,
any action will surely succeed.
Furthermore,
Yèdū is rich and prosperous,
a bulwark of the state.
Now its chief commander has gone to the capital,
leaving the military government without a leader.
Your servant secretly recalls the saying 'lax storage invites theft'
and the meaning of 'a brave man strengthens his defenses.'
'Lax storage invites theft'
is a saying from the Yì Dàzhuàn (易大傳).
'A brave man strengthens his defenses'
is a saying by Shēn Gōng Wūchén (申公巫臣) in the Zuǒzhuàn (左傳).
'Cáng (藏)'
is pronounced 'cú làng fān.'
'Zhòng (重)'
is pronounced 'zhí lóng fān.'
This is to prevent treacherous schemes."
The emperor said to the messenger:
"For several days now,
I have been troubled and indecisive.
Now that I have seen your memorial,
it is as if I have awakened from a drunken stupor.
You need not worry about this."
Mǐn Wáng (閩王) Xī (曦) heard that Wáng Yánzhèng (王延政) had sent a letter to invite Wáng Jìyè (王繼業), the Inspector of Quánzhōu (泉州),
so he summoned Jìyè back
and granted him death outside the city.
This was outside Fúzhōu (福州).
Thirty *lǐ* outside the city was considered the suburb.
This means he was killed in the wilderness.
Earlier,
Jìyè was the Inspector of Tīngzhōu (汀州).
Yáng Yīfēng (楊沂豐), who was Sītú (司徒) and concurrently Ménxià Shìláng (門下侍郎) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事), served as an official in the Staff Section (shìcáo cānjūn).
He was close to Jìyè.
Someone accused Yīfēng of conspiring with Jìyè.
Yīfēng was at a banquet
when he was immediately arrested and imprisoned.
The next day, he was executed,
and his clan was exterminated.
Yīfēng
was the younger cousin of Shè (涉).
Yáng Shè (楊涉) served as a prime minister during the transition between the Táng (唐) and Liáng (梁) dynasties.
'Cóng (從)'
is pronounced 'cái yòng fān.'
The people of the state mourned him.
From then on, clan members and old meritorious officials were successively executed.
People could not protect themselves.
Huáng Jùn (黃峻), a Jiànyì Dàfū (諫議大夫), carried a coffin to the imperial court and remonstrated strongly.
Xī said:
"This old man is acting mad!"
He was demoted to Sīhù (司戶) of Zhāngzhōu (章州).
Xī was excessively licentious and extravagant,
and his expenses were not met.
He consulted with the Guójìshǐ (國計使) Nán'ān (南安) Chén Kuāngfàn (陳匡範).
Nán'ān County
was established in the Suí (隋) dynasty.
In the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Quánzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) says it is forty-seven *lǐ* north of the prefecture.
Xī was pleased
and promoted Kuāngfàn to Lǐbù Shìláng (禮部侍郎).
Kuāngfàn increased taxes on merchants several times over.
Xī feasted his officials
and raised his wine cup to Kuāngfàn, saying:
"Bright pearls and beautiful jade
