In the ninth month of that year,
Yáng Yánxún was an envoy to the Qìdān.
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
Zhāng Jiànwǔ, the Inspector of Jìzhōu, and others captured Zhàozhōu.
Both Jì and Zhào prefectures were under Ān Zhòngróng's jurisdiction.
(35) The Hàn ruler fell ill.
A Hu monk told the Hàn ruler that his name, Gōng (龔), was inauspicious.
The Hàn ruler then created
the character "yǎn" (龑)
for his name,
deriving its meaning from
"flying dragon in the sky."
The *Yì* states: "The flying dragon in the sky,
it is auspicious to see the great man."
(36) On the *gēngxū* day,
an imperial edict appointed Qián Hóngzuǒ as Military Governor of Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng Armies, concurrently Grand Chancellor, and King of Wúyuè.
Punctuation by Dèng Guǎngmíng, collated by Niè Chóngqí.
Compiled by Sīmǎ Guāng
by imperial command.
Hòu Xuétiāntái (postscript by Xuétiāntái).
The 7th year of Tiānfú (Rén'yín, 942).
1. Spring,
First month,
On the *dīngsì* day,
a staff officer from Zhènzhōu led the imperial army into the city through the Xīguō Shuǐniǎn Gate,
killed twenty thousand defending civilians,
captured Ān Zhòngróng,
and beheaded him.
Dù Zhòngwēi killed the guide
and claimed the merit for himself.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
Zhòngróng's head arrived at Yèdū.
The emperor ordered it lacquered
and sent in a box to the Qìdān.
2. On the *guǐhài* day,
Zhènzhōu was renamed Héngzhōu,
and Chéngdé Army was renamed Shùnguó Army.
Zhènzhōu was originally Héngzhōu.
The Táng changed its name to avoid the personal name of Mùzōng.
Now, because of Ān Zhòngróng's rebellion,
the prefecture's name was changed back to its old one,
and the army's designation was also changed.
Héng [恆],
pronounced Hú Dēng.
3. On the *bǐngyín* day,
Zhào Yíng, Minister of the Secretariat and Grand Chancellor, was appointed Minister of the Imperial Household.
Dù Zhòngwēi was appointed Military Governor of Shùnguó and concurrently Minister of the Imperial Household.
Ān Zhòngróng's private wealth and the treasury of Héngzhōu
were all taken by Zhòngwēi,
and the emperor knew but did not question it.
Furthermore, Zhòngwēi recommended Wáng Yú of Fànyáng, Assistant Minister of the Court of the Imperial Gards, as his deputy.
Yú heavily taxed the people for him,
and the people of Héng could not bear their suffering.
4. Zhāng Shì's father, Duó, went to the palace to plead for justice.
The matter of Zhāng Yànzé killing Zhāng Shì is recorded in the previous volume for the previous year.
On the *rénwǔ* day,
Wáng Zhōu, Military Governor of Héyáng, was appointed Military Governor of Zhāngyì,
replacing Zhāng Yànzé.
5. The Mǐn ruler Xī established Empress Lǐ,
daughter of Zhēn, Grand Chancellor.
She was fond of wine and obstinate.
Xī favored and feared her.
6. Dīng Shěnqí, Military Governor of Zhāngwǔ,
maintained a thousand personal retainers
whom he allowed to commit atrocities within the territory.
Military officer Hè Xíngzhèng conspired with various Hú tribes to cause rebellion,
attacking Yánzhōu.
The emperor dispatched Hé Chóngjiàn, Defense Commissioner of Cáozhōu, to lead troops to rescue it.
Reinforcements from Tóng and Fū arrived subsequently,
and only then was it saved.
In the second month,
on the *guǐsì* day,
Chóngjiàn was appointed Acting Military Governor of Zhāngwǔ,
and Shěnqí was summoned back to court.
Chóngjiàn
was a Hú person from the Yún and Shuò region.
7. Sòng Qíqiū, Left Chancellor of Táng, firmly requested to participate in political affairs.
The Táng ruler allowed him to enter the Secretariat.
He further requested to lead the Department of State Affairs,
so Prince Shòu Jǐngsuì was dismissed from supervising the Department of State Affairs,
which was then led by the Secretariat and Chancellery.
Qíqiū was appointed to manage affairs of the Department of State Affairs.
Affairs of all three departments were to be decided with the participation of Prince Qí Jǐng.
This was to restrain Sòng Qíqiū.
His close subordinate Xià Chāngtú stole three thousand *mín* of official money.
Qíqiū judged to commute his death sentence.
The Táng ruler was greatly angered
and beheaded Chāngtú.
Qíqiū feigned illness
and requested to be relieved of his duties,
which was granted.
8. Jìngzhōu reported sending its guard officer Chén Yánhuī with an imperial edict to Liángzhōu.
The generals and officials in the prefecture asked Yánhuī to be the Military Governor.
9. In the third month,
the Mǐn ruler Xī established Prince Chánglè Yàchéng as King of Mǐn.
10. Zhāng Yànzé was in Jìngzhōu.
He dispatched troops to attack various Hú tribes,
but all his troops were defeated and lost.
He levied over a thousand horses from the people to compensate for the losses.
When he returned to Shǎn,
he returned to Shǎn from his replacement at Jìngzhōu.
Huán [還],
pronounced Cóng Xuān.
Shǎn [陝],
pronounced Shī Rǎn.
While drunk, he severed their hands and feet and then beheaded them.
Wáng Zhōu reported twenty-six instances of Yànzé's greed, cruelty, and unlawful acts during his governorship,
resulting in over five thousand households of displaced commoners.
Wáng Zhōu replaced Yànzé,
hence he was able to report on his actions while in office.
The emperor, considering his military achievements
and his marital connection with Yáng Guāngyuǎn,
released him without questioning.
The *Ōu Shǐ* states that
Zhāng Yànzé was connected by marriage to the emperor
and had also distinguished himself in suppressing Fàn Yánguāng.
Summer,
Fourth month,
On the *jǐwèi* day,
Zhèng Yìyì, Right Remonstrance Grand Master, submitted a memorial stating:
"The reason Yáng Hóng was massacred
was that last year Your Majesty sent Zhāng Shì to Yànzé,
allowing him to act on his will,
which caused Yànzé to dare to commit such savage atrocities
without any scruples.
All who heard or witnessed it gnashed their teeth,
yet Your Majesty did not even stir,
and made no inquiries or reprimands.
Good and evil were indistinguishable,
and rewards and punishments were without order.
Both within and outside the court, everyone says that Your Majesty accepted a hundred horses offered by Yànzé
and permitted him to act in this manner.
I secretly lament this ill repute for Your Majesty,
and beg you to enforce the law against Yànzé to cleanse Your sacred virtue."
The memorial was submitted
but kept in the palace.
Yìyì
was the nephew of Cóngdǎng.
Zhèng Cóngdǎng is mentioned in the annals of Táng Xīzōng.
Dǎng [讜],
pronounced Dǎng.
19 Mǐn Fùshā Wáng Yánzhèng attacked Tīngzhōu.
After forty-two battles,
he returned without success.
His generals Bāo Hóngshí and Chén Wàng,
led a naval force to resist the army from Fúzhōu.
On the *Dīngyǒu* day,
they met at Yóukǒu.
This refers to Yóuxīkǒu.
Diviners said the time was unfavorable, so
they held their troops and did not move.
Hóngshí and others led their troops ashore,
attacking by land and water.
They killed Jìngzhōng,
and captured or beheaded two thousand men.
Lín Shǒuliàng and Huáng Shàopō both fled back.
20 On the *Gēngzǐ* day,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
21 On the *Guǐmǎo* day,
Jǐng Yán'guǎng was granted the concurrent title of *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*,
and also *Shìwèi Mǎbù Dūzhīhuīshǐ*.
This was in reward for his merit in making decisive plans.
This laid the groundwork for Jǐng Yán'guǎng to seize power, control the emperor, and instigate conflict with the Khitans.
22 All the veteran officials wished to reinstate the *Shūmìshǐ*.
The abolition of the *Shūmìshǐ* was mentioned in the previous volume, last year.
They requested to relinquish their old *Shūmì* positions.
The *Shūmì* (Bureau of Military Affairs) was merged into the *Zhōngshū* (Central Secretariat).
Therefore, the duties originally managed by the *Shūmìyuàn* were called "old positions."
23 A spirit descended into a commoner's house in Bóluó Xiàn.
Bóluó
was an ancient Han dynasty county.
During the Tang dynasty, it belonged to Xúnzhōu,
and at this time was Han territory.
The *Jùnguó Zhì* says: Xúnzhōu has Bóluó Shān.
It floated across the sea
and attached itself to Luóshān,
hence the name Bóluó.
In the Song dynasty, Bóluó Xiàn belonged to Huìzhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* says: It is forty-five *lǐ* north of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Bóluó Xiàn is adjacent to Luóshān,
hence it is called Bóluó.
To the east it borders Lóngzhōu,
to the south Xīpíng,
and to the west the boundary of Zēngchéng.
People from all walks of life went to consult the spirit for good or ill fortune,
and it was often accurate.
The county official Zhāng Yùxián served it very respectfully.
At that time, bandits rose everywhere in Xúnzhōu,
but none were unified.
The bandit chiefs prayed together to the spirit.
The spirit spoke loudly, saying:
"Zhāng Yùxián should be your lord."
Thereupon,
they all honored Yùxián,
proclaiming him *Zhōngtiān Bāguó Wáng*,
changing the era name to Yǒnglè,
and establishing an official hierarchy.
They plundered the coastal regions.
The area southeast of Xúnzhōu, stretching to Cháozhōu and Huìzhōu,
are both coastal areas.
He had no other strategies;
his generals merely reported their advances and retreats.
The Han lord appointed Yuè Wáng Hóngchāng as *Dūtǒng*,
with Xún Wáng Hónggǎo as his deputy, to suppress them.
They fought at Qiánbógǔan.
The Han forces were at a disadvantage,
and both princes were surrounded by the bandits.
Commander Chén Dàoxiáng and others fought bravely to rescue them,
and they escaped.
Many eastern prefectures and counties were captured by Yùxián.
Eastern prefectures and counties
refer to the prefectures and counties east of Pānyú,
namely the lands of Huì and Cháo.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* says: From Guǎngzhōu east to Huìzhōu is three hundred fifteen *lǐ*.
And from Huìzhōu east to Cháozhōu is eight hundred ten *lǐ*.
He was from Duānzhōu.
24 Gāo Xíngzhōu had besieged Xiāngzhōu for over a year,
but it had not fallen.
Last year, in the eleventh month,
Gāo Xíngzhōu besieged Xiāngzhōu.
This event was first mentioned in the previous volume.
Qūzhōu Wáng Qīng, the *Fèngguó Jūn Dū Yúhòu*, said to Xíngzhōu:
Qūzhōu Xiàn
belonged to Míngzhōu.
In the third year of Xīníng of the Song dynasty,
Qūzhōu Xiàn was abolished as a county and made a town,
merged into Jīzé Xiàn.
"The enemy city is already in peril,
our army is already weary,
and the people's strength is exhausted.
If we do not press them soon,
what more are we waiting for!"
He and Yuánchéng Liú Cí, the *Fèngguó Dūzhīhuīshǐ*, led their troops to be the first to ascend.
Yuánchéng Xiàn bordered Wèizhōu.
The character *shuài*
is read as *lǜ*.
They captured it.
Ān Cóngjìn's entire clan immolated themselves.
25 On the *Jiǎzǐ* day,
Zhào Yíng was appointed *Zhōngshūlìng*.
26 Mǐn lord Xī sent an envoy with a handwritten edict, nine hundred gold artifacts, ten thousand strings of cash, and six hundred forty official proclamations for generals and officers,
seeking peace with Fùshā Wáng Yánzhèng.
Yánzhèng refused.
On the *Bǐngyín* day,
Mǐn lord Xī feasted all his ministers at the Jiǔlóng Diàn.
His nephew Jìróu could not drink,
but was forced to.
Jìróu secretly reduced his wine,
which angered Xī,
who then beheaded him and the accompanying general.
Wáng Xī's debauchery and tyranny
were similar to those of Sūn Hào.
The character *jiāng*
is read as *liàng*.
27 The people of Mǐn cast large iron coins called Yǒnglóng Tōngbǎo,
each worth a hundred lead coins.
28 The Han dynasty buried Emperor Tiānhuáng Dàdì at Kānglíng.
His temple name was Gāozǔ.
29 The Tang lord, acting as prime minister of Wú,
promoted benefits and eliminated harms, changing many old laws.
In the fourth year of Zhēnmíng of Liáng Jūn Wáng,
the Tang lord first obtained control of Wú politics,
which was the fifteenth year of Wú Wáng Lóngyǎn.
He ordered legal officials and the Ministry of Rites to compile *Shēngyuán Tiáo* in thirty volumes.
At this time, the Tang used Shēngyuán as an era name.
On the *Gēngyín* day,
they were put into effect.
30 Mǐn lord Xī appointed Yú Tíngyīng of Hòuguān, who held the title of *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*, as governor of Quánzhōu.
Tíngyīng was corrupt and greedy,
abducting women,
falsely claiming he was ordered to select them for the imperial harem.
When the matter was discovered,
Xī sent an censor to investigate him.
Tíngyīng, in fear,
went to Fúzhōu to surrender himself.
Xī interrogated and reproached him,
intending to hand him over to officials.
Tíngyīng retreated,
then offered ten thousand strings of cash as "banquet money."
Xī was pleased.
The next day, he summoned Tíngyīng
and said:
"The banquet has been purchased,
where are the Empress's tribute items?"
Tíngyīng again presented money to Empress Lǐ,
and then he was sent back to Quánzhōu.
From then on, all prefectures separately presented tribute to the Empress.
Not long after,
Tíngyīng was recalled to serve as prime minister again.
31 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the *Bǐngzǐ* day,
Zhāng Yùxián captured Xúnzhōu
and killed Liú Chuán, the Han governor.
32 Chǔ Wáng Xīfàn built the Tiāncèfǔ.
Wáng Jǔ's *Tiānxià Dàdìng Lù* says: Xīfàn built the Tiāncèfǔ to the northwest of the prefecture city,
constructing sixteen towers including Tiāncè and Guāngzhèng,
and also five halls including Tiāncè and Qínzhèng.
Windows, doors, railings, and banisters were all decorated with gold and jade.
Hundreds of thousands of *jīn* of cinnabar were used to paint the walls.
Cinnabar came from Chén, Xī, Xù, Jǐn prefectures and various valleys and caves,
all within Chǔ territory.
The *Běncǎo Tújīng* says: Cinnabar grows in deep mountain rocky cliffs.
Locals dig dozens of feet into the ground
before seeing its 'seedling,'
which is white stone,
called a cinnabar bed.
The cinnabar grows on the stone;
larger pieces are like chicken eggs, smaller ones like pomegranate seeds,
shaped like hibiscus buds or connected arrowheads on the bed.
It is dark purple like iron,
but bright and clear.
When broken,
it forms sharp walls
or resembles mica flakes that can be split.
The less stone, the better.
Beyond this, it is obtained by washing it from earth and stone.
In spring and summer, horn mats were used.
Horn mats
were made by splitting bamboo into fine strips,
then weaving them.
The knots were hidden, and the outer skin removed,
making them smooth and lovely.
Some southern barbarians also made them from white rattan.
Kapok
is now abundant in the south.
In mid-spring, it is planted in raised beds.
By late summer and early autumn, it bears fruit.
By mid-autumn,
the outer skin of the fruit splits into four,
and white, cotton-like fibers
emerge from within.
Local people harvest it and spin it
into cloth.
It is fine, dense, thick, and warm,
suitable for keeping warm in winter.
33 In the eleventh month,
on the *gēngyín* day,
Emperor Shèngwén Wǔmíngdé Xiào was buried in Xiǎnlíng mausoleum.
The mausoleum is in Shòu'ān County, Hénán Fǔ.
34 Previously, officials in various prefectures north and south of the Hé Nán sold sea salt themselves,
collecting 170,000 *mín* in cash annually.
They also distributed silkworm salt and collected money from the people.
Silkworm salt was used to dry cocoons.
In the second year of Tiānchéng of the Táng dynasty,
an edict was issued: "Silkworm salt shall be distributed once every second month of the year,
and payment collected by the deadline for summer taxes."
Sòng Bái said: In the third year of Xiǎndé of the Zhōu dynasty,
an edict ordered that silkworm salt in Qízhōu be distributed during the autumn harvest,
known as *chátóu*,
with 3,000 cash collected for every *shí* of salt.
In Cāng, Dì, Bīn, Zī, and Qīng prefectures,
one bolt of silk was collected for every *shí*.
Later, Qízhōu's levy was halved,
and the silk collected in the five prefectures was doubled.
Previously,
all of it was overturned.
It was better to allow private trade,
and annually collect from the people an amount equivalent to the money the government made from selling salt,
which was called "eating salt money."
Gāozǔ followed this.
Soon after, the price of salt plummeted,
reaching ten cash per *jīn*.
By this time,
Dǒng Yù, the Commissioner of the Three Bureaus, wanted to increase profits,
but found it difficult to suddenly change the former law.
So, he heavily taxed salt merchants.
Those passing through paid seven cash,
while those who stayed to sell paid ten cash.
Consequently, salt merchants almost disappeared,
and the government resumed selling it itself.
The "eating salt money"
is still collected as before.
In the *Wǔdài Huìyào*: At the time, those who spoke on affairs of state requested that the "eating salt money" be distributed among the prefectures and circuits,
calculating by household, with each household paying one *guàn* to two hundred (cash) in five grades,
and then allowing people to trade freely as they wished,
which would neither diminish government revenue
nor harm the people.
The imperial court implemented this,
while the various saltworks and bureaus remained as before.
Soon after, the price of salt plummeted,
and in prefectures and counties far from the salt-producing areas,
it was no more than twenty per *jīn*.
Those in charge found it difficult to suddenly change the law again,
and proposed re-imposing the tax.
This was apparently to stop private trade
and return the profits to the government.
Although the saltworks sold a lot of salt,
the households' "eating salt money" was not waived,
and the people suffered greatly.
35 Lǐ Rénwù, the Salt and Iron Commissioner of Mǐn and Right Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
was Mǐn's son.
Lǐ Mǐn
was the father of Mǐn Lord Chǎng's principal consort, the Duchess of Liáng.
Rénwù was young,
handsome in appearance,
and favored by Xī.
He enjoyed the favor of Lóngyáng.
Rénwù was made Left Director of the Imperial Secretariat and concurrently Minister of the Central Secretariat.
Lǐ Guāngzhǔn, a Hanlin Academician and Minister of Personnel, was made Minister of the Central Secretariat and concurrently President of the Ministry of Revenue,
both holding the title of Co-Chancellor.
Xī was debauched and excessive.
Once, during a night banquet,
Guāngzhǔn, being drunk, offended the emperor's will.
Xī ordered him seized, sent to the marketplace, and beheaded.
The clerks dared not kill him and imprisoned him.
The next day,
at court,
he was summoned and reinstated to his position.
That evening,
another banquet was held,
and Zhōu Wéiyuè, a Hanlin Academician, was arrested and imprisoned.
The clerks brushed off a bed and waited for him,
saying:
"His Excellency slept here last night,
so Your Worship need not worry."
He was released when he sobered up.
Another day,
at another banquet,
all the attendant officials left drunk,
only Wéiyuè remained.
Xī said:
"Wéiyuè is quite small,
why does he drink so much?"
Someone on his left or right said:
"Alcohol has a separate intestine;
this is a common folk saying."
Xī was delighted,
ordered Wéiyuè dragged down from the hall,
intending to dissect him to inspect his "alcohol intestine."
Someone said:
"If Wéiyuè is killed,
there will be no one
to attend Your Majesty for heavy drinking."
So, he spared him.
36 When the Emperor first ascended the throne,
the grand ministers debated whether to present a memorial, declare themselves vassals, and announce the mourning to the Qìdān.
Jǐng Yán-guǎng requested sending a letter referring to themselves as grandsons, not vassals.
Jǐng Yán-guǎng's proposal was based on the Qìdān ruler's command three years prior for Gāozǔ to call himself the "Son Emperor,"
and to write letters using family etiquette.
"To humble oneself for the sake of the state,
what shame is there?
If Your Majesty acts thus,
one day you will surely have to don armor yourself
and fight the Qìdān,
and then regret will be of no use."
"*Yú shí*" means "at that time."
Féng Dào equivocated on the matter.
The Emperor ultimately followed Yán-guǎng's proposal.
The Qìdān were furious
and sent an envoy to rebuke them,
saying:
"How dare you not first seek approval
and abruptly ascend the throne?"
Yán-guǎng again replied with insolent words.
Zhào Yánshòu, the Military Commissioner of Lúlóng for the Qìdān, wanted to replace the Jìn Emperor as ruler of China.
The desire of Zhào Yánshòu and his son to rule China
was already evident when they were stationed at Tuántuán Bó.
The Qìdān ruler was quite pleased with this.
Eighth year of Tiānfú (Guǐmǎo, 943 CE)
1 Spring,
first month.
On the *guǐmǎo* day,
the Shǔ ruler appointed Tián Jìngquán, the Commissioner of Xuanhui and concurrently Commissioner of Palaces and Gardens, as Military Commissioner of Yǒngpíng.
Jìngquán was an eunuch.
He cited Wáng Chéngxiū of Former Shǔ as a precedent and appointed him.
Former Shǔ ruler Wáng Yǎn made the eunuch Wáng Chéngxiū governor of Qínzhōu.
This event can be found in volume 273, second year of Táng Zhuāngzōng's Tóngguāng reign.
The poem says: "The mirror of Yin is not far off,
it is in the time of the Xiàhou."
Mèng Chǎng failed to take the fall of Former Shǔ as a warning,
and instead cited Wáng Chéngxiū as a precedent to elevate eunuchs to high ranks.
His state eventually fell to Sòng,
but it was too late!
2 The Emperor heard that the Qìdān were about to invade.
In the second month,
on the *jǐwèi* day,
he departed from Yèdū.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
he arrived at Dōngjīng.
The Emperor had ascended the throne in front of the coffin at the Bǎochāng Hall in Yèdū;
it was only now that he returned to Biàn.
No month was left empty.
3 Lǐ Jǐngdá, Prince Xuānchéng of Táng,
was resolute and straightforward.
Lièzǔ loved him
and repeatedly wanted to make him his successor.
Lièzǔ
refers to the Táng ruler.
When the Táng ruler died,
his temple name was Lièzǔ;
the *Tōngjiàn* recorded it based on his national history.
The Táng ruler stopped because Qí Wáng Jǐng was older.
Jǐng resented Qí Qiū because of this.
He resented him for supporting the plot to usurp the succession
and was angry at him for contending for power and ruining the country.
Sòng Qíqiū therefore could not escape.
The Táng ruler's youngest son, Lǐ Jǐngtì,
whose mother was Lady Zhǒng, was favored.
Qí Wáng Jǐng's mother, Empress Sòng, rarely got to see the ruler.
When the Táng ruler visited Jǐng's palace,
he encountered Jǐng personally tuning musical instruments.
He was furious
and reproached him for several days.
Lady Zhǒng seized the opportunity to say
that Jǐngtì, though young, was intelligent
and could be made the successor.
The Táng ruler angrily said:
"If a son errs,
the father instructs him,
which is a common matter.
How can a woman presume to know about important national affairs?"
He immediately ordered her to be married off.
Historians say that the Táng ruler was clear-sighted and decisive,
and not swayed by female favorites.
Táng Zhǔ once dreamt of swallowing a spiritual elixir.
The next morning, a fangshì, Shǐ Shǒuchōng, presented an elixir recipe,
which Táng Zhǔ considered divine and consumed.
Gradually, he became irritable and impatient.
Since Shūsūn Bào's time,
many have brought disaster upon themselves by acting on ominous dreams.
He did not listen.
Once, he bestowed medicine upon Lǐ Jiànxūn.
Lǐ Jiànxūn said:
"Your subject has taken it for several days,
and already feels restless and hot,
let alone taking more!"
Táng Zhǔ said:
"I have been taking it for a long time."
When his officials submitted reports,
he often erupted in rage;
however, if someone argued with righteous indignation and reason,
he would also compose himself, apologize, and comply.
Táng Zhǔ asked the Daoist Wáng Qīxiá:
"What Dao can lead to great peace?"
He replied:
"A king must first govern his heart and body,
then he can govern his family and state.
Currently, Your Majesty cannot yet rid yourself of hunger and anger, or be sated with joy.
How can you speak of great peace!"
Empress Sòng praised him from behind the curtain,
deeming it profound truth.
Whatever Táng Zhǔ bestowed upon him,
Qīxiá never accepted.
Qīxiá often presented memorials for others.
Táng Zhǔ wished to build an altar for him.
He declined, saying:
"The state's resources are currently depleted,
how can there be time for this!
Wait until the memorials I burn do not transform into ash [and ascend],
then I shall request it."

Hóng requested an audience, but was declined with the excuse of an afternoon nap.
Hóng told the guest-general (kèjiàng) Ōu Hóngliàn:
“The King indulges his desires and spurns advice.
I foresee his family, a thousand mouths, will be scattered before long.”
People often refer to an entire family as "a hundred mouths";
here it says "a thousand mouths"
because he was a feudal lord,
speaking grandly.
Thereafter, he never saw him again for the rest of his life.
37 Mǐn Zhǔ Xī married off his daughter,
and took out the staff roster (bānbù) to review it;

He had all of them beaten in the imperial hall.
Because Censor-in-Chief (yùshǐ zhōngchéng) Liú Zàn had not impeached anyone,
he was also about to be beaten.
Zàn, upholding righteousness, refused to suffer such humiliation
and intended to commit suicide.
Policy Advisor (jiànyì dàfū) Zhèng Yuánbì remonstrated, saying:
“In ancient times, punishment was not inflicted upon high-ranking officials.
This cites the words of the Qūlǐ.
Shàng,
pronunciation for Shí Zhǎng.
How can it be appropriate to inflict flogging upon them!”
Xī, with a stern expression, said:
“Do you wish to emulate Wèi Zhēng?”
Yuánbì replied:
“I consider Your Majesty to be Táng Tàizōng,
hence I dare to emulate Wèi Zhēng.”
Xī’s anger gradually subsided,
and he released Zàn.
Zàn nevertheless died of sorrow.
Kāiyùn First Year (jiǎchén, 944)
The reign era was changed in the seventh month of this year.
1 In spring,
the first month,

is another term for “biānzhèn.”

He said:

Heaven is weary of the Wáng clan;
it is proper to choose a virtuous person to enthrone instead."
No one dared to speak.
Chóngyù then pushed Wénjìn onto the throne,
where he put on the imperial robe and crown,
and led all the officials to bow twice facing north, declaring themselves subjects.
Wénjìn declared himself the ruler of Mǐn.
He rounded up all members of the Wáng imperial clan, over fifty people, young and old, from Yánxǐ downwards,
and killed them all.
Yánxǐ
was the Mǐn ruler's younger brother.
Shào (少)
is read *shǐ zhào* (詩照).
Cháng (長)
is read *zhī liǎng* (知兩).
He was posthumously given the title Ruìwén Guǎngwǔ Míngshèng Yuándé Lóngdào Dàxiào Huángdì,
with the temple name Jǐngzōng.
Chóngyù was made the commander of the Six Armies.
The Minister of Rites and acting Commissioner of the Three Bureaus, Zhèng Yuánbì, spoke out defiantly and refused to submit,
so he was demoted and returned to his hometown.
He intended to flee to Jiànzhōu,
wanting to flee to Wáng Yánzhèng.
Wénjìn issued an order
to release palace women
and halt construction projects,
reversing Xī's policies.
Yīn ruler Yánzhèng sent the General Commander Wú Chéngyì to lead troops to attack Wénjìn,
but he was unsuccessful.
Wénjìn appointed the Privy Councilor Bào Sīrùn as co-equal with the Grand Chancellor,
and made the Yǔlín General Commander Huáng Shàopō the Prefect of Quánzhōu,
and the Left Army Commander Chéng Wénwěi the Prefect of Zhāngzhōu.
Xǔ Wénzhěn of Tíngzhōu Prefecture, Tong'an,
surrendered his entire prefecture to him.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: "Tong'an County in Quánzhōu is 135 *lǐ* west of the prefecture seat."
It was probably established by the Wáng clan.
Sòng Bái said: "In Kāiyuán 19th year (731), four townships from Nán'ān County in Quánzhōu were separated to establish Dàtóng Farm.
The King of Mǐn elevated it to Tong'an County."
Zhěn (稹)
is read *zhāng rěn* (章忍).
10 On the day Dīnghài,
an edict ordered the troops from Tàiyuán, Héng, and Ān
to return to their respective garrisons.
This was because the Qìdān had already retreated.
11 On the day Xīnmǎo,
Mǎ Quánjié attacked the Qìdān's Tàizhōu
and captured it.
The Wǔdài Huìyào states: "In Tiānchéng 3rd year (928) of the Later Táng, Fènghuà Commandery was elevated to Tàizhōu,
with Qīngyuàn County as its administrative seat.
In Kāiyùn 2nd year (945), 9th month, of the Jìn dynasty, its administrative seat was moved to Mǎnchéng County;
in Guǎngshùn 2nd year (952), 2nd month, of the Zhōu dynasty, the prefecture was abolished,
and Mǎnchéng County was ceded to Yìzhōu."
At this time, Mǎ Quánjié attacked Tàizhōu from Dìngzhōu.
12 An imperial decree ordered that militiamen be registered throughout the realm;
every seven households were to jointly provide weapons and supplies for one soldier.
13 Qinzhōu troops rescued Jiēzhōu,
coming out of Huángjiē Lǐng,
and defeated the Shǔ troops at Xīpíng.
14 The Hàn appointed Chén Wò, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue, as co-equal with the Grand Chancellor.
In the 15th summer,
in the fourth month,
on the Dīngwèi day,
Liáng Jìn, the巡檢使 (patrol inspector) along the river, with village militia, recaptured Dézhōu.
Village militia [xiāng shè bīng]
are民兵 (people's militia).
At that time, the Qìdān were raiding and plundering,
and the people along the river
equipped themselves with weapons,
each following their village,
formed into associations,
to protect themselves.
When the Qìdān captured Dézhōu and returned north,
Liáng Jìn seized the opportunity of their departure to recapture it.
On the Jǐyǒu day,
orders were given for Gāo Xíngzhōu, the Guīdé Jiédùshǐ, and Wáng Zhōu, the Bǎoyì Jiédùshǐ, to remain stationed at Chánzhōu.
On the Gēngxū day,
the Emperor departed from Chánzhōu;
on the Jiǎyín day,
he arrived at Dàliáng.
Jǐng Yán'guǎng, the Shìwèi Mǎbù Dūzhīhuīshǐ, Tiānpíng Jiédùshǐ, and Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
was already disliked by both high and low.
"High" [shàng]
refers to the generals, ministers, and high officials;
"low" [xià]
refers to the soldiers and common people.
惡 [è] is pronounced 'wū lù fān'.
Sāng Wéihàn brought up his crime of not saving Qīchéng.
"引" [yǐn]
means "to pull".
To bring up his crime,
is like someone pulling out a rolled-up garment from their sleeve.
On the Xīnyǒu day,
Yán'guǎng was given the additional title of Shìzhōng,
and sent out as the Xī Jīng Liúshǒu (Resident Commissioner of the Western Capital).
When Jìn moved its capital to Biàn,
Hénán Fǔ was designated as the Western Capital.
Yán'guǎng was dejected and discontented.
A stubborn petty person,
when in power, becomes arrogant, overbearing, and acts on impulse;
when out of power, becomes dejected and discontented –
this is his usual way.
He began to worry about the country's ruin and his own danger,
and so indulged in wine day and night.
Knowing he had no hope of survival,
he merely sought momentary pleasure.
The court, due to the Qìdān invasion,
saw national expenditures further depleted. They again dispatched thirty-six envoys to various routes to levy people's wealth,
each sealed with a sword and given to them.
The envoys often brought subordinate officials and soldiers,
carrying chains, shackles, knives, and staffs into people's homes.
Both young and old were terrified,
and had nowhere to seek death.
Local officials again took advantage of the situation to commit malpractices.
Hénán Fǔ contributed 200,000 strings of cash;
this was the amount it was required to contribute.
Jǐng Yán'guǎng increased the levy by 170,000,
intending to keep it for himself.
Lú Yì said to Yán'guǎng:
"You, sir,
hold positions as both general and prime minister,
your wealth and honor are extreme.
Now the state is unfortunate,
the treasuries are empty,
and it has no choice but to take from the people.
How can you bear to seek profit from this again,
and become a burden to your descendants?"
Yán'guǎng felt ashamed and stopped.
Historians say that Jǐng Yán'guǎng was slightly better than Dù Chóngwēi.
Previously,
an imperial edict, due to Yáng Guāngyuǎn's rebellion,
ordered Yǎnzhōu to repair its defenses.
Qīng and Yǎn were neighboring prefectures,
hence the order to prepare.
"先" [xiān] is pronounced 'xī jiàn fān'.
Under the pretext of repairing the battlements,
they levied people's wealth to fill private coffers.
Zhāng Rén'yuàn, the Dàlǐ Qīng, was the levy envoy.
Upon arriving at Yǎnzhōu,
he levied 100,000 strings of cash.
It happened that Shěn Xìn was not present.
"Not present" [bù zài zhě]
means not currently in the prefecture.
He simply took one granary full of cash,
which already met the required amount.
Historians say that the Jìn's藩鎮 (frontier garrisons)
profited from the country's difficulties,
exploiting the people to enrich their families.
On the 16th Wùyín day,
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn, the Shìwèi Mǎbù Jūn Dūyúhòu and Tàiníng Jiédùshǐ, was ordered to lead 20,000 infantry and cavalry to attack Yáng Guāngyuǎn in Qīngzhōu.
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn likely replaced Ān Shěnxìn as the commander of Tàiníng.
This was to prepare against the Qìdān.
The Qìdān dispatched troops to relieve Qīngzhōu.
Xuē Kěyán of Tángyáng, the Qízhōu Fángyùshǐ, intercepted and attacked them,
defeating them.
Tángyáng county belonged to Jìzhōu.
In the fourth year of Huángyòu of Sòng,
the county was abolished and became a town,
incorporated into Nángōng county.
The Jiǔyù Zhì says: "The land is south of the Táng River."
"敗" [bài] is pronounced 'bǔ mài fān'.
On the 17th Bǐngxū day,
an imperial edict ordered that the village militia registered in all prefectures
be designated Wǔdìng Jūn,
totaling over 70,000 people.
At that time, after the ravages of war,
there was this further disturbance,
and the people could not make a living.
On the 18th Dīnghài day,
Zhāng Cóng'ēn, the Yèdū Liúshǒu, submitted a memorial saying:
"Although Zhào Yánzhào occupies Bèizhōu,
his subordinate soldiers, having been away for a long time, yearn to return.
It is advisable to quickly advance and attack him."
An edict appointed Cóng'ēn as the Bèizhōu Xíngyíng Dū Bùshǔ (Commander-in-Chief of the Bèizhōu Expeditionary Camp),
to oversee the generals in attacking him.
On the Xīnmǎo day,
Cóng'ēn reported that Zhào Yánzhào set fires, plundered greatly,
abandoned the city and fled,
stationing himself between Yíng and Mò,
and fortifying himself with water as a barrier.
There are many marshes between Yíng and Mò,
hence Zhào Yánzhào used them as a barrier for fortification.
Yíng and Mò are 110 *lǐ* apart.
Zhū Wénjìn sent an envoy to Táng.
The Táng ruler imprisoned the envoy,
intending to attack him.
The Táng ruler wanted to punish Zhū Wénjìn for the crime of regicide.
In the sixth month, on the Xīnyǒu day,
the government army captured Zīzhōu,
and executed its Cìshǐ (prefect), Liú Hàn.
Zīzhōu
was a prefecture under Yáng Guāngyuǎn's jurisdiction.
Féng Dào, the Tàiwèi and Shìzhōng, although he was the prime minister,
Féng Dào had already been formally appointed as one of the Three Ducal Ministers during the time of Lù Wáng of Táng.
When Gāozǔ of Jìn entered Luò,
he employed him as prime minister,
and his position and authority were above those in government.
He had no power to make decisions.
This was Féng Dào's method of self-preservation and securing his position,
which he used throughout his life.
"操" [cāo] is pronounced 'qī dāo fān'.
"Féng Dào is
a good prime minister in times of peace;
but in these difficult times,
it is like making a Chan monk fly an eagle."
It means that Chan Buddhism takes tranquility and stillness as its principle,
and monks take compassion and non-killing as their teaching.
While a Chan monk
may be endlessly eloquent,
they are unable to adapt to circumstances.
Making them fly an eagle for hunting
is not their task.
On the Guǐmǎo day,
Dào was appointed Kuāngguó Jiédùshǐ,
and concurrently Shìzhōng.
Féng Dào was sent out to govern Tóngzhōu,
intending to appoint another prime minister.
On the Yǐsì day,
the Hàn ruler imprisoned Qí Wáng Hóngbì in his private residence.
Someone said to the Emperor:
"Your Majesty, if you wish to resist the northern barbarians [Běi Dí] and bring peace to the realm,
it cannot be done without Sāng Wéihàn."
The request to dismiss Féng Dào and
the request to employ Sāng Wéihàn
came from the same person.
Earlier histories state that Wéihàn hired someone to speak to the Emperor;
the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn always uses
"or" [huò]
because the source is uncertain.
On the Bǐngwǔ day,
the Shūmìyuàn was reinstated.
The abolition of the Shūmìyuàn is seen in volume 282, Gāozǔ Tiānfú 4th year.
All matters, big or small,
were entrusted to it.
Within a few months,
the court was somewhat better governed.
On the 24th [day], the Yellow River breached its banks in Huázhōu,
submerging the prefectures of Biàn, Cáo, Shàn, Pú, and Yùn,
encircling Liángshān and joining the Wèn River.
Liángshān is located in Shòuzhāng County, Yùn Prefecture.
The Wèn River comes from the northeast
and converges with the Jǐ River northeast of Liángshān.
Now, the waters from the breached river spread widely,
encircling Liángshān and joining the Wèn.
Shàn,
pronounced *shàn*.
Pú,
pronounced *bǔ*.
Huán,
pronounced *huàn*.
Wèn,
pronounced *wèn*.
When the breach was finally sealed,
the Emperor wished to carve a stele to commemorate the event.
Yáng Zhāojiǎn, a Secretariat Drafter, remonstrated, saying:
"Your Majesty carving a stone to record merits
is not as good as issuing an edict of sorrow;
praising in writing
is not as good as distributing a document acknowledging your faults."
The Emperor approved his words and desisted.
Initially, Gāozǔ ceded territory in the northern border to bribe the Qìdān;
this event is recorded in volume 280, Gāozǔ, Tiānfú 1st year.
Fǔzhōu administered one county, Fǔgǔ.
The Later Táng established it on the riverside land northeast of Línzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Fǔzhōu was originally Fǔgǔ Garrison in the Western River barbarian territory.
The local man Zhé Sìlún
served as the garrison commander for generations.
In Tiānyòu 7th year of Zhuāngzōng of Later Táng,
the garrison was elevated to Fǔgǔ County;
in the 8th year,
Fǔzhōu was established to control the barbarian frontier,
and Sìlún’s son, Cóngyuǎn, was made刺史 (cìshǐ).
Zhé,
a surname;
Cóngyuǎn,
a given name.
Brief guide to surnames: Zhé,
pronounced *cháng liè fān*.
The people of the prefecture were greatly alarmed.
Cóngyuǎn then relied on the stronghold to resist them.
When the Emperor broke ties with the Qìdān,
he sent an envoy to instruct Cóngyuǎn to attack the Qìdān.
Cóngyuǎn led his troops deep [into their territory],
capturing over ten forts.
On *wùwǔ* day,
Cóngyuǎn was appointed Fǔzhōu Regimental Commissioner.
Cóngyuǎn was a native of Yúnzhōu.
Ōu Shǐ says: Zhé Cóngyuǎn was a native of Yúnzhōng,
probably referring to the general area of the ancient Yúnzhōng Commandery.
On *jiǎzǐ* day,
the Hanlin Academicians were reinstated.
The abolition of Hanlin Academicians
is recorded in volume 282, Tiānfú 5th year.
On *wùchén* day,
Lǐ Shènyí, Right Sanqi Changshi, was appointed Vice Minister of War and Hanlin Academician Grand Imperial Secretary.
Liú Wēnsǒu, Director of the Department of Public Works, and Xú Táifú, Director of the Department of Finance and Compiler of Imperial Edicts,
(Wǔqiáng County belongs to Shēnzhōu.
*Jiǔyù Zhì* states: it is sixty *lǐ* northeast of the prefecture.)
were all appointed Academicians.
Wēnsǒu was the son of Yuè.
Liú Yuè is mentioned in volume 250, Táng Míngzōng, Tiānchéng 1st year.
In autumn,
7th month,
*xīnwèi* *shuò*,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed.
The era name was changed to Kāiyùn.
On *jǐchǒu* day,
Liú Xù, Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince, was appointed Minister of Works concurrently Menxia Shilang and Grand Academician.
In the 8th month,
*xīnchǒu* *shuò*,
Liú Zhīyuǎn, Military Commissioner of Hédōng, was appointed Supreme Commander of the Northern Front Expeditionary Army,
and Dù Wēi, Military Commissioner of Shùnguó, was appointed Grand Commander of Recruitment and Suppression,
to oversee thirteen military commissioners to prepare for the Qìdān.
Sāng Wéihàn twice held power in court,
sending Yáng Guāngyuǎn and Jǐng Yánguǎng out to the provinces.
(Yáng Guāngyuǎn and Jǐng Yánguǎng
had both previously commanded the Palace Guards.
In early Tiānfú,
Sāng Wéihàn held power and sent Yáng Guāngyuǎn away;
at this time, he again held power and sent Jǐng Yánguǎng away.)
Cháo,
pronounced *zhí yáo fān*.
The fifteen military commissioners dared not disobey.
(Liú Zhīyuǎn, Dù Wēi, and the thirteen military commissioners make fifteen people.
According to Xuē Shǐ, the thirteen military commissioners recorded are:
Zhāng Cóng'ēn of Yùn Prefecture, acting as Commissioner of Infantry and Cavalry;
Jǐng Yánguǎng, Resident Commissioner of Xījīng, acting as Commander of Battle Formations;
Zhào Zàilǐ of Xúzhōu, acting as Commander of the Imperial Guard;
Ān Shūqiān of Jìnzhōu, acting as Commander of the Left Flank Battle Formations;
former Commander of Yǎn, Ān Shěnxìn, acting as Commander of the Right Flank;
Ān Shěnqí of Hézhōng, acting as Commander of Infantry and Cavalry;
Fú Yànqīng of Héyáng, acting as Commander of the Left Flank Cavalry;
Huángfǔ Yù of Huázhōu, acting as Commander of the Right Flank;
Zhāng Yànzé, Commander of the Right Shénwǔ Army, acting as Commander of Cavalry Battle Formations;
Wáng Tíngyìn of Cāngzhōu, acting as Commander of the Left Flank Infantry;
Sòng Yánjūn of Shǎnzhōu, acting as Commander of the Right Flank;
former Commander of Jīn, Tián Wǔ, acting as Commander of the Left Flank Infantry Battle Formations;
Pān Huán, Commander of the Right Lóngwǔ Army, acting as Commander of the Right Flank.)
Fényáng, Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng, submitted a memorial stating that he was not old and still capable,
but the imperial rescript had overlooked him.
Wéihàn issued an imperial edict to the Academicians in the Inner Court,
(Those Academicians in the Inner Court
were so named because they were summoned by imperial edict.
Academicians in the Inner Court
were Academicians who served in the forbidden palace.)
saying, "It is not that the imperial rescript forgot,
but rather that Shuòfāng is a critical area,
and without you, it cannot be controlled.
I was considering transferring you to the interior,
but a replacement also requires an extraordinary talent."
"Shòu"
should be
"shòu".
Fényáng was greatly pleased.
At that time, military and state affairs were numerous,
and requests from all departments and envoys converged like spokes to a hub.
Wéihàn made decisions on each matter,
at first seemingly without much thought,
leading people to suspect his carelessness;
but after he retired and they discussed it thoroughly,
they still could not change it.
However, as a prime minister, he was quite swayed by his likes and dislikes,
always repaying a favor, no matter how small, and an insult, no matter how slight,
which caused people to belittle him.
(The histories praise Sāng Wéihàn's strengths while also mentioning his weaknesses,
thus clarifying right and wrong
and serving as a warning.)
Yá,
pronounced *wǔ xiè fān*.
Zì,
pronounced *shì xiè fān*.
Shào,
pronounced *shī zhào fān*.
When the Qìdān invaded,
the Emperor again ordered Liú Zhīyuǎn to gather troops in Shāndōng.
(Tàiyuán considered the area north of the Yellow River as Shāndōng.)
The Emperor initially ordered Liú Zhīyuǎn to march from Túmén to Héngzhōu,
and then later ordered him to gather troops in Xíngzhōu,
both mentioned above.
The Emperor suspected him
and said to his confidants:
"Tàiyuán is not helping me at all.
He must have other plans.
If he truly has a claim,
why doesn't he act quickly!"
(He meant, if he has a claim to be Son of Heaven,
why doesn't he act quickly.
These were words of anger.)
Fèn,
pronounced *fú wèn fān*.
Yet, he had no real power to control,
and was excluded from confidential and major plans.
Zhīyuǎn also knew he was being sidelined,
but merely acted cautiously and maintained his own position.
Guō Wēi saw Zhīyuǎn's worried expression
and said to him:
"Hédōng's mountains and rivers are dangerous and fortified.
(Hédōng's seat was Jìnyáng.
To the east, it was blocked by Mount Tàiháng and Chángshān;
to the west, it was bordered by Lóngmén and Xīhé;
to the south, it had the strategic passes of Mount Huòtài and Quèshǔ Valley;
to the north, it had the dangers of Yànmén and the Wǔtái Mountains.
Hence the saying.)
The land produces many warhorses.
This is what is meant by relying on dangerous terrain and horses.
The people are accustomed to military life.
These are the resources of a hegemon and king.
What is there to worry about!"
Zhū Wénjìn declared himself Acting Military Governor of Wēiwǔ
and provisionally managed the affairs of Mǐnguó,
sending an envoy to submit a memorial pledging allegiance to Jìn.
On *guǐchǒu* day,
Wénjìn was appointed Military Governor of Wēiwǔ and Manager of Mǐnguó Affairs.
31 On *Guǐhài* day,
Zhènníng Army was established in Chánzhōu.
Púzhōu was subordinated to it.
Púzhōu, which belonged to Tiānpíng Circuit, was detached and subordinated to Zhènníng Army.
32 Initially,
Liú Jīn, the Cìshǐ of Háozhōu under Wú, died.
His son Rén’guī succeeded him.
Rén’guī died.
His son Chóngjùn succeeded him.
Emperor Lièzǔ of Táng established Dìngyuǎn Army in Háozhōu.
Táng established Dìngyuǎn Army in Háozhōu.
The *Zīzhì Tōngjiàn* records this in the third month of the eighth year of Tiānfú, after Yuánzōng's enthronement;
see the previous volume.
Coincidentally, Yáo Jǐng, the Jiédùshǐ of Qīnghuái Circuit, died.
Táng established Qīnghuái Army in Shòuzhōu.
He requested to concurrently govern Shòuzhōu.
The Táng ruler feigned ignorance of his intention
and transferred Chóngjùn to be the Jiédùshǐ of Qīnghuái Circuit,
appointing Liú Yànzhēn, the Cìshǐ of Chǔzhōu, as the Guāncháshǐ of Háozhōu,
and sent him rushing to replace Chóngjùn.
Chóngjùn regretted it.
Yànzhēn
was Xìn's son.
Liú Xìn served the Yáng clan of Wú
and had distinguished himself in battle for four generations.
33 In the ninth month,
on the *Gēngwǔ* day which was the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
34 On *Bǐngzǐ* day,
Khitans raided Suìchéng and Lèshòu.
Suìchéng County
belonged to Yìzhōu.
In the sixth year of Tàipíng Xīngguó of Sòng,
Wēilǔ Army was established.
In the first year of Jǐngdé,
it was renamed Guǎngxìn Army.
It was eighty *lǐ* southeast of Yìzhōu,
controlling the strategic points of Wǔhuí Ridge and Láng Mountain.
Jīn established Suìzhōu there.
Lèshòu County belonged to Shēnzhōu.
Sòng transferred it to Yíngzhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: it is eighty *lǐ* south of Yíngzhōu.
35 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on *Bǐngwǔ* day,
the Hàn ruler poisoned Zhèn Wáng Hóngzé in Yōngzhōu.
36 Yīn ruler Yánzhèng sent his general Chén Jìngquán with three thousand troops to garrison Yóuxī and Gǔtián.
In the second year of Yǒngtài of Táng,
Gǔtián County was established by dividing Hòuguān and Yóuxī.
It belonged to Fúzhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: it is one hundred eighty *lǐ* northwest of the prefecture.
Yóuxī County is one hundred ninety-five *lǐ* south of Nánjiànzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: According to Yóuxī County's administration,
it is now two hundred forty *lǐ* southeast of Yánpíng,
and eight hundred thirty-five *lǐ* northwest of Fúzhōu.
Its territory borders Zhāngzhōu's Lóngyán County, Jiànzhōu's Shāxiàn, and Fúzhōu's Hòuguān County in three places.
The mountains and caves are deep and secluded,
and the shoals and streams are treacherous and steep.
Within it lies a thousand *lǐ* of land.
Many fugitives from various regions seek refuge in these caves.
In the twenty-eighth year of Kāiyuán,
Jīnglüèshǐ Táng Xiūzhōng pacified its people,
and it was named a county after that.
This source was originally called Yóuxī,
hence its name.
Gǔtián County was also established in the twenty-ninth year of Kāiyuán by opening up mountain caves.
In the sixth year of Wǔdé of Táng,
Chángxī County was established,
belonging to Fúzhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: it is three hundred forty-five *lǐ* northeast of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Chángxī County was originally part of Hàn's Mǐn County.
Táng established Wēnmá County,
named after the Wēnmá Stream within the county.
In the ninth year of Tiānbǎo,
it was renamed Chángxī County.
From Quánzhōu, the Sǎnyuán Commander Liú Cóngxiào from Táolín
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Quánzhōu has Táolín Stream,
which was probably where Liú Cóngxiào resided.
Sǎn (*sà*), formerly pronounced *dàn*.
Said: "Zhū Wénjìn slaughtered and exterminated the Wáng clan

13 On the *jǐchǒu* day,
Yèdū was again made Tiānxíong Army.
In the first year of Táng Zhuāngzōng's Tóngguāng reign (923 CE),
Wèizhōu was made Dōngjīng Xīngtáng Fǔ,
and the Tiānxíong military governorship was abolished.
In the third year,
Dōngjīng was abolished and made Yèdū.
When Jìn rose,
it followed this,
changing Xīngtáng Fǔ to Guǎngjìn Fǔ.
Now it is restored to Tiānxíong Army.
14 Zhāng Hànzhēn of Mǐn reached Fúzhōu
and attacked its east pass.
Huáng Rénfěng, hearing that his family had been exterminated,
opened the gates and fought fiercely,
routing the Mǐn army.
He captured Hànzhēn,
entered the city,
and executed him.
Zhuó Yánmíng had no other strategy;
he merely sprinkled water and scattered beans in the main hall,
performing various rituals.
He also sent an envoy to welcome his father from Pútián.
In the early Wǔdé reign of the Táng dynasty (618-626 CE),
Nán'ān County was divided,
and Pútián County was established,
belonging to Quánzhōu.
In the fourth year of Sòng Tàipíng Xīngguó (979 CE),
Xīnghuà Army was established by division,
located one hundred and sixty *lǐ* northeast of Quánzhōu.
Lǐ Réndá, having installed Yánmíng,
personally managed the affairs of the Six Armies and various guards,
sent Huáng Rénfěng to garrison the west gate,
and Chén Jìxún to garrison the north gate.
Rénfěng calmly said to Jìxún:
"What makes a person human
is loyalty, trustworthiness, benevolence, and righteousness.
I once rendered service to Fùshā,
but later betrayed it,
which was not loyalty;
people entrusted their nephews to me, but I conspired with others to kill them,
which was not trustworthiness;
Wáng Jìchāng
was the nephew of Mǐnzhǔ Yánzhèng.
All those I killed were old acquaintances from my hometown,
which was not benevolence;
abandoning my wife and children
and letting others prey on them,
which was not righteousness.
This body has sunk nine times out of ten,
and I will have unending shame even in death!"
Thereupon, he beat his chest and wept bitterly.
Jìxún said:
"A great man pursues fame and achievement,
why care for wife and children!
You should put this matter aside,
lest it bring disaster."
Lǐ Réndá heard of this,
and sent people to accuse Rénfěng and Jìxún of plotting rebellion,
and had them both killed.
From this, military power entirely returned to Lǐ Réndá.
In the 5th month,
on the *bǐngshēn* day,
a general amnesty was issued.
Dù Wēi, the Jiédùshǐ of Shùnguó,
had long garrisoned Héngzhōu.
In the 7th year of Tiānfú under Gāozǔ,
Dù Wēi first took charge of Héngzhōu;
see Volume 283.
Relying on his status as a distinguished relative,
Dù Wēi was married to Gāozǔ's sister, the Sòngguó Zhǎnggōngzhǔ.
He always used border defense as an excuse
to extort money and silk from officials and common people to fill his private coffers.
If wealthy families possessed precious goods, famous beauties, or fine horses,
he would seize them all;
or he would falsely accuse them of crimes and have them killed,
confiscating their families' property.
Moreover, he was excessively cowardly.
Whenever dozens of Qìdān cavalry entered the border,
Dù Wēi would already have closed the gates and mounted the ramparts.
Or when a few Qìdān riders drove thousands of captured Hàn people past the city walls,
Dù Wēi would only glare and crane his neck to watch them,
with no intention of intercepting them.
Consequently, the barbarians had no fear,
and many subordinate cities were massacred by them.
Dù Wēi would not send out a single soldier to rescue them.
Within a thousand *lǐ*,
bones lay exposed like wild growth.
"Exposed bones like wild growth"
is a phrase from the *Zuǒzhuàn*.
"Like wild growth" means
like grass growing profusely in a vast wilderness.
Dù Wēi saw his territory was devastated
and that he was resented by the populace.
Fearing the strength of the Qìdān,
he repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to enter the court,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
Dù Wēi did not wait for a reply,
and abruptly abandoned his post to enter the court.
When the court heard of this,
they were alarmed.
Sāng Wéihàn spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"Dù Wēi indeed disobeyed imperial orders,
abandoning his border garrison.
He habitually relied on his past merits and old connections,
seeking lenient treatment.
When there were many incidents at the frontier,
he had no intention of defending it.
It is fitting to dismiss him at this time,
so as to avoid future troubles."
The Emperor was displeased.
Wéihàn said:
"If Your Majesty cannot bear to dismiss him,
then you should grant him a small post near the capital,
and not again entrust him with a powerful feudal domain."
The Emperor said:
"Dù Wēi
is a close relative of mine,
and surely harbors no disloyal intentions;
meaning he has no other ambitions.
Do not doubt him, Duke!"
From then on, Wéihàn dared not speak again on state affairs,
and resigned his position due to a foot ailment.
Dù Wēi could not be removed, yet Sāng Wéihàn sought to leave;
Jìn was in peril.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
Dù Wēi arrived at Dàliáng.
On the *dīngsì* day,
Lǐ Réndá conducted a grand review of his warriors,
and invited Zhuó Yánmíng to supervise it.
Lǐ Réndá secretly instructed his soldiers to rush forward and ascend the steps,
assassinating Yánmíng.
Lǐ Réndá feigned alarm,
and fled in a panic;
the soldiers together seized Lǐ Réndá
and made him sit in Yánmíng's seat.
Lǐ Réndá then proclaimed himself Wēiwǔ Liúhòu,
using the Bǎodà era name.
This year
was the 3rd year of Bǎodà of the Nán Táng.
He also sent envoys to pay tribute to Jìn;
and killed Yánmíng's father.
The Táng appointed Lǐ Réndá as Wēiwǔ Jiédùshǐ and Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
bestowed upon him the name Hóngyì,
and enrolled him in their clan registry.
Because they shared the same surname,
he was enrolled in their clan registry and given the name Hóngyì,
ranking him among their sons.
This laid the groundwork for Lǐ Réndá to betray Táng and align with Wú-Yuè.
On the *jǐwèi* day,
Dù Wēi presented his divisions of infantry and cavalry, totaling 4,000 men, along with their armor and weapons.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
he also presented 100,000 *hú* of grain
and 200,000 bundles of fodder,
claiming they were all within his territory.
This meant they were all in Héngzhōu.
If he truly possessed them,
they were all cruelly extorted from the people.
In his hasty departure from the garrison,
they could not be transported to fill his private coffers,
hence he offered them.
The infantry belonged to Hùguó,
and Dù Wēi again requested them to be his personal guard,
with all their provisions and stipends to be supplied by the county officials.
Dù Wēi's fooling of the court was like this,
yet the Emperor could not discern his treachery,
which thus led to the Zhōngdù incident in Héngzhōu.
He sought the *Jiéyuè* of Tiānxióng,
and the Emperor granted it.
and repeatedly defeated Quánzhōu forces.
The Quánzhōu forces
were those led by Dǒng Sī'ān and Wáng Zhōngshùn to relieve Jiànzhōu.
They captured its general Shí Hòuqīng.
on the *guǐyǒu* day,
Dù Wēi was appointed Tiānxióng Jiédùshǐ.
The Qìdān invasions
began last year in the 1st month with the fall of Bèizhōu.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states: Shēngōng Wūchén sent a letter to Zǐzhòng and Zǐfǎn, saying: "I will surely make you weary from rushing to battles until you die."
"Rushing to battles" means
when there is an emergency at the border,
rushing to provide aid.
Many Qìdān people and livestock also died,
and the people of the country were weary of the suffering.
Empress Dowager Shùlǜ said to the Qìdān Lord:
"If Hàn people were to be barbarian lords,
would that be acceptable?"
He replied:
"No."
The Empress Dowager said:
"Then why do you wish to be the Hàn Lord?"
He replied:
"The Shí clan was ungrateful,
and cannot be tolerated."
The Empress Dowager said:
"Although you may now gain Hàn territory,
you will not be able to dwell there;
later events indeed proved Empress Dowager Shùlǜ's words.
What will regret avail you then!"
She also said to her subordinates:
"How can the Hàn people sleep so soundly!
When a person cannot sleep comfortably,
they toss and turn, unable to fall asleep;
but to sleep soundly
means their sleep is undisturbed.
I have not heard of barbarians and Hàn making peace.
If the Hàn people can truly change their minds,
why should I begrudge making peace with them!"
Sāng Wéihàn 屢 (repeatedly) advised the Emperor to resume peace talks with the Qìdān to alleviate the national crisis.
The Emperor granted Zhāng Huī, a general of Kāifēng Prefecture, the title of Gòngfèngguān,
a general of Kāifēng Prefecture,
being a general of Kāifēng Fǔ.
He apologized humbly.
The Qìdān ruler said:
"If Jǐng Yánguǎng and Sāng Wéihàn come themselves,
and we are ceded the two circuits of Zhèn and Dìng to be subordinated to us,
then peace can be made."
The imperial court, angered by the Qìdān's words,
believed they had no intention of peace,
and thus stopped.
When the Qìdān ruler entered Dàliáng,
he said to Lǐ Sōng and others:
"If the Jìn envoy had come again previously,
then the north and south would not have gone to war."
History states that the entire Qìdān nation, high and low, was inherently weary of war.
22nd autumn,
seventh month,
some Mǐn people reported that the Fúzhōu relief troops were plotting rebellion.
In the first month of this year,
the Mǐn ruler had dispatched Fúzhōu troops to Jiànzhōu to resist Táng.
When they were sent back,
an ambush was laid in a defile,
and all were slaughtered.
Over eight thousand people died,
and their flesh was dried and taken back for food.
Táng's Biān Hào captured Tánzhōu,
Tánzhōu is 180 *lǐ* east of Jiànzhōu.
All eagerly approved.
The constant demands for supplies exhausted the treasury,
and the people of Hóng, Ráo, Fǔ, and Xìn suffered particularly.
Yánzhèng sent an envoy to present a memorial, declaring himself a subject to Wúyuè,
requesting to be a vassal in exchange for aid.
23rd, Chǔ King Xīfàn suspected Jìngjiāng *Jiédùshǐ* and concurrently *Shìzhōng*, *Zhī Lǎngzhōu* Xīgǎo had gained popular support,
and sent people to spy on him.
Xīgǎo, fearful,
feigned illness and requested to return home,
but was not permitted;
an physician was sent to examine his illness,
and consequently poisoned him.
The matter of Xīfàn's jealousy of Xīgǎo began in volume 280, Gāozǔ Tiānfú Yuánnián.
Annotated by Zhāng Xīchēn, proofread by Niè Chóngqí
Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by Imperial Edict
Hòuxué Tiāntái
Kāiyùn 2nd year (Yǐsì, 945 CE)
1. Eighth month,
Jiǎzǐ *shuò* (first day of the lunar month),
there was a solar eclipse.
2. Bǐngyín,
the Right *Púyè* concurrently *Zhōngshū Shìláng* and *Tóng Píngzhāngshì* Hé Níng was dismissed from his current post;
*Shūmìshǐ* and *Hùbù Shàngshū* Féng Yù was promoted to *Zhōngshū Shìláng* and *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*.
All matters, great or small,
were entrusted to him.
Since the victory at Yángchéng, the Emperor
believed the realm to be free from worries,
and became increasingly extravagant and arrogant.
The victory at Yángchéng is mentioned in the previous volume, last year.
That victories are not to be relied upon is an ancient truth.
Zhòu of the Shāng dynasty achieved a hundred victories yet ultimately had no successor;
Fūchā won many battles,
yet ultimately lost his state.
The victory at Sāngtián was a precursor to the destruction of Guó;
the triumph at Fāngchéng was the foundation for the defeat of Yōng.
Xiàng Liáng died at Dìngtáo, yet Yíng Qín was ruined;
Yǔwénhuàjí was crushed at Líyáng, yet Lǐ Mì was defeated;
all these were calamities resulting from relying on victory.
The Battle of Yángchéng
was won after a perilous situation.
The Qìdān returned north with broken wings,
their resentment growing deeper,
their plans becoming more profound.
Yet the Jìn ruler reclined at ease, believing there were no more troubles.
The ancestral temple of the Shí clan
deserved not to be worshipped.
All went into the imperial treasury;
many exquisite objects were made,
palaces were expanded,
the imperial garden was sumptuously decorated,
something unmatched by recent dynasties;
"Recent dynasties"
refers to recent eras,
such as Liáng and Táng.
Cháo,
read *zhí yáo*.
Several hundred weavers were employed,
and it took a full year to complete;
moreover, actors were rewarded without limit.
Sāng Wéihàn remonstrated, saying:
"Previously, Your Majesty personally led troops against the Hu barbarians,
referring to the Battle of Chányáng in the first year,
detailed in the previous volume.
The rewards were no more than a few bolts of silk.
Now, a single pleasant remark or laugh from an actor
often earns bundles of silk, ten thousand coins, brocade robes, and silver belts.
According to Táng regulations,
ten bolts of silk make a bundle.
How can the soldiers not feel resentful,
saying: 'We risked our lives in battle,
our sinews severed and bones broken,
yet we are not even as meritorious as a single remark or laugh!'
If this continues,
the soldiers will lose morale,
and with whom will Your Majesty protect the altars of state?"
The Emperor did not listen.
Féng Yù was always good at flattering the Emperor,
and thus received even more favor.
Once, when he was ill at home,
the Emperor said to his chancellors:
"No appointments, from *Cǐshǐ* upwards,
may be made until Féng Yù recovers."
Such was the extent of his reliance.
Dòu Guǎngdé had virtuous conduct.
Emperor Wén of Hàn, because Dòu Guǎngdé was his empress's younger brother,
feared that the world would criticize his favoritism,
and dared not appoint him prime minister.
What kind of person was Féng Yù,
that Jìn Emperor Chū openly declared his trust in him at court to show his close reliance!
Rulers facing chaos,
each consider their own ministers worthy.
Is this what is meant?
Bribes and gifts from all directions
converged at his door.
Consequently, court governance further deteriorated.
Historians say that the doom of Jìn was already set.
Cháo,
read *zhí yáo*.
3. The Táng army had besieged Jiànzhōu for a long time.
In the second month of this year,
the Táng army's attack on Jiànzhōu was first mentioned in the previous volume.
Someone said to Dǒng Sī'ān:
Wèi,
meaning to advise him.
"You should decide your course of action soon."
Sī'ān said:
"Our family has served the Wáng clan for generations.
If I betray them in their peril,
who in the world would tolerate me!"
The crowd was moved by his words,
and no one defected.
Dīnghài,
Táng vanguard bridge-and-road commander, Wáng Jiànfēng, the Prince of Shàngyuán, was the first to ascend the walls.
Shàngyuán was originally Jiāngníng County,
renamed during the Shàngyuán era of Táng Sùzōng,
attached to Jiāngníng Fǔ.
Mǐn ruler Yánzhèng surrendered.
Mǐn, since Wáng Cháo gained Fújiàn at the end of Táng,
passed through Shěn Zhī, Yán Hàn, Lín, Chǎng, Xī,
until Yánzhèng and then fell.
Dǒng Sī'ān gathered his troops and fled to Quánzhōu.
Historians say the two generals of Quánzhōu served the Mǐn ruler with consistency.
Initially,
when the Táng army arrived,
the people of Jiàn suffered from the chaos of the Wáng clan and the heavy taxes of Yáng Sīgōng.
Yáng Sīgōng's heavy taxes are mentioned in volume 283, Tiānfú 8th year.
Liǎn,
read *lì shàn*.
After Jiànzhōu was taken, the soldiers were allowed to plunder extensively,
burning all palaces, houses, and dwellings;
that night, with cold rain,
the frozen dead lay piled upon each other,
and the people of Jiàn were disappointed.
The Táng ruler, considering their merits,
did not question them.
4. The Hàn ruler killed Sháo Prince Hóngyǎ.
Hóngyǎ was the Hàn ruler's younger brother.
5. Ninth month,
Xǔ Wénzhěn with Tíngzhōu,
Wáng Jìxūn with Quánzhōu,
and Wáng Jìchéng with Zhāngzhōu,
all surrendered to Táng.
Xúnzǐ once said:
"Unifying is easy,
but solidifying is difficult."
Táng could take Mǐn,
but could not permanently possess Mǐn.
This sets the stage for the Mǐn people's rebellion against Táng.
6. Bǐngshēn,
Jǐng Yánguǎng, the Western Capital Commissioner and concurrently *Shìzhōng*, was appointed Deputy Commander of the Northern Front Campaign.
7 Diànzhōngjiān Wáng Qīnzuò (殿中監王欽祚) was provisionally appointed to oversee affairs in Héngzhōu (恆州).
At that time, there was a shortage of military provisions,
so an imperial edict ordered Qīnzuò (欽祚) to requisition grain from the common people.
Dù Wēi (杜威) had over 100,000 hú (斛) of grain in Héngzhōu (恆州).
Qīnzuò (欽祚) compiled a registry of it and reported it.
Wēi (威) was furious,
and submitted a memorial stating:
"What crime have I committed,
that Qīnzuò (欽祚) should confiscate my grain?!"
The imperial court, on account of this, recalled Qīnzuò (欽祚).
Was Dù Wēi's (杜威) grain in Héngzhōu (恆州)
not the same amount that he had previously offered in a memorial?
Even if it were beyond what he had offered in a memorial,
it was still extorted from what the military and people had accumulated.
To list it and confiscate it,
what fault was there in that?
If the laws of the imperial court
do not apply to the noble and favored,
but only oppress the poor and humble to meet demands,
then the state is no longer its state.
為 (wéi),
read as yú wěi fān.
還 (huán),
read as cóng xuān fān.
8 On the day wù shēn (戊申),
the Wēixìn Jūn (威信軍) was established in Cáozhōu (曹州).
9 Lǐ Shǒuzhēn (李守貞), the Shìwèi Mǎbù Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ (侍衞馬步都指揮使), was dispatched to garrison Chánzhōu (澶州).
10On the day yǐ mǎo (乙卯),
Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤), the Zhāngdé Jiédùshǐ (彰德節度使), was dispatched to garrison Héngzhōu (恆州).
11The Hàn Zhǔ (漢主) executed Liú Sīcháo (劉思潮), Lín Shǎoqiáng (林少強), Lín Shǎoliáng (林少良), and Hé Chāngtíng (何昌廷).
As for Zuǒ Púyè Wáng Yùn (左僕射王翷),
he had once conspired with Gāozǔ (高祖) to establish Hóngchāng (弘昌).
The details are found in volume 283, Tiānfú (天福) seven years.
Yīngzhōu (英州)
was the land of Zhēnyáng Xiàn (湞陽縣), Guìyáng Jùn (桂陽郡) under Hàn (漢).
During the Táng (唐) dynasty, Zhēnyáng Xiàn (湞陽縣) was subordinate to Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
Hàn Zhǔ Liú Yǎn (漢主劉龑) divided Zhēnyáng Xiàn (湞陽縣) to establish Yīngzhōu (英州).
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: From Guǎngzhōu (廣州) north to Yīngzhōu (英州) is 420 lǐ (里).
He was granted death.
Both within and outside the court, everyone feared for their safety.
12In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day guǐ sì (癸巳),
the Zhèn'ān Jūn (鎮安軍) was established in Chénzhōu (陳州).
13Táng Yuánjìng Sòng Tàihòu (唐元敬宋太后) passed away.
14Wáng Yánzhèng (王延政) arrived at Jīnlíng (金陵).
The Táng Zhǔ (唐主) appointed him as Yǔlín Dàjiàngjūn (羽林大將軍).
Yáng Sīgōng (楊思恭) was executed to apologize to the people of Jiàn (建).
This was because Yáng Sīgōng (楊思恭) had heavily extorted wealth.
He promoted refined governance with leniency and simplicity,
and the people of Jiàn (建) then became peaceful.
To pacify the desolate remnants,
such governance was appropriate.
Since Gài Gōng (蓋公) transmitted this method to Cáo Cān (曹參),
Cān (參) used it as chancellor in Qí (齊),
and again as chancellor in Hàn (漢),
but later generations rarely knew this method.
治 (zhì),
read as zhí zhī fān.
15Initially,
Gāolí Wáng Jiàn (高麗王建) used military force to annex neighboring states,
and became quite powerful.
Details are found in volume 281, Gāozǔ Tiānfú (高祖天福) first year.
麗 (lí),
read as lì zhī fān.
"Bóhǎi (勃海) is our marital kin.
Its king was captured by the Qìdān (契丹).
I request to jointly attack and retrieve him with the imperial court."
Gāozǔ (高祖) did not respond.
When the Emperor became an enemy of the Qìdān (契丹),
Wàluō (襪囉) mentioned it again.
The Emperor wanted to make Gāolí (高麗) harass the Qìdān's (契丹) eastern border to divide their military strength.
Coincidentally, Jiàn (建) died,
and his son Wǔ (武) declared himself provisionally in charge of state affairs.
He submitted a memorial reporting the death.
In the eleventh month,
on the day wù xū (戊戌),
Wǔ (武) was appointed Dàyì Jūnshǐ (大義軍使) and Gāolí Wáng (高麗王).
The Tōngshì Shèrén (通事舍人) Guō Rénwù (郭仁遇) was dispatched to his country
to convey the instruction to attack the Qìdān (契丹).
Fearing that the Qìdān (契丹) would know,
it was not put into an official edict,
but merely conveyed through an imperial instruction.
Seeing that their military was extremely weak,
Wàluō's (襪囉) previous words
were merely Jiàn's (建) exaggeration;
he truly did not dare to be an enemy of the Qìdān (契丹).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: During the Tiānfú (天福) reign of the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
a Western Regions monk, Wàluō (襪囉), came to court.
He was skilled in divination by fire.
Soon, he took leave of Gāozǔ (高祖)
and requested to travel to Gāolí (高麗).
Wáng Jiàn (王建) treated him with great respect.
At that time, the Qìdān (契丹) had already occupied the land of Bóhǎi (勃海) for many years.
Jiàn (建) then casually said to Wàluō (襪囉):
"Bóhǎi (勃海) was originally a relative state of ours.
Its king was captured by the Qìdān (契丹).
I wish to attack and retrieve it for the imperial court,
and also to settle old grievances.
When you return,
please speak to the Son of Heaven for me;
we should schedule a joint attack."
Wàluō (襪囉) returned
and fully reported it,
but Gāozǔ (高祖) did not respond.
When the Emperor and the Qìdān (契丹) engaged in battle,
Wàluō (襪囉) reported it again.
The Emperor sent Guō Rénwù (郭仁遇) with a swift edict to instruct Jiàn (建)
to deeply attack their territory to pressure them.
Coincidentally, Jiàn (建) had already died.
Wǔ (武) was in charge of state affairs,
and did not get along with his father's ministers;
they were devouring each other.
The internal difficulties were somewhat resolved,
but military might had not yet been established.
Moreover, the barbarian people were timid and weak.
Wàluō's (襪囉) words
were all Jiàn's (建) vain boasting.
Wǔ (武) then offered other reasons as an explanation.
He offered an explanation to defend himself.
16On the day yǐ mǎo (乙卯),
Wúyuè Wáng Hóngzuǒ (吳越王弘佐) executed the Nèidūjiānshǐ (內都監使) Dù Zhāodá (杜昭達).
On the day jǐ wèi (己未),
he executed the Nèiyá Shàng Tǒngjūnshǐ (內牙上統軍使) and Míngzhōu Cǐshǐ (明州刺史) Kàn Fán (闞璠).
Zhāodá (昭達)
was the grandson of Jiànhuī (建徽).
Dù Jiànhuī (杜建徽) had rendered meritorious service assisting Wúyuè Wáng Qián Liú (吳越王錢鏐).
Chéng Zhāoyuè (程昭悅), a wealthy man from Qiántáng (錢塘), used bribes to cultivate a relationship with the two men,

Zhāoyuè (昭悅) was cunning and deceitful,

favoring him more than the old generals.
Fán (璠) was displeased;
Zhāoyuè (昭悅), knowing this,
went to Fán (璠) and prostrated himself, apologizing.
Fán (璠) reprimanded him for a long time,
then said:
"Initially, I was determined to kill you;
but now that you have repented,
I am also relieved."
Zhāoyuè (昭悅) was afraid
and plotted to remove Fán (璠).
Fán (璠) was dictatorial and stubborn,
and many people in the state detested him.
Zhāoyuè (昭悅) wanted to send Fán (璠) out,
fearing Fán (璠) would realize it.
He privately said to the Yòu Tǒngjūnshǐ (右統軍使) Hú Jìnsī (胡進思):
"Now, I want to appoint you and Fán (璠) as governors of your respective prefectures.
Would this make Fán (璠) unsuspecting?"
Jìnsī (進思) agreed,
so Fán (璠) was appointed Míngzhōu Cǐshǐ (明州刺史),

Kàn Fán (闞璠)
was from Míngzhōu (明州);

"Sending me out

Fán (璠) then accepted the appointment.
Soon after, Jìnsī (進思) was retained for other reasons.
The mother of Nèi wài Mǎbù Dūtǒngjūnshǐ (內外馬步都統軍使) Qián Rénjùn (錢仁俊)

Zhāoyuè (昭悅) then slandered Fán (璠) and Zhāodá (昭達),

After Fán (璠) and Zhāodá (昭達) were executed,

Thereupon, Zhāoyuè (昭悅) purged Fán's (璠) and Dù's (杜) faction.
Anyone whose authority

The people of the state feared him and eyed him with apprehension.

治 (zhì),

Hú Jìnsī (胡進思) alone was spared,

Shèn (慎)

Shèn Wēnqí (慎溫其) was promoted from a prefectural official to a national official.

In the twelfth month of the 17th year,
on the Yǐchǒu (乙丑) day,

The Táng (唐) dynasty changed Wèizhōu (魏州) to Xīngtáng Fǔ (興唐府);

He was a member of Fēng Yù’s (馮玉) faction;

Consequently, requests and bribes

In the 19th year,

the Emperor was ill,

this refers to the first day of the first month of this year.

Ruì (睿)

Wéihàn (維翰) then claimed a foot ailment,
hoping to avoid court attendance

This was also to distance himself from suspicion.
Fù (復)

Someone said to Fēng Yù (馮玉):
"Sāng Gōng (桑公) is an elder statesman;
now that he has been relieved of his key duties,
even if he is not retained in a chancellery position,

Why make him Prefect of the Capital (Yǐn Jīng 尹京)
to personally handle trivial matters?"
Wěi (猥) means "miscellaneous."
"I fear he might rebel."
This means the reason Wéihàn (維翰) was not given a major command
was the fear that he would use military force to rebel.
"How can a scholar rebel!"
Yù (玉) said:
"Even if he does not rebel himself,
I fear he might incite others."
This refers to Wéihàn’s (維翰) approval of Jìnzǔ’s (晉祖) plan to raise troops in Jìnyáng (晉陽).
In the 20th year, the hermit Dài Yǎn (戴偃) from Xiāngyīn (湘陰), Chǔ (楚).

Chǔ (楚) King Xīfàn (希範) imprisoned him;

In the 21st year, Xiè Zhòngxuān (謝仲宣), a subordinate of Qí (齊) King Jǐngdá’s (景達) administration, said to Jǐngdá (景達):

The Táng (唐) ruler then had Jǐngdá (景達) personally go to Qīngyáng (青陽) to summon him.
Qíqiū (齊丘) was living in seclusion in Qīngyáng (青陽), as seen in volume 283, Tiānfú (天福) fourth year.
In the 1st year, in spring,
the first month,
Qíqiū (齊丘) was made Grand Tutor (Tàifù 太傅) concurrently Central Secretariat Director (Zhōngshū Lìng 中書令),
but he merely attended court requests
and did not participate in government affairs.
He only attended court assemblies and responded to summons.
Along with Central Secretariat Attendant (Zhōngshū Shìláng 中書侍郎) Fēng Yánjǐ (馮延己), they were both made Joint Administrators of Affairs (Tóng Píngzhāngshì 同平章事).
Jiànxūn (建勳) was experienced in official matters,

Yánjǐ (延己) was skilled in writing,

Gāo Yuè (高越), a Director in the Ministry of Public Works (Shuǐbù Lángzhōng 水部郎中),

Earlier,

The Táng (唐) ruler said to Mèngxī (夢錫):

History says that when righteousness and evil are mixed,

on the Rénxū (壬戌) day, the first day of the month,

Jìn (晉) changed Jīngzhào Fǔ (京兆府) to Jìnchāng Jūn (晉昌軍).
Wherever he went, he was greedy and tyrannical;
his family wealth was the greatest among all the commanders.
The Emperor coveted his wealth,

Wáng Jìxūn (王繼勳) and Lǐ Hóngyì (李弘義) both served Southern Táng (Nántáng 南唐);

Lǐ Hóngyì (李弘義) used this as a pretext for war.

The three clans of Tuòbá Yànchāo, Shí Cún, and Yěsībāo,

Liú Cóngxiào installed Wáng Jìxūn (see previous volume, previous year).

Two hundred *lǐ* northwest of Dìngzhōu there was Lángshān.

She misled the public with sorcery.
Her predictions were quite accurate,

Sūn Fāngjiǎn, a man from Zhōngshān,

At this time, Jìn and the Qìdān severed good relations.
Taxes and corvée labor on the northern border were burdensome,

Fāngjiǎn and Xíngyǒu thereupon led the strong and influential people of their locality.

When the Qìdān invaded,
Fāngjiǎn led his followers to intercept and attack them.
He captured quite a lot of their armor, weapons, cattle, horses, and military supplies.
The number of people who brought their families to join him increased daily.

they reached over a thousand families,

Fearing they would be suppressed by officials,

The imperial court also valued his resistance against invaders,

Fāngjiǎn often entered Qìdān territory to plunder and loot,

Afterwards, he made incessant demands.
If the imperial court slightly failed to satisfy his wishes,

In the border regions,
there were treacherous people like this,

The Táng people called them

In the area between Yǎn, Yùn, Cāng, and Bèi (prefectures),

At first,
after the Táng people had conquered Jiànzhōu,
