his words and demeanor were very disdainful.
He treated him coldly.
Jué did not dare to mention the matter of coming to court and returned.
(This lays the groundwork for Chén Jué raising troops to attack Fúzhōu, suffering defeat, and returning.)
(The character 還,
is pronounced *cóngxuānfān*,
or as written.)
In the 11th year, autumn,
in the 7th month,
the Hé river burst its banks at Yángliú,
flowing west into Xīnxiàn,
becoming forty *lǐ* wide,
then flowing north from Cháochéng.
Xīnxiàn is east of Wèizhōu,
Cháochéng is southeast of Wèizhōu,
forty *lǐ* apart.
廣 (*guǎng*),
read like *kuàng* in ancient pronunciation.
There was someone who came from Yōuzhōu,
saying that Zhào Yánshòu intended to return to the state;
the Grand Councillors Lǐ Sōng and Féng Yù believed him,
and ordered Dù Wēi, the Military Commissioner of Tiānxíong, to send a letter to Yánshòu,
fully stating the imperial decree,
and tempting him with rich rewards.
Zhào Xíngshí, a military commander from Luòzhōu,
had previously served Yánshòu.
He was dispatched to secretly carry the letter and deliver it.
Yánshòu wrote back saying:
"Having been in a foreign land for a long time,
I long to return to the Central Plains.
I beg for a large army to be sent to meet and receive me,
so that I may extract myself and go south."
His words were sincere and earnest.
The imperial court was delighted,
and again sent Xíngshí to Yánshòu
to arrange a meeting.
The Jìn people from this point fell into Zhào Yánshòu's scheme.
read like *fú yòu*.
In the 8th month,
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn reported:
"I encountered more than a thousand Qìdān cavalry north of the Great Wall."
This refers to the Great Wall built by Yān during the Warring States period,
located south of Gù'ānxìan in Zhuōzhōu.
Xuē Shǐ says: Lǐ Shǒuzhēn reported that the main army reached Wàngdūxiàn,
and subsequently arrived north of the Great Wall,
where they encountered the barbarians and engaged in battle.
Their chieftain, Xièlǐ, was beheaded.
A great number of the remaining troops were driven into the water and drowned.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
an imperial edict ordered Lǐ Shǒuzhēn to return and garrison Chánzhōu.
Since the Emperor had broken off good relations with the Qìdān,
he repeatedly summoned the Tǔyùhún chieftain, Bái Chéngfú, to court,
entertaining and rewarding him generously.
Chéngfú accompanied the Emperor in the battle against the Qìdān at Chánzhōu,
and also garrisoned Huázhōu with Zhāng Cóng'ēn.
As the year was unusually hot,
he was sent with his tribe back to Tàiyuán,
to pasture livestock in the territory of Lán and Shí prefectures.
Many of the tribe committed unlawful acts,
but Liú Zhīyuǎn did not tolerate any leniency;
the tribe knew the imperial court was weak,
and also feared Zhīyuǎn's strictness,
so they conspired to flee back to their old lands.
The Tǔyùhún tribe, knowing the imperial court was weak,
and also fearing Liú Zhīyuǎn's strictness;
yet dared not cause trouble in Tàiyuán
because they dreaded Liú Zhīyuǎn's prestige and strategy,
and had no means to indulge their treachery,
thus they wished to flee back to their old lands.
Bái Kějiǔ, whose rank was second only to Chéngfú,
led his department in deserting first to the Qìdān.
The Qìdān appointed him as Observer of Yúnzhōu,
to lure Chéngfú.
Zhīyuǎn discussed with Guō Wēi, saying:
"Today, the world is in turmoil,
keeping these people in Tàiyuán
is a hidden danger to our heartland;
it is better to eliminate them."
Chéngfú's family was very wealthy;
they used silver troughs to feed their horses.
Wēi persuaded Zhīyuǎn to execute him
and confiscate his wealth to provision the army.
Zhīyuǎn secretly memorialized:
"The Tǔyùhún are treacherous and unreliable;
I request that they be relocated to the interior."
The Emperor sent an envoy to dispatch one thousand nine hundred people from their tribe,
distributing them among Héyáng and other prefectures.
Zhīyuǎn sent Wēi to lure Chéngfú and others to live inside Tàiyuán city.
Then he falsely accused Chéngfú and five clans of plotting rebellion,
surrounded them with troops and killed them,
totaling four hundred people,
and confiscated their family property.
An imperial edict praised and rewarded him.
The Tǔyùhún thus declined.
The Wǔdài Huìyào states: Among the Tǔyùhún chieftains was Hèlián Duó.
During the Xiántōng era of the Táng dynasty,
he assisted Kāng Chéngxùn, the Military Commissioner of Tàiyuán, in pacifying Xúfāng, and was meritorious.
The imperial court appointed him Military Commissioner of Zhènwǔ.
He later illegally occupied Yúnzhōng.
After Emperor Tàizǔ of Later Táng expelled him,
he returned to Lǐ Kuāngchóu of Yōuzhōu;
his tribe scattered and resided in Wèizhōu territory,
alternately having their own leaders,
their surnames not constant.
There was Bái Chéngfú,
who, from the Tóngguāng era, successively served as Commandant.
He established a stockade relying on Shímén north of Zhōngshān.
Emperor Zhuāngzōng bestowed on it the plaques of the Níngshuò and Fènghuà prefectures,
and made the commandant a Military Commissioner,
also granting Chéngfú the surname Lǐ
and the name Shàolǔ.
His livestock
would seek out good water and grass,
and his able-bodied men often numbered several thousand.
His sheep and horses multiplied,
entering the markets of the Central Plains,
and the imperial court always cared for them.
In the third year of Qīngtài of King Lù,
Bái Kějiǔ became the Níngshuò and Fènghuà Resident Administrator,
first appearing in history.
In the first year of Tiānfú of Jìn,
Gāozǔ, because the Qìdān had helped him ascend the throne,
ceded the land north of Yànmén and Yōuzhōu to bribe them,
thus the Tǔyùhún tribes were all subordinated to the Qìdān.
Afterwards, suffering from the harsh rule of the Qìdān,
they were again lured by Ān Chóngróng, the Military Commissioner of Zhènzhōu,
and thus turned against the Qìdān,
leading their tents, wagons, sheep, and horses to return to the state via the Wǔtái road.
The Qìdān were furious,
and, because the imperial court harbored deserters,
sent an envoy to rebuke them.
In the first month of the sixth year,
Gāozǔ ordered Gòngfèngguān Zhāng Chéng and others to lead two thousand soldiers
to search the valleys of Bìng, Zhèn, Xīn, and Dài prefectures for Tǔyùhún,
and return them to their old lands;
however, also because the Qìdān's demands were insatiable,
he was displeased at heart,
and ordered Hàn Gāozǔ to be stationed in Tàiyuán,
secretly comforting and appeasing them.
In the fifth month of that year,
the great chieftain Bái Chéngfú and his subordinates came to court;
in the ninth month,
he again sent chieftain Bái Kějiǔ to court.
The Young Emperor succeeded to the throne,
severed relations with the Qìdān,
and repeatedly summoned their chieftains to court,
bestowing generous gifts.
During every grand banquet,
they were ordered to be seated alongside the meritorious officials.
When repelling the barbarians at Chánzhōu during the Kāiyùn era,
Chéngfú and others were summoned to lead their tribes and follow.
As that year was exceptionally hot,
many of their subordinates died,
so they were sent back to Tàiyuán,
and their tents moved to Lán and Shí prefectures.
However, Chéngfú had no discipline over his subordinates,
and they frequently violated military orders.
His kinsman, Bái Kějiǔ,
who was Chéngfú's second-in-command,
took advantage of grazing horses
to lead his own tents and flee north.
The Qìdān bestowed official titles and ranks upon him,
and again sent him to secretly lure Chéngfú.
Chéngfú also wished to rebel and leave,
but the matter was not yet accomplished.
Hànzǔ, knowing this,
then surrounded his tribe with soldiers,
captured Chéngfú and his kinsmen Bái Tiěguì, Hèlián Hǎilóng, and five other families,
totaling over four hundred people,
and executed them.
Their cattle and horses were confiscated,
and another chieftain, Wáng Yìzōng, was ordered to lead the remaining members.
Mùróng Yànchāo, the Prefect of Púzhōu, was punished for illegally levying taxes
and illicitly taking five hundred *hú* of government wheat to make *qū* (fermenting agent),
which he distributed to the local people.
Lǐ Yàntāo had long held a grudge against Yànchāo,
exposed his actions,
and the crime warranted death.
Yàntāo urged Féng Yù to have him killed,
but Liú Zhīyuǎn submitted a memorial arguing for his rescue.
Mùróng Yànchāo was Liú Zhīyuǎn's younger brother by the same mother,
so he rescued him.
上 (*shàng*),
read like *shí zhǎng*.
"Crimes like Yànchāo's
are committed by all regional commanders in the empire today.
If the law were fully applied to them,
I fear that no one would feel secure."
On the *jiǎxū* day,
an imperial edict pardoned Yànchāo from death,
stripped him of his official titles and ranks,
and exiled him to Fángzhōu.
15 Táng Chén Jué (陳覺) returned from Fúzhōu (福州),
arriving at Jiànzhōu (劍州).
Jiànzhōu (劍州)
was the Tánzhōu (鐔州) established by Yīn (殷) ruler Wáng Yánzhèng (王延政).
After Southern Táng (南唐) conquered Jiànzhōu (建州),
it divided Yánpíng (延平), Jiànpǔ (建浦), and Fùshā (富沙) three counties to establish Jiànzhōu (劍州).
When Sòng (宋) unified the realm,
because there was also a Jiànzhōu (劍州) in Shǔ (蜀) region,
it added
the character
"Nán" (南) to make it Nánjiànzhōu (南劍州).
He was ashamed that he had boasted of inviting Lǐ Hóngyì (李弘義) to court but failed to achieve it.
Shìwèi guān (侍衞官)
refers to guards stationed directly by the ruler's side,
similar to the Shìguān (侍官) of the flourishing Táng (唐) dynasty.
Chén Jué (陳覺) dispatched troops and garrison soldiers from Tíng (汀), Jiàn (建), Fǔ (撫), and Xìn (信) prefectures,
ordering the Jiànzhōu (建州) supervisor of the army, Féng Yánlǔ (馮延魯), to lead them,
and hasten to Fúzhōu (福州) to welcome Hóngyì (弘義).
Yánlǔ (延魯) first sent a letter to Hóngyì (弘義),
informing him of the consequences (fortune and misfortune).
Hóngyì (弘義) replied, requesting battle,
and sent the Louchan Zhihuishi (樓船指揮使), Yáng Chóngbǎo (楊崇保), to lead the prefectural army to resist them.
One version
of "zhōushī" (州師)
writes
"zhōushī" (舟師).
The Jiànxī (建溪) river flows eastward through Jiànzhōu (劍州) to Fúzhōu (福州),
all part of a great river,
so locals also referred to it as a river.
"Fúzhōu (福州) is isolated and precarious;
it can be captured any day."
The Táng (唐) ruler was very angry at Jué (覺) for taking decisions independently;
many of his trusted ministers said:
"The troops have already reached the city walls,
it is impossible to stop them;
we must send reinforcements to assist them."
On the day of dīngchǒu (丁丑),
Jué (覺) and Yánlǔ (延魯) defeated Yáng Chóngbǎo (楊崇保) at Hòuguān (候官).
The two counties, Mǐn (閩) and Hòuguān (候官),
both administered Fúzhōu (福州) outside the city walls.
This battle took place within the Hòuguān (候官) county borders.
"Bài" (敗),
read bù mài fān.
On the day of wùyín (戊寅),
they capitalized on their victory and attacked the western gate of Fúzhōu (福州).
Hóngyì (弘義) sallied forth,
utterly defeated them,
and captured Yáng Kuāngyè (楊匡鄴), the Táng Zuǒ Shénwēi Zhǐhuīshǐ (唐左神威指揮使).
The Táng (唐) ruler appointed Wáng Chóngwén (王崇文), the Yǒng'ān Jiédùshǐ (永安節度使), as Dōngnánmiàn Dūzhāotǎoshǐ (東南面都招討使).
In the tenth month of last year,
Táng (唐) established the Yǒng'ān (永安) military command in Jiànzhōu (建州).
Yánlǔ (延魯) was made Nánmiàn Jiānjūnshǐ (南面監軍使),
and they gathered troops to attack Fúzhōu (福州),
capturing its outer wall.
Hóngyì (弘義) strongly defended the second wall.
It was the second layer of the city wall.
16 Féng Huī (馮暉) led his troops across the dry sea (hànhǎi),
arriving at Huīdé (輝德).
Zhāng Jì (張洎) said: "From Wēizhōu (威州) to Língzhōu (靈州) lies seven hundred *lǐ* (里) of dry sea (hànhǎi),
a salty, barren marsh
with no streams, brooks, or river valleys."
Huīdé (輝德)
is a place name,
south of Língwǔ (靈武).
Zhāng Shùnmín (張舜民) said: "The current dry river plain is the dry sea (hànhǎi),
north of Qīngyuǎn Jūn (清遠軍)."
Zhào Xún (趙珣) in his *Jùmǐ tújīng* (聚米圖經) said: "Between Yán (鹽), Xià (夏), and Qīngyuǎn Jūn (清遠軍),
it is all sandy desert,
commonly called the dry sea (hànhǎi)."
From Huánzhōu (環州), exiting through Qīnggāng Chuān (青剛川),
was originally the main road to Língzhōu (靈州).
From here, passing Měilì Zhài (美利寨),
gradually entering Píngxià (平夏),
traversing the dry sea (hànhǎi),
it was difficult to find water sources.
To Yàodé Qīngbiān Zhèn (耀德清邊鎮) entering Língzhōu (靈州).
Tuòbá Yànchāo (拓跋彥超)'s forces numbered several tens of thousands,
arranged in three formations,
blocking key routes,
and occupying water sources to await them.
Great fear arose in the army.
Huī (暉) sought peace with Yànchāo (彥超) through bribery,
and Yànchāo (彥超) agreed.
From dawn until noon,
emissaries went back and forth several times,
but the troops had not disengaged.
Yào Yuánfú (藥元福) said:
"The barbarians know we are hungry and thirsty;
they are pretending to agree to peace to wear us down.
If it reaches evening,
then we will be captured.
Although the barbarians are numerous now,
their elite troops are not many;
those arrayed along the Western Mountains are the elite.
The rest of the infantry
are not a concern.
I ask you, my lord, to maintain a strict formation and await me."
"Yánchén" (嚴陳) means
to arrange troops in a strict formation.
"If I achieve a minor victory, I will raise a yellow banner,
and the main army should join forces and strike them;
we will surely defeat them."
Thereupon, he led his cavalry forward,
fighting fiercely with short weapons.
Yànchāo (彥超) retreated slightly;
Yuánfú (元福) raised the yellow banner,
and Huī (暉) led his troops to him.
Yànchāo (彥超) was utterly defeated.
Féng Huī (馮暉) had imprisoned Tuòbá Yànchāo (拓跋彥超) within Língwǔ (靈武) city,
and Yànchāo (彥超) knew the reason and harbored resentment.
When Huī (暉) left the garrison, Yànchāo (彥超) was released.
Once Yànchāo (彥超) was released, Huī (暉) returned.
A tiger released from its cage,
if it could retaliate,
would stop at nothing.
If he did not defeat him through force of battle,
Féng Huī (馮暉)'s authority could not be re-established in Shuòfāng (朔方).
"Shuài" (帥),
read "shuài".
Huī (暉) entered Língzhōu (靈州).
17 In the ninth month,
the Qìdān (契丹) with thirty thousand invaded Hédōng (河東);
on the day of rénchén (壬辰),
Liú Zhīyuǎn (劉知遠) defeated them in Yángwǔ Gǔ (陽武谷),
beheading seven thousand.
18 After Hàn (漢) Liú Sīcháo (劉思潮) and others died,
Chén Dàoxiáng (陳道庠) felt uneasy internally.
Chén Dàoxiáng (陳道庠)
was among those who assassinated Hàn (漢) ruler Hóngdù (弘度) with Liú Sīcháo (劉思潮) and others.
The killing of Liú Sīcháo (劉思潮) and others was seen in the ninth month of last year.
According to Lù Zhèn (路振)'s *Jiǔguó Zhì* (九國志),
Chén Dàoxiáng (陳道庠)'s father, Dāng (璫),
had old ties with Dèng Shēn (鄧伸),
hence this situation.
Shēn (伸) said:
"You foolish fellow!
This book contains the stories of executing Hán Xìn (韓信) and mincing Péng Yuè (彭越);
you should read it carefully!"
When the Hàn (漢) ruler heard this,
he exterminated Dàoxiáng (道庠)'s and Shēn (伸)'s clans.
19 Lǐ Hóngyì (李弘義) declared himself Wēiwǔ Liúhòu (威武留後),
changed his name to Hóngdá (弘達),
and presented a memorial to the Jìn (晉) for appointment;
Lǐ Hóngyì (李弘義)'s original name was Rén'ér (仁達);
Hóngyì (弘義) was the name bestowed by Táng (唐);
having rebelled against Táng (唐),
he then changed his name.
On the day of jiǎwǔ (甲午),
Hóngdá (弘達) was appointed Wēiwǔ Jiédùshǐ (威武節度使) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事),
in charge of the affairs of Mǐnguó (閩國).
20 Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤) reported defeating the Qìdān (契丹) north of Dìngzhōu (定州),
and again defeated them at Tàizhōu (泰州),
beheading two thousand.
21 On the day of xīncǒu (辛丑),
Fúzhōu (福州)'s Páichénshǐ (排陳使), Mǎ Jié (馬捷),
led Táng (唐) troops from Mǎmùshān (馬牧山), capturing their encampment and entering,
reaching the Shànhuàmén Qiáo (善化門橋).
Dūzhǐhuīshǐ (都指揮使) Dīng Yànzhēn (丁彥貞) resisted them with a hundred soldiers.
Hóngdá (弘達) retreated to defend Shànhuàmén (善化門),
as both outer city walls were occupied by Táng (唐) troops.
Hóngdá (弘達) changed his name to Dá (達).
Hóngdá (弘達) changed his name to Dá (達),
because the name of the Wúyuè (吳越) king had *hóng* (弘) at the beginning,
so he avoided it.
"Zhòng" (重),
read zhí lóng fān.
"Gèng" (更),
read gōng héng fān.
He requested aid from Wúyuè (吳越).
22 Chǔ (楚) King Xīfàn (希範), knowing the Emperor preferred luxury and extravagance,
repeatedly offered treasures as tribute,
seeking the title of Dū Yuánshuài (都元帥);
on the day of jiǎchén (甲辰),
Xīfàn (希範) was appointed Zhū Dào Bīngmǎ Dū Yuánshuài (諸道兵馬都元帥).
On the day of bǐngchén (丙辰),
the Yellow River breached its banks at Línhuáng (臨黃) in Chánzhōu (澶州).
Línhuáng (臨黃) was
a town on the river in Wèi (衞) during the Spring and Autumn period,
known as Guān Xiàn (觀縣) in Dōng Jùn (東郡) during the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
where Wèi (衞) Xuāngōng's (宣公) new terrace was located.
The Later Wèi (後魏) established Línhuáng Xiàn (臨黃縣),
which belonged to Chánzhōu (澶州) in the Táng (唐) dynasty;
in the first year of Duāngǒng (端拱) of Sòng (宋), Línhuáng (臨黃) was absorbed into Guānchéng Xiàn (觀城縣).
The Qìdān envoy to Yíngzhōu, Inspector Liú Yánzuò, sent a letter to Wáng Luán, the Supervising Commissioner of Lèshòu,
asking him to offer the city in submission.
It also said:
"The Qìdān soldiers in the city are less than a thousand.
We beg the imperial court to send light troops to attack them,
and I will act as an internal confederate.
Furthermore,
this autumn has seen much rain.
From Wǎqiáo northward,
the accumulated water is boundless.
The Qìdān lord has already returned to his imperial tent.
Although he has heard of changes south of the pass,
Yíng and Mò prefectures,
which Jìn ceded to the Qìdān,
are south of Wǎqiáo Pass.
They cannot be rescued."
Luán and Dù Wēi, the Military Governor of Tiānxíong and concurrently Grand Councilor, repeatedly memorialized that Yíng and Mò could be taken at this opportune moment.
Inspector Mùróng Qiān of Shēnzhōu presented a map of Yíng and Mò.
Féng Yù and Lǐ Sōng believed it to be true
and wished to dispatch a large army to welcome Zhào Yánshòu and Yánzuò.
Previously, Zhào Yánshòu had also falsely offered submission.
Previously,
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn, the Commander of the Imperial Guards (Cavalry and Infantry) and Military Governor of Tiānpíng, had repeatedly led troops past Guǎngjìn.
Dù Wēi treated him generously,
bestowing gold, silk, armor, and weapons,
totaling tens of thousands.
Shǒuzhēn, therefore, became close with Wēi.
When Shǒuzhēn came to court,
the Emperor comforted him, saying:
"I hear that as a general, you often spend your private wealth to reward your soldiers."
He replied:
"This is all due to Dù Wēi's loyalty to the state,
supplying me with gold and silk.
How could I claim such merit for myself!"
He then said:
"If Your Majesty uses troops another day,
I wish to join forces with Wēi to pacify the desert."
The Emperor, therefore, also considered him worthy.
When the northern campaign was about to be launched,
the Emperor discussed with Féng Yù and Lǐ Sōng
to make Wēi the Grand Marshal
and Shǒuzhēn his deputy.
Zhào Yíng privately said to Féng and Lǐ:
"Commander Dù is a royal relative
(meaning he married a princess)
yet his desires are not satisfied,
and his heart is often discontent
(he holds positions of general and minister,
meaning he governs a major town and is concurrently Grand Councilor).
(Not satisfied means his desires are not yet met.)
(Discontent also means dissatisfaction.)
(Qiè, pronounced kǔ diàn.)
If there is indeed an affair in the north,
it would be better to appoint Shǒuzhēn alone."
Dù Wēi's true intentions
were known even to Zhào Yíng.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Xīnwèi day,
Wēi was appointed Grand Commander of the Northern Campaigning Army.
Shǒuzhēn was appointed Supervising Commissioner of the Cavalry and Infantry.
Ān Shěnqí, Military Governor of Tàiníng, was appointed Commander of the Left and Right Wings.
Fú Yànqīng, Military Governor of Wǔníng, was appointed Commander of the Left Wing of the Cavalry.
Huángfǔ Yù, Military Governor of Yìchéng, was appointed Commander of the Right Wing of the Cavalry.
Liáng Hànzhāng, Military Governor of Yǒngqīng, was appointed Grand Vanguard Commander of the Cavalry.
Sòng Yànjūn, former Military Governor of Wēishèng, was appointed Commander of the Left Wing of the Infantry.
Wáng Ráo, Commander of the Left Wing of the Féngguó Army, was appointed Commander of the Right Wing of the Infantry.
Xuē Huáiràng, Training Commissioner of Míngzhōu, was appointed Grand Vanguard Commander.
An imperial edict was also issued, stating:
"A large army is specially dispatched
to pacify the cunning barbarians.
First, Yíng and Mò shall be taken
to stabilize the region south of the pass;
next, Yōu and Yàn shall be recovered
to pacify the region north of the frontier."
It also said:
"Whoever captures the barbarian lord
shall be made a Military Governor of a superior circuit,
rewarded with ten thousand strings of cash,
ten thousand bolts of silk,
and ten thousand taels of silver."
Easier said than done!
The ruler and officials of Jìn,
relying on the victory at Yángchéng,
had a contemptuous attitude towards the Qìdān.
Arrogant troops are defeated;
this has been true since ancient times.
By this time, it had not stopped.
The movement of the army and its provisions was extremely difficult.
The Tang general Lín Zànyáo of Zhāngzhōu revolted,
killing Supervising Commissioner Zhōu Chéngyì and Inspector Chén Huì of Jiànzhōu.
Inspector Liú Cóngxiào of Quánzhōu raised an army to drive out Zànyáo,
appointing Dǒng Sī'ān, a sub-general from Quánzhōu, to provisionally govern Zhāngzhōu.
The Tang ruler made Sī'ān Inspector of Zhāngzhōu.
Sī'ān declined, citing his father's name, Zhāng.
The Tang ruler renamed Zhāngzhōu to Nánzhōu
and ordered Sī'ān and Liú Cóngxiào to lead their provincial troops to jointly attack Fúzhōu.
On the Gēngchén day,
they besieged it.
Envoys from Fúzhōu arrived at Qiántáng,
seeking a relief army.
Qiántáng was the capital of the Wúyuè kingdom.
Everyone said:
"The road is treacherous and distant;
it is difficult to rescue."
Only Shuǐqiū Zhāoquàn of Lín'ān, the Inner Palace Overseer, believed they should rescue it.
Shuǐqiū is a compound surname.
(The Hè family's Xìngyuàn states that in the Hàn dynasty, there was Shuǐqiū Cén, Prefect of Sīlì.)
(Today, it is a prominent surname in Lín'ān.)
"If the lips are gone, the teeth will be cold;
there are many such ancient sayings.
If we cannot even rescue a neighboring province,
what good will it do us!
Are you gentlemen only concerned with stuffing yourselves
and sitting idly?"
On the Rénwǔ day,
Zhāng Jūn
and Zhào Chéngtài, commanding generals, were dispatched with thirty thousand troops
by land and water to rescue Fúzhōu.
(When Wúyuè rescued Fúzhōu, one could reach Fúzhōu by sailing downstream from Wù and Qú to Jiàn and Jiàn.)
(At this time, Jiàn and Jiàn were already held by Southern Táng,
so this route was impassable.)
(They must have taken the route from Píngyáng in Wēnzhōu, crossing the sea to the border of Fúzhōu.)
Previously, troops were recruited,
but for a long time, no one responded.
Hóngzuǒ ordered them to be rounded up,
saying:
"Those who are rounded up into soldiers
will have their rations and rewards halved."
The next day,
those who volunteered gathered like clouds.
Hóngzuǒ ordered Zhāoquàn to exclusively manage military affairs.
Zhāoquàn, being wary of Chéng Zhāoyuè,
yielded the military command to him.
(Chéng Zhāoyuè was at that time favored and trusted by Hóngzuǒ,
which is why Shuǐqiū Zhāoquàn was wary and yielded to him.)
And he entrusted military strategy to Yuán Dézhāo.
(Dézhāo was the son of Wēi Zǐchàng.)
(Wēi Zǐchàng is mentioned in Volume 263, during the third year of Kāipíng under Emperor Tàizǔ of Liáng.)
Hóngzuǒ discussed casting iron coins to increase the stipends and rewards for his generals and soldiers.
His younger brother, Hóng Yì, the Palace Interior Supervising Commander, remonstrated, saying:
"Casting iron coins has eight disadvantages: Once new coins are circulated,
all old coins will flow into neighboring countries – this is one;
(old coins refer to copper coins)
then merchants will not travel,
and all goods will not circulate – this is two;
the prohibition on copper is very strict,
yet people still illicitly cast coins,
let alone when every household has pots and pans,
and the fields have plows and shares,
many will surely violate the law – this is three;
the Mǐn people cast iron coins and perished in chaos,
which is not a good example – this is four;
(the Mǐn's casting of iron coins is seen in Volume 283, Tiānfú 7th year and the previous volume, 1st year)
this is five;
(meaning, when neighboring countries hear of it,
they will surely think that the state's finances are empty, hence casting iron coins)
this is six;
laws change and become corrupt,
and cannot be quickly restored – this is seven;
'Qián'
is the national surname,
changing it would be inauspicious – this is eight."
Hóngzuǒ then ceased.
Dù Wēi and Lǐ Shǒuzhēn joined forces at Guǎngjìn and marched north.
(Lǐ Shǒuzhēn led his troops to join Dù Wēi in Wèizhōu,
and together they marched north.)
He requested more troops,
(the princess refers to Princess Sòngguó, Dù Wēi's wife,
who was the Emperor's aunt.)
saying: "Now that we are deep in enemy territory,
we must rely on a large force."
Consequently, all imperial guard armies were placed under his command.
(Dù Wēi's plan was the same as Zhào Déjūn's plan to merge Fàn Yánguāng's army.
Déjūn did not get his request, but Wēi did.)
(Their ambitions were beyond what was proper, and both led to the ruin of the state and their own destruction.)
And the palace guards were left empty.
In the eleventh month,
on the Dīngyǒu day,
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn was provisionally appointed to oversee the affairs of the Yōuzhōu Branch Office.
On the *jǐhài* day,
Dù Wēi and others arrived at Yíngzhōu.
The city gates were wide open,
but it was so silent it was as if there were no one there.
Wēi and the others dared not enter.
They heard that the Khitan general Gāo Móhàn had already led his troops out stealthily.
Wēi dispatched Liáng Hànzhāng with two thousand cavalry to pursue them,
and they encountered the Khitans at Nányángwù,
where they were defeated and died.
Hearing this, Wēi and the others
led their troops southward.
At that time, several counties including Shùchéng requested to surrender.
Shùchéng,
a county of Shùzhōu in the Hàn dynasty,
was called Shùchéng in the Suí dynasty,
and belonged to Yíngzhōu in the Táng dynasty.
In the sixth year of Xīníng of the Sòng dynasty,
Shùchéng County was abolished and became Shùchéng Town,
belonging to Héjiān County.
They plundered their women and returned.
On the 27th *jǐyǒu* day,
Wúyuè troops arrived at Fúzhōu.
From Zēngpǔ, they secretly entered the city from the south.
Táng troops advanced to occupy Dōngwǔmén.
Lǐ Dá and the Wúyuè troops jointly resisted them,
but were unsuccessful.
From then on, communication between inside and outside was cut off,
and the city became increasingly perilous.
The Táng ruler dispatched Wáng Jiànfēng, the Inspector of Xìnzhōu, to assist in attacking Fúzhōu.
At that time, although Wáng Chóngwén was the Marshal,
Chén Jué, Féng Yánlǔ, and Wèi Cén contended for power.
Liú Cóngxiào and Wáng Jiànfēng were stubborn and disobedient.
Liú Cóngxiào rose from Quánzhōu,
beheaded Huáng Shàopō,
and defeated Lǐ Hóngtōng,
so the Táng people feared his prestige;
Wáng Jiànfēng, though originally a Táng general,
relied on his achievement of being the first to scale Jiànzhōu;
therefore, both were stubborn and disobedient.
read *jūe*.)
read *qiáng*.)
Their advances and retreats did not coordinate.
Because of this, the officers and soldiers all disintegrated,
and therefore the city could not be conquered.
The Táng ruler appointed Dù Chāngyè, the Surveillance Commissioner of Jiāngzhōu, as Minister of Personnel,
and concurrently acting Director of the Department of State Affairs.
Previously, Chāngyè had been Minister of War and acting Director of the Department of State Affairs,
before being sent out to Jiāngzhōu.
(Acting Director of the Department of State Affairs
means acting Director of the Department of the Grand Secretariat.)
He reviewed the account books,
and, leaning on the desk, sighed,
"In less than a few years,
what has been
consumed is half!"
(This means that in the interim between Chāngyè's appointments,
in less than a few years,
the accumulated wealth in the imperial treasury
had been consumed by half.)
(This means it could not sustain itself for long.)
(The history states that the Táng treasury
was depleted by military campaigns.)
On the 28th, the Khitan ruler launched a large-scale invasion,
advancing from Yì and Dìng towards Héngzhōu.
Dù Wēi and others arrived at Wǔqiáng.
(*Jiǔyù Zhì* says: Wǔqiáng County is forty-five *lǐ* west of Shēnzhōu.)
Sòng Bái said: Wǔqiáng
was Wǔsuì during the Warring States period,

The old city was thirty *lǐ* northeast of the current county seat,
which was Hàn Wǔqiáng County.
(*Jùnguó Xiàndào Jì* says: The old Wǔqiáng County city
was twenty-five *lǐ* southwest of the current county seat,

Gāo Qí moved the county seat to the old city of Wǔyì Commandery of the Later Wèi,
which is the current county seat.)
They were about to proceed south from Bèi and Jì.
Zhāng Yànzé, the Jìedùshǐ of Zhāngdé, was at Héngzhōu at the time.
(In September of last year,
Zhāng Yànzé was sent to garrison Héngzhōu to guard against the Khitans.)
read *héng*.)
He spoke of how the Khitans could be defeated;
Wēi and others then headed towards Héngzhōu again,
with Yànzé as the vanguard.
(*Kǎoyì* says: *Bèishǐ* says:
"Yànzé was a wolf cub,
his heart had secretly already changed.
He made overtures to Yélǜ,
asking to be the guide,
and then urgently persuaded Wēi to lead his army along the Hūtuó River to reinforce Chángshān from the west.
When they reached Zhēndìng Dōngyuán Ford,
he secretly conspired with Wēi,
first sending the infantry across the water,
but not rescuing them,
leading to their defeat,
intending to demoralize the army to execute a treacherous plan,
and then urged the supervisor Gāo Xūn to surrender to the barbarians."
However, if Yànzé and Wēi had already made overtures to the Khitans,
then why did Yànzé still seize the bridge?
And why did the Khitans still discuss retreating?
Therefore, this account is not adopted.)
On the *jiǎyín* day,
Wēi and others reached Zhōngdù Bridge.
(The Hūtuó River flows southeast of Héngzhōu.
The people of Héngzhōu established various fords as they pleased.
This one being called Zhōngdù [Middle Ford]
indicates that there were also fords upstream and downstream.)
Yànzé led cavalry to contend for it,
and the Khitans burned the bridge and retreated.
The Jìn troops and Khitans encamped on opposite sides of the Hūtuó River.
Initially,
the Khitans, seeing the large Jìn army arrive
and failing to win the contention for the bridge,
feared that the Jìn army would quickly cross the Hūtuó River
and combine forces with Héngzhōu to attack them,
so they discussed withdrawing their troops.
But upon hearing that the Jìn army was building ramparts for a prolonged campaign,
they stayed.
(They knew the Jìn army dared not fight.)
On the 29th, Tián Xínggāo, the Inspector of Shīzhōu of Shǔ, rebelled.
Gěng Yànxún, an imperial attendant, was dispatched with troops to suppress him.
On the 30th, although Dù Wēi was a senior general by virtue of being an imperial relative,
he was timid and weak by nature.
His subordinate generals were all Jìedùshǐ.
(From Lǐ Shǒuzhēn to Sòng Yànjūn,
they were all Jìedùshǐ.)
He would hold banquets and amuse himself,
rarely discussing military affairs.
Lǐ Gǔ, the Inspector of Cízhōu and concurrent Northern Transport Commissioner, advised Wēi and Lǐ Shǒuzhēn, saying:
"Now our main army is a stone's throw from Héngzhōu,
with campfires visible to each other.
If we place many three-pronged wooden stakes in the water,
and pile firewood and earth on top,
a bridge can be built quickly.
(Three-pronged wooden stakes
are made by binding three pieces of wood together,
crossed,
with their lower parts spread open to form three legs,
to be placed in the water.)
At night, recruit soldiers and officers to hack into the barbarian camp,
and with forces converging from inside and out,
the barbarians will surely flee."
All the generals thought this was a good idea,
but Dù Wēi alone disagreed,
and sent Gǔ south to Huái and Mèng to supervise military provisions.
The Khitans deployed their main force in front of the Jìn army,
and secretly dispatched their generals Xiāo Hàn and the interpreter Liú Chóngjìn with a hundred cavalry and weak soldiers,
to move along the western mountains to the rear of the Jìn army,
cutting off the Jìn supply route and retreat path.
Those gathering firewood and foraging who encountered them
were all plundered;
those who escaped back
all spoke of the great strength of the barbarian forces,
causing fear in the army.
Hàn and others reached Luánchéng.
The thousand-plus garrison soldiers in the city
were unaware of their arrival,
and surrendered in panic.
The Khitans captured Jìn civilians,
tattooed "By imperial decree, no killing"
on their faces,
and released them to flee south;
transport workers on the road who encountered them
abandoned their carts and fled in disorder.
(Hàn was the uncle of the Khitan ruler.)
(All Khitan empresses' families adopted Xiāo as their surname.)
(Ōu Shǐ says: Hàn was
a great Khitan clan,
their title was Ābō.)
(Hàn's sister was also married to the Khitan ruler Déguāng.)
(And Ābō originally had no surname;
the Khitans called Hàn "Guójìu" [imperial uncle].)
(After entering Biàn,
when he was about to return north,
he was made Jìedùshǐ of Xuānwǔ.
Lǐ Sōng created the name Xiāo Hàn for him,
and thus he first adopted the surname Xiāo.)
(Sòng Bái says: Xiāo Hàn
was the son of Shùlǜ Ābō.)
In the twelfth month,
on the *Dǐngsì* day which was the first day of the month,
Lǐ Gǔ personally wrote a secret memorial,
fully explaining the critical situation of the grand army,
requesting the imperial carriage to proceed to Huázhōu,
sending Gāo Xíngzhōu and Fú Yànqīng to escort it,
and dispatching troops to guard Chánzhōu and Héyáng to prepare for the *lǔ*'s assault;
he sent military officer Guān Xūn to gallop and present it.
Gāo Xíngzhōu and Fú Yànqīng
were famous generals of that era.
Huá, Chán, and Héyáng
were crucial strongholds along the Yellow River.
If the Jìn emperor had been able to follow Lǐ Gǔ's advice,
how could there have been the disaster of Zhāng Yànzé's light cavalry entering Biàn?!
"To gallop and present it"
means an urgent report.
From the Bǎoyuán and Kāngdìng eras onwards in the Sòng dynasty,
border garrisons generally had "galloping acceptance" officials.
*Cóng* (從)
is pronounced *cái yòng fān*.
*Chán* (澶)
is pronounced *shí lián fān*.
*Shàng* (上)
is pronounced *shí liǎng fān*.
On the *Jǐwèi* day,
the Emperor first heard that the grand army was encamped at Zhōngdù;
on the *Jiǎyín* day,
Dù Wēi and others arrived at Zhōngdù;
on the *Jǐwèi* day,
Dàliáng first heard of it.
A powerful enemy had deeply penetrated,
and all the armies were isolated and vulnerable,
yet the postal report only arrived after seven days.
The state of Jìn's military can be imagined from this.
Guān Xūn arrived.
On the *Gēngshēn* day,
Dù Wēi memorialized, requesting more troops.
An edict ordered all guards of the palace to be dispatched, amounting to several hundred people,
to go to his aid.
Since ancient times,
those who emphasized attack over defense
have never failed to be defeated.
Dispatching several hundred people
was insufficient to augment the strength of the grand army,
and it weakened the defense of the palace.
"Five hundred thousand"
refers to the combined numbers of Shù and Shí.
Everywhere was in turmoil.
On the *Xīnyǒu* day,
Wēi again sent his follower Zhāng Zuò and others to report the emergency.
Zuò and the others, on their return,
were captured by the Qìdān.
From then on, communication between the court and the front lines was completely cut off.
At that time, all the imperial guards were at the expeditionary camp,
and people's hearts were filled with apprehension,
not knowing what to do.
Sāng Wéihàn, the Prefect of Kāifēng,
seeing the state in imminent danger,
sought an audience with the Emperor to discuss affairs;
the Emperor was then in the imperial garden training falcons.
"Training falcons"
means teaching and domesticating them,
making them tame and attached to humans.
Sāng Wéihàn then went to the executive officials to speak of it,
but the executive officials did not take it seriously.
"Executive officials"
refers to Féng Yù, Lǐ Yàntāo, and others.
Sāng Wéihàn said to his close associates:
"The Jìn clan will not offer blood sacrifices again!"
He meant that Jìn would surely perish, and its ancestral temples would not be worshipped.
The collapse of the Jìn clan
was not only known to Sāng Wéihàn,
but to the entire nation.
The Emperor wanted to lead a northern expedition himself,
but Lǐ Yàntāo remonstrated and stopped him.
At that time, although Fú Yànqīng held duties in the expeditionary camp,
the Emperor kept him
to garrison Jīngzhōukǒu.
On the *Rénxū* day,
an edict appointed Gāo Xíngzhōu, the Jìedùshǐ of Guīdé, as the Northern Sector Grand Commander,
with Yànqīng as his deputy,
to jointly guard Chánzhōu;
and appointed Jǐng Yánguǎng, the Resident Overseer of Xījīng, to garrison Héyáng,
also to create a show of force.
The history records that these three generals garrisoned the river crossings,
but although they made a show of force, their military strength was very weak.
Wáng Qīng, the Commander-in-Chief of Fèngguó, said to Dù Wēi:
"Now the grand army is five *lǐ* from Héngzhōu.
What are we doing defending this place?
The camp is isolated, food is running out,
and it will likely collapse on its own.
I request to take two thousand infantry as the vanguard;
to seize the bridge and clear the path.
You, sir, can then lead the armies to follow.
If we can enter Héngzhōu,
then we will have no worries."
Wēi agreed,
and sent Qīng to advance with Sòng Yànjūn.
Qīng fought very bravely,
and the Qìdān could not withstand him,
their勢 slightly retreated;
the generals requested to follow with the main army,
but Wēi refused.
Yànjūn was defeated by the Qìdān,
and escaped by floating across the water to the bank.
Qīng alone led his subordinates, formed a line north of the water, and fought fiercely.
There were mutual casualties,
and he repeatedly requested rescue from Wēi,
but Wēi did not send even a single cavalryman to assist him.
Qīng said to his troops:
"The senior general holds the army,
and sits idly watching us in distress without rescuing us.
This must be due to ulterior motives.
We must repay the nation with our lives!"
The troops were moved by his words,
and none retreated.
By dusk,
the battle did not cease.
The Qìdān continued with fresh troops,
and Qīng and his soldiers all died.
Lǐ Gǔ drew up plans for Dù Wēi but they were not implemented;
one could still say that it is easy to speak and hard to act.
But as for Wáng Qīng fighting bravely and not being rescued,
then Dù Wēi's desire to betray the country for his own benefit
was clearly exposed,
and everyone knew it.
Qīng
was from Míngzhōu.
On the *Jiǎzǐ* day,
the Qìdān remotely encircled the Jìn camp with troops,
cutting off communication inside and out,
and food in the army was almost exhausted.
Dù Wēi conspired with Lǐ Shǒuzhēn and Sòng Yànjūn to surrender to the Qìdān.
Wēi secretly sent his trusted confidants to the Qìdān chieftain's tent
to demand a heavy reward.
The Qìdān ruler tricked him, saying:
"Zhào Yánshòu's prestige is always shallow;
I fear he cannot be emperor of China.
If you truly surrender,
I will make you emperor."
Wēi was pleased,
and so decided on the surrender plan.
Zhào Yánshòu and his son thus fell into the Qìdān's trap.
Dù Wēi's talent and wisdom were not sufficient to aspire to Yánshòu's position,
so his falling into the Qìdān's scheme
is not surprising.
Tracing the same tracks,
could it be the will of Heaven?!
On the *Bǐngyín* day,
Wēi hid armed men and summoned all the generals,
bringing out the surrender document and showing it to them,
making them sign it.
The generals were startled and shocked,
none dared to speak,
but merely nodded in obedience.
Wēi sent Gāo Xūn, the Palace Gate Envoy, to deliver it to the Qìdān.
The Qìdān ruler issued an edict to comfort and accept them.
On this day,
Wēi ordered all soldiers to array outside.
The soldiers were all excited,
thinking they were about to fight.
Wēi personally explained to them, saying:
"Now our food is exhausted and our path is blocked;
we must seek a way to survive together with you all."
Thereupon, he ordered them to lay down their arms.
All the soldiers wept bitterly,
their cries shaking the plains.
The history records that the Jìn army did not want to surrender to the Qìdān,
but were forced by their commander to obey.
"The Emperor has lost virtue,
trusts wicked and cunning individuals,
and is suspicious of us."
All who heard this gnashed their teeth.
The Qìdān ruler sent Zhào Yánshòu, dressed in an ochre robe, to the Jìn camp
to comfort and appease the soldiers,
saying:
"They are all your property."
Dù Wēi and his subordinates
all welcomed and paid respects before his horse;
the Qìdān ruler also dressed Wēi in an ochre robe to show the Jìn army,
but in reality, he was merely toying with them.
The Qìdān ruler was not only toying with Dù Wēi and Zhào Yánshòu,
but also deceiving the Jìn army.
In his heart, he knew that the Jìn army was not truly submissive,
so he claimed that he would make a Chinese person the ruler of China,
and these two individuals would certainly be one of them.
The Jìn people said they had lost their ruler but gained a ruler,
and they were both Chinese,
hence they did not rebel.
His strategy was clever.
However, although the Qìdān ruler was clever in his deception,
after entering Biàn,
he could not control Hédōng on a large scale,
nor could he control the petty bandits on a small scale.
Is this not an instance where those who rely on schemes and tactics sometimes fail?
*Yī* (衣)
is pronounced *yú jì fān*.
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn was Sītú.
Dù Wēi led the Qìdān ruler to the foot of Héngzhōu city,
and notified Wáng Zhōu, the Jìedùshǐ of Shùnguó, of his surrender.
Wáng Zhōu also surrendered.
On Wùchén day,
the Qìdān ruler entered Héngzhōu.
He dispatched troops to attack Dàizhōu;

The Qìdān used their victorious power to coerce Dàizhōu into surrender,
but Tàiyuán remained unmoved,

Previously, the Qìdān had repeatedly attacked Yìzhōu,
but the Cìshǐ, Guō Lín, staunchly defended it.
Each time the Qìdān ruler passed by the city,
he would point to it and sigh:
"I can conquer the world,
but I am thwarted by this man!"
When Dù Wēi had surrendered,
the Qìdān ruler sent the Tōngshì Gěng Chóngměi to Yìzhōu,
to entice and persuade its populace.
All the people surrendered;
Guō Lín could not control them,
and was subsequently killed by Gěng Chóngměi.
History says that when a great mansion collapses,
it cannot be supported by a single beam.
(He was) a native of Xíngzhōu.
Lǐ Yīn, the Jìedùshǐ of Yìwǔ,
and Fāng Tài, the Liúhòu of Ānguó,
both surrendered to the Qìdān.
The Qìdān ruler appointed Sūn Fāngjiǎn as the Jìedùshǐ of Yìwǔ,

Sòng Bái said: Má Dā's
original name was Jiělǐ,
and he was a cousin of Ābǎojī.
His father was named Sālā,
who defected to Liáng,
and died in Biàn.
Zhāng Lì, the Qìdān Hànlín Chéngzhǐ and Lìbù Shàngshū, spoke to the Qìdān ruler, saying:
"Now that the Great Liáo has obtained the empire,
(In the second year of Tiānfú of Gāozǔ,

it is not appropriate to use northern people or your close attendants.
If government decrees are flawed,

it will still be lost."
The Qìdān ruler did not heed him.
If the Qìdān ruler had followed Zhāng Lì's advice,
things might have turned out differently.
Leading his troops south from Xíng and Xiāng,
the Qìdān army descended along the mountains to approach Jìn.
Xiāng,
pronounced Xī Liàng.
He sent Zhāng Yànzé with 2,000 cavalry to first take Dàliáng,
and to pacify the officials and common people,
with the Tōngshì Fù Zhù'ér as the Dūjiān.
When Dù Wēi surrendered,
Huángfǔ Yù was initially not privy to the plan.
The Qìdān ruler wanted to send Huángfǔ Yù to lead troops into Dàliáng first,
but Huángfǔ Yù declined;
he withdrew
and said to his confidants:
"My position is that of a general and prime minister.
Having failed, I could not die;
how can I bear to conspire against my lord again?"
Upon reaching Píngjí,
(Píngjí was an ancient county in the Hàn dynasty,
and belonged to Zhàozhōu in the Táng dynasty.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: The old city of Píngjí was Jípú邑 in the Spring and Autumn period.
The Shísānzhōu Zhì says: During the Warring States period, it was renamed Píngjí.)
"I have not eaten for several days,
what face do I have to go south again?"
Thereupon he strangled himself to death.
Zhāng Yànzé marched rapidly, doubling the usual pace,
and crossed Báimǎjīn at night.
(Because Zhāng Yànzé knew there were garrison troops in Chán and Mèng,
he crossed from Báimǎjīn.)
On Rénshēn day,
the Emperor first learned of the surrender of Dù Wēi and others;
that evening,
he further heard that Zhāng Yànzé had reached Huázhōu.
He summoned Lǐ Sōng, Féng Yù, and Lǐ Yàntāo into the palace to discuss matters,
intending to issue an edict to Liú Zhīyuǎn to dispatch troops for reinforcement.
Tàiyuán is 1,200 lǐ from Luòyáng,
and Luòyáng is another 380 lǐ from Dàliáng.
Even if Liú Zhīyuǎn had heard the command and immediately sprang into action,
it would have been too late.
On Guǐyǒu day,
before dawn,
Zhāng Yànzé broke through the gate at Fēngqiūmén and entered.
Lǐ Yàntāo led 500 imperial guards to meet him,
but could not stop him.
Zhāng Yànzé stationed his troops outside Míngdémén.
(The Wǔdài Huìyào states: Míngdémén was the south gate of the imperial city of Dàliáng.
Xuē Shǐ states: In the third year of Tiānfú, tenth month,
the Dànínggōng gate was renamed Míngdémén.)
The Emperor started a fire in the palace,
and personally holding a sword, drove more than ten women of the imperial harem towards the fire,
but was restrained by Xuē Chāo, a general of the imperial guards.
Shortly after, Zhāng Yànzé entered through Kuānrénmén, conveying a letter from the Qìdān ruler to the Empress Dowager to comfort and reassure her.
(The Wǔdài Huìyào states: The east gate of the imperial city of Dàliáng was Kuānrénmén.)
The Emperor then ordered the fire extinguished
and all the palace city gates opened.
The Emperor sat in the imperial garden,
weeping with the Empress,
and summoned Hànlín Xuéshì Fàn Zhì to draft an instrument of surrender,
in which he referred to himself as
"your grandson and subject, Chóngguì.
Misfortune has struck, my spirit is bewildered;
my destiny is exhausted, Heaven wills my demise.
Now, I, together with the Empress Dowager and my wife, Fēng Shì,
and my entire clan, are awaiting punishment, bound in the suburbs.
I send my sons, Yánxù, the Jìedùshǐ of Zhènníng,
and Yánbǎo, the Jìedùshǐ of Wēixìn,
to present one state seal
and three golden seals in welcome."
(The state seal
was the Seal of Receiving Mandate made by Gāozǔ in the third year of Tiānfú.
Xù,
pronounced Yū Jù.)
"Your new daughter-in-law, concubine Lǐ Shì."
Such humiliation as "subject and concubine"
was seen only in Jìn and Sòng.
Alas,
how painful!
Shàng,
pronounced Shí Zhǎng.
Fù Zhù'ér entered to proclaim the Qìdān ruler's command.
The Emperor removed his yellow robe,
wore a plain shirt,
bowed twice to receive the proclamation,
and those around him all wept silently.
The Emperor sent for Zhāng Yànzé,
wanting to consult with him.
Zhāng Yànzé said:
"Your subject has no face to see Your Majesty."
The Emperor summoned him again,
but Zhāng Yànzé merely smiled and did not respond.
Someone urged Sāng Wéihàn to escape.
Sāng Wéihàn said:
"I am a high official,
where can I escape to?"
He sat and awaited his fate.
Zhāng Yànzé summoned Sāng Wéihàn by imperial command.
When Sāng Wéihàn reached Tiānjiē,
(The main street outside the south gate of the imperial city
was called Tiānjiē,
a thoroughfare.)
he had not finished speaking after dismounting,
when a military official bowed before his horse and invited Sāng Wéihàn to the Shìwèisī.
(Inviting him to the Shìwèisī
indicated that he was to be imprisoned.
Another account says: At that time, Zhāng Yànzé was staying in the Shìwèisī office.)
He looked at Lǐ Sōng and said:
"Shìzhōng holds state power,
(Lǐ Sōng's official title was Shìzhōng.)
but instead lets Wéihàn die.
Why is this?"
Lǐ Sōng showed a look of shame.
Zhāng Yànzé sat casually when he saw Sāng Wéihàn.
Sāng Wéihàn reproached him, saying:
"Last year, I rescued you from among criminals,
and you again commanded a major garrison,
and were entrusted with military power.
(During Gāozǔ's time, the court and populace all requested Zhāng Yànzé's execution.
He was dismissed from Jīngzhōu and returned to serve as imperial guard;
last year, Sāng Wéihàn rescued him and enabled him to jointly resist the Qìdān,
and he again commanded the Jìedùshǐ of Zhāngguó,
leading troops to garrison Chángshān.)
Zhāng Yànzé had no reply,
and sent soldiers to guard him.
Mèng Chénghuì, the Xuānhuīshǐ,
had always been favored by the Emperor due to his flattery and cunning.
At this point,
the Emperor summoned Mèng Chénghuì,
wishing to consult with him,
but Mèng Chénghuì hid and did not appear;
Zhāng Yànzé captured and killed him.
Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤) let his soldiers plunder extensively.
The poor, taking advantage of the chaos,
also rushed into wealthy households,
killing people and taking their goods.
This continued for two days before stopping,
leaving the capital city empty.
The wealth accumulated in Zhāng Yànzé’s (張彥澤) residence
piled up like mountains.
He considered himself to have rendered meritorious service to Qìdān (契丹).
Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤) regarded his rapid entry into Biàn (汴) as a meritorious achievement.
When he went out, he was always accompanied by several hundred horsemen and attendants.
His banners were all inscribed with
"Loyal to the Lord with a Red Heart" (赤心為主).
Those who saw them laughed.
When soldiers brought criminals before him,
Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤) did not ask about their offenses,
but merely glared with wide eyes and raised three fingers,
then ordered them to be dragged out and beheaded.
Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤) had long been at odds with Gāo Xūn (高勳), the Director of the Palace Gate Bureau.
When he was drunk, he went to Gāo Xūn’s (高勳) house,
killed his uncle and younger brother,
and left their bodies at the gate.
The gentry and common people shivered without being cold.
Lǐ Tāo (李濤), a Scholar of the Central Secretariat, said to someone:
"Rather than hiding in ditches and still not escaping,
it's better to go and see him."
So he sent in his calling card to request an audience with Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤), saying:
"Lǐ Tāo (李濤), the one who submitted a memorial requesting the execution of the Grand Commandant,
has respectfully come to ask for death."
Lǐ Tāo’s (李濤) request to kill Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤) is recorded in Volume 283, under the seventh year of Tiānfú (天福) of Gāozǔ (高祖).
Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤) said to Lǐ Tāo (李濤):
"Is the Scholar afraid today?"
Lǐ Tāo (李濤) replied:
"My fear today
is like your fear in previous years.
If Gāozǔ (高祖) had followed my words then,
how could things have come to this!"
Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤) laughed heartily
and ordered wine to be served to him.
Lǐ Tāo (李濤) drained his cup and left,
acting as if no one else was there.
Lǐ Tāo (李濤) was
a great-grandson of the Huí (回) clan.
He was articulate and courageous,
truly of a noble lineage.
On the Jiǎxū (甲戌) day,
Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤) moved the Emperor to Kāifēng Fǔ (開封府).
Not a moment was allowed for delay,
and there was weeping in the palace.
The Emperor, Empress Dowager, and Empress rode in palanquins,
with more than ten palace women and eunuchs following on foot.
Those who saw them shed tears.
The shame of a fallen nation,
those who speak of it feel heartbroken,
how much more so those who witnessed it!
This is what Chéng Zhèngshū (程正叔) called true understanding.
Heaven,
and mankind!
Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤) sent someone to subtly advise the Emperor, saying:
"When the Qìdān (契丹) ruler arrives,
these treasures cannot be hidden."
The Emperor returned all of them,
and also divided some to give to Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤).
Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤) selected the rare treasures,
and sealed the rest to await the Qìdān (契丹).
Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤) dispatched Lǐ Yún (李筠), the Commander of the Crane-Controlling Guards, with troops to guard the Emperor,
cutting off all internal and external communication.
The Emperor’s paternal aunt, Wūshì Gōngzhǔ (烏氏公主), bribed the gatekeepers
to enter and bid farewell to the Emperor,
then returned to her residence and hanged herself.
The memorials presented by the Emperor and Empress Dowager to the Qìdān (契丹) ruler
all had to be shown to Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤) first
before they dared to dispatch them.
The Emperor sent for several bolts of silk from the inner treasury,
but the official in charge would not give them,
saying:
"These are not the Emperor's property."
He also asked Lǐ Sōng (李崧) for wine,
but Lǐ Sōng (李崧) also declined, citing other reasons, and did not present it.
He also wanted to see Lǐ Yàntāo (李彥韜),
but Lǐ Yàntāo (李彥韜) also refused to go.
The Emperor was dejected for a long time.
At this time,
the officials of the Jìn (晉) dynasty
already regarded the abdicated Emperor as a stranger on the road.
Even if he was dejected, what good would it do?
Chóu (惆) is pronounced as Chǒu Jiū (丑鳩).
Fēng Yù (馮玉) flattered Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤)
and requested to personally deliver the Imperial Seal,
hoping that Qìdān (契丹) would reappoint him.
Such was the understanding of a minister of a fallen state.
Fù (復) is pronounced as Fú Yòu (扶又).
Madame Dīng (丁氏), the Lady of Chǔ (楚國夫人),
was Yánxù’s (延煦) mother,
and she was beautiful.
Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤) sent someone to take her.
The Empress Dowager hesitated and did not immediately comply;
Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤) cursed and scolded,
then immediately had her taken away.
That night,
Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤) killed Sāng Wéihàn (桑維翰).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Xuē Shǐ* (薛史) says:
"The Emperor recalled Sāng Wéihàn (桑維翰)’s advice during his premiership,
repeatedly offering strategies,
and requesting peace with the barbarians.
When the Lord of Lú Róng (盧戎) arrived in the capital, it would expose his own faults.
He wanted to kill Sāng Wéihàn (桑維翰) to silence him,
and so ordered Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤) to kill him."
However, at this time, how could Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤) still obey the young Emperor's command!
Therefore, this account is not adopted.
Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤) reported to the Qìdān (契丹) ruler
that Sāng Wéihàn (桑維hàn) had hanged himself.
The Qìdān (契丹) ruler said:
"I had no intention of killing Sāng Wéihàn (桑維翰),
why did this happen!"
He ordered his family to be generously treated.
Gāo Xíngzhōu (高行周) and Fú Yànqīng (符彥卿) both went to the Qìdān (契丹) royal tent to surrender.
The two had come from Chánzhōu (澶州) to surrender.
When interrogated,
regarding the Battle of Yángchéng (陽城),
see the previous volume, previous year.
"Děi" (敗) is pronounced as Bǔ Mài (補賣).
"Jié" (詰) is pronounced as Qù Jí (去吉).
They said:
"At that time, your servant only knew to exert all his strength for the Jìn (晉) ruler. Today, life or death is up to fate."
The Qìdān (契丹) ruler smiled and released them.
Fú Yànqīng (符彥卿)'s words were straightforward,
and the Qìdān (契Dān) ruler had no reason to blame him.
"Wéi" (為) is pronounced as Yú Wěi (于偽).
On the Jǐmǎo (己卯) day,
Yánxù (延煦) and Yánbǎo (延寶) returned from the royal tent.
The Qìdān (契丹) ruler bestowed a handwritten imperial edict upon the Emperor,
and also sent Jiělǐ (解里) to tell the Emperor:
"Grandson, do not worry.
I will certainly ensure you have a place to eat."
The Emperor's heart felt slightly at ease,
and he submitted a memorial to express his gratitude.
The Qìdān considered the presented Chuánguó Bǎo to be crudely carved,
and it did not correspond to previous historical records,
suspecting it was not genuine.
They interrogated the Emperor with an imperial edict,
demanding he present the real one.
Lǐ Xīnchuán said: The Qín Xǐ,
was Lǐ Sī's "insect-and-fish seal script,"
its circumference was four cùn.
According to the Yùxǐ Tú, this seal was carved from the Zhào Bì,
the bì originally being the uncarved jade presented by Biàn Hé,
and it was the one Lìn Xiāngrú reclaimed.
I once examined it according to ritual regulations:
a bì of five cùn with a hole
could not be re-carved into a seal;
so this theory is fallacious.
The Qín Xǐ, reaching the Hàn dynasty, was called the Chuánguó Xǐ.
From then until the Hàn dynasty,
what emperors cherished and used
was the Qín Xǐ;
what Zǐ Yīng surrendered,
what Empress Dowager Yuán threw,
what Wáng Xiàn obtained,
what the Chìméi presented,
all were this same object.
It was lost during Dǒng Zhuó's rebellion.
The Wú Shū states that Sūn Jiān found it in the Zhēnguān Well in Luòyáng,
then it was seized by Yuán Shù,
and Xú Qiú obtained it and presented it.
This is probably not true.
If it were so,
why would the Wèi clan not cherish and use it, but instead carve their own seal?
After that, successive generations all used its name.
During the Yǒngjiā zhī Luàn, it was lost to Liú Shí.
What returned to the Jiāngzuǒ during the Yǒnghé era
was the Jìn Xǐ.
When the Wèi clan established their state,
they carved a Chuánguó Xǐ with the same inscription as the Qín.
However, the Qín Xǐ was read from the right,
while the Wèi Xǐ was read from the left.
When the Jìn ruled the empire,
they also carved their own seal,
its inscription read:
"Received Mandate from Heaven,
Emperor's Longevity and Prosperity."
The Yúfú Zhì of this book mistakenly took it for the Qín Xǐ transmitted by the Hàn.
This is a grave error.
This seal passed through Liú Cōng and Shí Lè.
When Shí Zhī died,
his minister Jiǎng Gàn sought aid from Xiè Shàng,
and thus sent the seal to Jiāngnán.
Wáng Biāozhī identified it,
and also did not claim it was the Qín Xǐ.
At the end of the Tàiyuán era,
it was obtained from Xī Yān.
It passed through the Six Dynasties,
and reached the Suí dynasty;
it was the Mùróng Yān Xǐ.
In the nineteenth year of Jìn Xiàowǔ's Tàiyuán era,
Yǒng, the ruler of Xī Yān, sought aid from Qiè Huī,
and presented a jade seal.
It was six cùn square,
and four cùn and six fēn high;
its inscription was like that of the Qín Xǐ.
From then on, it was cherished by the Sòng, Qí, and Liáng dynasties.
After Hóu Jǐng died,
Xīn Shù of Běi Qí obtained it in Guǎnglǐng,
and presented it to the Gāo clan.
Later, it passed through the Zhōu and Suí dynasties,
and was mistakenly identified as the Qín Xǐ.
After Jiāngnán was pacified,
it was realized that it was not,
and so it was renamed the Shén Xǐ.
When Liú Yù launched his Northern Expedition,
he obtained it in Guānzhōng.
It passed through the Jìn and Chén dynasties,
and then again became possessed by the Suí;
it was the Yáo Qín Xǐ.
In the thirteenth year of Jìn Yìxī,
Liú Yù entered the pass,
obtained the Chuánguó Xǐ and presented it.
It was four cùn in size,
its inscription was the same as the Qín,
but it was raised relief and not deeply carved.
The Suí obtained this after destroying Chén,
and identified it as the true seal,
consequently deeming the Shén Xǐ transmitted by the Yǔwén clan as false.
Knowledgeable people also said that ancient seals were deeply carved,
for pressing into clay,
while later ones had raised relief,
for pressing onto paper.
Therefore, the one with raised relief was not the Qín Xǐ.
The Yáo clan merely took its inscription and made it.
During the Kāiyùn zhī Luàn,
it was lost to the Yēlǜ.
What the Nǚzhēn obtained and regarded as a great treasure
was the Shí Jìn Xǐ.
In the sixteenth year of Táng Tàizōng's Zhēnguàn era,
he carved a Shòumìng Xǐ,
its inscription read:
"The Emperor's Auspicious Mandate,
those with virtue prosper."
Later it belonged to Zhū Quánzhōng,
and when Cóng Kē immolated himself,
the seal was also lost with him.
When Déguāng entered Biàn,
Chóngguì presented the seal to him,
saying,
"Carved by the former emperor."
This probably referred to Jìngtáng.
It seems that during the Táng era, everyone mistakenly believed it to be the Qín Xǐ,
but the Qín Xǐ had been lost long ago.
Now, examining this,
"Shí Zhī died,"
should be written as
"Rǎn Mǐn died."
Lǐ Xīnchuán's account differs from the Táng Liùdiǎn.
Now both are presented,
to await those who know.
When it reached the Zhōu dynasty,
two more treasures were made.
What the officials presented,
their account also followed the Liùdiǎn,
detailed notes are provided later.
"Jié" (interrogate)
"Recently, King Cóng Kē immolated himself.
This event is found in volume 280, first year of Gāozǔ's Tiānfú era.
It must have been incinerated with him.
This treasure was made by the former emperor.
This event is found in volume 281, third year of Tiānfú.
How could I, your subject, dare to hide a treasure today!"
Then he stopped.
The Emperor heard that the Qìdān Zhǔ was about to cross the river,
and wished to formally welcome him with the Empress Dowager on the way;
Zhāng Yànzé reported this beforehand,
but the Qìdān Zhǔ did not allow it.
The officials also wanted the Emperor to carry a bì and lead a sheep,
with ministers carrying coffins,
to welcome him outside the city.
They first prepared the ritual procedures and informed the Qìdān Zhǔ.
The Qìdān Zhǔ said:
"I sent elite troops to take Dàliáng directly,
not to accept a surrender."
He also did not allow it.
He also issued an edict that all civil and military officials of Jìn
should remain as before;
and the court system
should entirely adopt Hàn rituals.
The Qìdān Zhǔ replied:
"I am currently wearing armor and commanding the army,
and the ceremonial guard of the Grand Minister of Ceremonies,
I do not have time to implement them."
He rejected them all.
Earlier, when the Qìdān Zhǔ reached Xiāngzhōu,
he immediately sent troops to Héyáng to capture Jǐng Yánguǎng.
Yánguǎng was in such a rush that he had nowhere to flee or hide,
not expecting to be captured so suddenly.
"You caused the two rulers to be displeased with each other,
all this was your doing.
Where are your 'one hundred thousand horizontally-honing swords' now!"
He summoned Qiáo Róng,
and had them debate and testify against each other,
concerning ten matters.
Yánguǎng initially refused to admit guilt,
but Róng showed him the words recorded on paper.
Each time he admitted to a matter,
a tally stick was given.
When it reached eight tallies,
Yánguǎng merely prostrated himself on the ground and begged for death,
so he was put in chains.
On the last day of the bǐngxū cycle,
all officials lodged at Fēngshàn Sì.
This was to welcome the Qìdān Zhǔ.
Fēngshàn Sì is to the east of Dàliáng city.
Punctuated by Zhāng Xīchēn, collated by Niè Chóngqí.
